body: Yavne's municipality has drawn a line under months of behind-the-scenes wrangling over the city's senior football set-up, brokering a formal merger between its two adult clubs, Maccabi Tzvi Yavne and Beitar Yavne, ONE reported.

The agreement was signed off at a meeting in the office of Mayor Roi Gabbay, bringing together two clubs that had both competed in Liga Alef South last season - one tier below Liga Leumit - and had increasingly found themselves competing for the same pool of players, sponsors and civic backing in a single small city.

Under the terms of the deal, the unified operation will play on under the Maccabi Tzvi Yavne name, with the club's existing badge and colours preserved. Beitar Yavne's registered association will stop fielding a separate senior team for the length of the agreement, folding its playing operation into its former cross-town rival.

The new leadership line-up blends figures from both sides. Asher Shetrit, who chaired Beitar Yavne, takes over as chairman of the merged body, while Asaf Ohana, formerly Maccabi's chief executive, stays on to run day-to-day and football operations. Felix Alimelech, Avi Ohion, Shalom Swissa and Avraham Biton were named to the board, with attorney Ram Sharon and Gal Pershker appointed to the audit committee, according to ONE.

Gabbay, who hosted the signing, framed the deal as a pooling of long-divided civic resources. "We successfully united forces and resources for one shared goal - to push Maccabi Yavne toward achievements," the mayor said.

The word "saga" in ONE's own framing points to a messier backdrop than a simple handshake. The merger comes after other Liga Bet clubs had separately pressed competing claims to Beitar Yavne's Liga Alef status, ONE reported, adding administrative uncertainty to a city that had ended up fielding two senior teams in the same division, sharing the same municipal stadium.

That overlap was itself a fairly recent development. Beitar Yavne reached Liga Alef for the first time in its history only ahead of the 2024-25 season, stepping into a vacancy left when Adom Ashdod withdrew from professional football, ONE reported at the time - a rapid rise that suddenly put two Yavne clubs in the same tier as Maccabi Tzvi Yavne, a club with a far longer history at that level.

For a city of under 60,000 people, running two parallel Liga Alef operations had strained both clubs' budgets and, at times, left playing squads on both sides thin - the kind of duplication municipal officials have periodically tried to resolve in Israel's lower leagues.

Practical details - fixtures, squad composition and exactly where the new Maccabi Tzvi Yavne will sit when Liga Alef South resumes - remain to be settled. But with the municipality's backing and a shared boardroom now in place, Yavne heads into the close season with one football club to build around rather than two competing for the same limited resources.

body: Bnei Sakhnin's manager, Yossi Abukasis, has admitted this summer's recruitment drive has left him frustrated, saying overseas targets keep turning down good offers to move to Israel.

"We are very short on players, we have young players from the youth ranks. There are things that are not in our control," Abukasis said, according to ONE. "We offer nice proposals to foreign players who decide not to come to Israel. It disappoints me."

Abukasis, who took over at Sakhnin in February, is currently overseeing a preseason training camp in Hungary as the club prepares for the return of Ligat Ha'Al action, with the squad still short of reinforcements in key positions.

The club is actively working to add both a defender and a forward from abroad. Among the names linked is striker William Agada, who spent a loan spell at Hapoel Haifa in the 2020-21 season and, per ONE, has again attracted interest from Haifa this summer — though a deal for Sakhnin has proven difficult to advance.

Reluctance among foreign players to relocate to Israel has been a recurring theme across the league since the outbreak of war in October 2023, and Abukasis's comments suggest it remains a live obstacle for a club outside the traditional top tier trying to compete for value signings.

On the players already through the door, ONE reports Lithuanian arrival Modestas Vorobjovas has made a stronger early impression than fellow new signing Carlitos, giving Abukasis at least some options as he shapes his squad for the campaign ahead.

With preseason friendlies approaching, the coach's frustration underlines the practical squeeze facing Sakhnin: a threadbare group leaning on academy graduates while trying to close gaps at both ends of the pitch before the new Ligat Ha'Al season gets under way.

body: Hapoel Jerusalem's summer rebuild has a new name attached to it: Itay Ahoud, the young Maccabi Haifa midfielder who has emerged as a target for the capital club as it looks to add depth before the new Ligat Ha'al season, ONE reports.

The interest is real, but the deal is not close. According to the report, Ahoud's move to Jerusalem cannot advance until Maccabi Haifa itself decides whether it even wants to loan the player out this season — a call the Haifa club has yet to make. Until then, Hapoel Jerusalem can only wait.

Ahoud, born on September 21, 2006, is one of Maccabi Haifa's own academy products and has been earmarked as a rare talent in the club's youth pipeline, having previously been named the club's outstanding player at youth level. He operates in central midfield, comfortable both screening the back four and stepping into possession.

He is not unfamiliar with senior football away from Haifa. Ahoud spent last season out on loan at Hapoel Kfar Saba, gaining regular first-team minutes, before returning to Sammy Ofer Stadium ahead of this campaign to compete for a place in the Haifa squad — which is precisely why the champions have been in no rush to sanction another loan.

For Hapoel Jerusalem, adding a combative young midfielder on loan would fit a squad still being reshaped after a difficult 2025/26 campaign, which ended with the club 12th and stuck in the bottom playoff group.

Part of that reshaping was enforced rather than chosen. Ziv Arie, the coach most closely identified with Hapoel Jerusalem over the past seven years, left the club in the spring and signed a one-year deal to take charge of Maccabi Petah Tikva in May.

The two clubs' paths are about to cross again regardless of how the Ahoud pursuit plays out. Hapoel Jerusalem are due to face Maccabi Petah Tikva in the Toto Cup, which will mark Arie's first game back against his former team since the split.

The club has chosen not to mark the occasion with a farewell ceremony at that fixture, judging a Toto Cup tie too low-key an occasion for a coach it regards as one of the defining figures in its recent history. Jerusalem instead intend to honour Arie properly at a league match later in the season, when the stadium is fuller and the stakes are higher.

title: Basketball association rejects Yinai's account of Oturu naturalization saga
dek: Hapoel Tel Aviv owner Ofer Yinai says the federation pushed him to naturalize Dan Oturu, then buckled to Maccabi pressure — the association says his version is simply wrong

verificationSources.label: ONE
Walla Sport
Wikipedia — Daniel Oturu

body: The Israel Basketball Association has publicly pushed back on Hapoel Tel Aviv owner Ofer Yinai, rejecting as inaccurate his claim that the federation itself proposed naturalizing American center Dan Oturu before quietly dropping the idea under pressure from rival clubs.

Yinai laid out his version in a video posted this week, telling fans that association chairman Amos Frishman had approached Hapoel Tel Aviv months earlier about making Oturu the national team's next naturalized player.

According to Yinai, that request came with a price tag: he says he spent roughly $2 million reworking Oturu's contract to strip out a buyout clause, a change he claims the association needed in place before naturalization could proceed.

Yinai went further, alleging that once Maccabi Tel Aviv and Maccabi Herzliya got wind that Oturu was the chosen player, they objected — and the plan was shelved. His argument was blunt: if the association acted independently rather than deferring to the sport's biggest ownership groups, Oturu would already be starting at center for Israel.

The federation's response, carried by ONE, flatly contradicts that timeline. The association says its chairman never approached Yinai or his representatives about naturalizing Oturu or any other player — and that the opposite happened: it was Hapoel Tel Aviv that sought a meeting and raised Oturu's naturalization on its own initiative.

The association also disputes the substance of what the naturalization committee actually discussed, saying its mandate was to set general procedures for the process rather than to evaluate any specific player, and that no naturalization decision was ever finalized for Oturu or anyone else.

Oturu himself is very much a going concern for Hapoel regardless of the dispute. The American-Nigerian center arrived from Anadolu Efes and has since signed a contract extension through the 2028-29 season, having established himself as one of the EuroLeague's more productive big men.

The naturalization question matters because Israel's senior national team has long relied on adding eligible foreign-born players to bolster its frontcourt, a practice that inevitably draws scrutiny — and lobbying — from the league's ownership groups whenever a specific name is floated.

This is not the first time Yinai has clashed publicly with Israeli basketball's governing bodies. He has previously filed a defamation suit against referees' association officials over a dispute stemming from a state cup semifinal, seeking damages of more than a million shekels.

For now, Oturu remains outside Israel's national team picture, and the two sides have offered irreconcilable accounts of who asked whom first. Attention will likely turn to whether the association releases any further detail on the naturalization committee's actual deliberations to settle the dispute over the record.

title: Lecce winger Banda goes silent as club warns he 'will pay the consequences'
dek: Technical director Stefano Trinchera says Lecce have had no word from Lameck Banda for days after the Zambian winger, sold to the club by Maccabi Petah Tikva in 2022, missed pre-season training and a scheduled medical.

body: Lecce have run out of patience with Lameck Banda. The Zambian winger, one of the club's most reliable performers over the past three seasons, has not shown up for pre-season training and has now missed a scheduled medical examination as well, according to ONE.

"Unfortunately, we haven't heard from Lameck Banda for several days," Lecce technical director Stefano Trinchera said, adding bluntly that the player "will pay the consequences of his behaviour" once the situation is resolved.

Banda was due at the BioLab clinic in Cutrofiano, near Lecce, for a routine pre-season medical check. He never turned up, and club staff say calls and messages to the 25-year-old have gone unanswered.

The saga has dragged on for more than a week. Banda initially told Lecce that bureaucratic and logistical problems were delaying his return to Italy from Zambia, but he was later reported to have been spotted leaving Lusaka's Kenneth Kaunda International Airport aboard an Ethiopian Airlines flight with his newly married wife — only for the club to say it still had not heard from him directly.

The disappearing act comes amid live transfer interest. Saudi Arabian club Al-Fateh have made an approach for Banda, but Lecce have so far rejected an opening offer of around €2.5 million as too low, leaving the winger's immediate future unresolved along with his whereabouts.

There is an Israeli financial interest in how this plays out. Banda arrived at Lecce in August 2022 in a permanent deal from Maccabi Petah Tikva, reportedly worth around €2 million, after a season on loan in Israel. According to ONE, the Israeli club retained a sell-on percentage on any future transfer fee above that €2 million mark — meaning a sale to Al-Fateh or elsewhere would trigger a payment back to Petah Tikva.

Banda made history on his Lecce debut as the first Zambian player to appear in Serie A, and he has been a fixture for the club ever since, contributing five goals and four assists last season as Lecce retained their top-flight status.
For now, Lecce are left waiting — for Banda to answer his phone, for a transfer offer they consider acceptable, and for clarity on a player who was supposed to be back in training weeks ago.

title: Courtois says he is pain-free and ready after World Cup injury scare
dek: The Real Madrid goalkeeper, hurt in Belgium's World Cup quarter-final exit to Spain, says he expects no lingering problems as he prepares to rejoin training.

body: Thibaut Courtois says the muscle injury that forced him out of Belgium's World Cup quarter-final against Spain has cleared up completely, and that he expects to report back for pre-season training with no restrictions, according to ONE.

The Real Madrid goalkeeper went off during the July 10 defeat to Spain unable to strike long kicks properly, a sign at the time that feared he had suffered something serious in the closing stages of Belgium's tournament.

Real Madrid ran tests on Courtois on July 13 at the club's Valdebebas training complex once he returned from international duty, and the results were reassuring: the muscle damage, in the quadriceps, was minor rather than the kind of tear that would have sidelined him for weeks.
"I'm no longer feeling any discomfort," Courtois said, according to ONE, adding that he intends to be ready to train as soon as his holiday ends and he rejoins the squad.

That timeline lines up with reporting from Managing Madrid and Football España, who say Courtois is on course to be fully available for Real Madrid's LaLiga opener against Real Sociedad next month. Spanish outlets add that the club may still hold him out of the August 1 pre-season friendly against Fiorentina as a precaution, even though the injury is not expected to cost him any meaningful pre-season work.

The scare comes at a significant moment for Courtois off the pitch as well. With Dani Carvajal's exit from the club, Real Madrid restructured its captaincy, and Courtois has moved up to third in the pecking order, outranked now only by new captain Fede Valverde and vice-captain Vinícius Júnior.

The 34-year-old has also made clear he sees his long-term future at the Bernabéu, saying he would like to remain at Real Madrid for another four or five years, remarks that come amid reports the club and his camp are already discussing a contract extension.

Courtois spent part of his recovery period away from the pitch entirely, attending the Tomorrowland festival in Belgium alongside his wife, the Israeli model Mishel Gerzig, a former IDF rescue-ship captain the goalkeeper married in 2023 and with whom he has a daughter, Ellie.

title: Nicosia, 29 October 2002: the night Haifa humbled Manchester United
dek: Exiled to a borrowed stadium in Cyprus, Itzhak Shum's Maccabi Haifa beat Manchester United 3-0 in the Champions League — still among the greatest results an Israeli club has ever produced in Europe.

body: The strangest thing about the greatest night in Maccabi Haifa's European history is that it did not happen in Haifa. It happened 250 kilometres across the Mediterranean, at the GSP Stadium in Nicosia, where Israel's champions were obliged to stage their 'home' fixtures. On 29 October 2002, in that adopted arena, Haifa beat Manchester United 3-0 in the group stage of the Champions League — a result contemporaries immediately called perhaps the finest ever recorded by an Israeli team in European competition.

The exile itself was part of the story. Haifa had made history that autumn simply by arriving: the first Israeli club ever to reach the Champions League group stage. But with the second intifada raging at home, UEFA refused to sanction matches in Israel on security grounds and forced the club to find a neutral venue abroad. Cyprus was the nearest willing host, and so a landmark campaign for Israeli football unfolded with its home crowd reduced to those supporters willing and able to make the short flight to Nicosia.

There had already been a taste of what this team could do. On the opening matchday at Old Trafford in September, Yaniv Katan had silenced 60,000 people after eight minutes — the first goal by an Israeli club in the Champions League group stage. United recovered emphatically, winning 5-2, with Ryan Giggs, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Juan Sebastián Verón, Ruud van Nistelrooy and a late Diego Forlán penalty overwhelming the visitors despite a second Haifa goal from Raffi Cohen. The scoreline stung, but the eight minutes mattered: Haifa had shown they would attack anyone.

By the time the return fixture came around, Sir Alex Ferguson's side had already secured their passage to the second group stage, and he used the occasion to rotate. Yet this was hardly a scratch team. Rio Ferdinand, Paul Scholes and Solskjaer all started, Forlán led the line, and the young goalkeeper Ricardo was given a night's work he would not forget. Against them, Itzhak Shum — who had taken over from Avram Grant that summer — sent out the core of his double-winning side: Dudu Aouate in goal, Arik Benado and Walid Badir in front of him, Katan and the Nigerian striker Yakubu Aiyegbeni in attack.

The breakthrough came five minutes before the interval, and it belonged, fittingly, to Katan. Picked out by Raimondas Žutautas, he skipped past John O'Shea and lashed his finish beyond Ricardo. If Old Trafford had been a cameo, this was the full performance: Haifa pressing, passing and believing against the champions of Europe of only three years earlier.

Eleven minutes into the second half, Žutautas turned provider into scorer, the Lithuanian midfielder striking spectacularly from long range to double the lead. Then, with thirteen minutes remaining, Yakubu completed the night from the penalty spot. Three-nil, and the Spanish referee Antonio López Nieto's final whistle confirmed a scoreline that flashed around Europe looking like a misprint: Maccabi Haifa 3, Manchester United 0.

The context made it heavier still. United had not lost a Champions League match in more than a year — not since Deportivo La Coruña won at Old Trafford in October 2001 — and it was the first time in over two years they had failed to score away from home in the competition. That the defeat was administered by a debutant club playing in a borrowed stadium, by a team assembled for a fraction of United's wage bill, was precisely what made the evening reverberate.

Haifa's campaign ended in honourable third place in Group F, with seven points — level terms with the continent's establishment, ahead of Olympiacos and behind only United and Bayer Leverkusen — and with it a parachute into the UEFA Cup. The season had a bittersweet coda: Shum's team surrendered the Israeli title to Maccabi Tel Aviv on goal difference, and the coach left for Greece that summer, where he promptly won a double with Panathinaikos.

More than two decades on, the Nicosia result remains the benchmark against which every Israeli European campaign is measured. Katan stayed to become a one-club Haifa icon; Yakubu's penalty was an early flourish from a striker England would soon come to know well; Aouate went on to a long career in Spain. And the match itself endures as a peculiarly Israeli kind of triumph — a famous home win that no one ever saw at home, delivered by a team that had to leave its country to show what its country's football could do.
facts: Maccabi Haifa beat Manchester United 3-0 at the GSP Stadium, Nicosia, on 29 October 2002, in the 2002-03 Champions League Group F.

title: Sanchez Vicario says her $41 million fortune vanished under ex-husband's watch
dek: The four-time Grand Slam champion says she trusted her husband with the finances for over a decade of marriage — only to see most of her tennis fortune disappear, with a Barcelona court finding them both guilty of hiding assets from a bank.

verificationSources.label: BBC Sport
ESPN
Yahoo Sports
Tennis.com

body: Arantxa Sanchez Vicario spent two decades as one of the fiercest competitors women's tennis has produced — four Grand Slam singles titles, the world No. 1 ranking and five Olympic Games worth of medals. She says none of it prepared her for what happened to the money she made along the way.

The Spaniard, now 54, says roughly $41 million (about €36 million) of her fortune has vanished, and she places the blame squarely on her ex-husband and former financial manager, Josep Santacana. The pair married in 2008, share two children and divorced in 2019.

"I focused on playing tennis and never handled my own financial affairs, because I simply didn't know how," she has said of the arrangement. "I trusted my husband completely — and the money vanished."

That trust became a criminal matter. In January 2024 a court in Barcelona found both Sanchez Vicario and Santacana guilty of fraud, ruling that the couple had concealed assets to dodge debts owed to Banque de Luxembourg.

Santacana, described in the case as the entrepreneur who ran the couple's finances, was handed the harsher punishment: three years and three months in prison. Sanchez Vicario was sentenced to two years, but as a first-time offender the term was suspended after she agreed to help repay what was owed.
The court also ordered the pair to pay a combined €6.6 million (roughly $7.1 million) in damages to the bank. Sanchez Vicario says she now hands over half of her earnings to chip away at that debt.

She has continued to present herself as a victim of the arrangement rather than a willing participant, insisting she was kept in the dark about the family's finances throughout the marriage. "I just expect the truth to be told and this to be over," she has said of the ordeal, which she describes as psychologically exhausting.

It is not the first time Sanchez Vicario's finances have landed her in legal trouble. In 2009, Spain's Supreme Court fined her $5.9 million over unpaid taxes from 1989 to 1993, a period in which she had claimed residency in Andorra rather than Spain.

None of it erases the résumé that made her one of the sport's most decorated figures: French Open titles in 1989, 1994 and 1998, a US Open crown in 1994, the year she also reached world No. 1, and medals across the 1992 Barcelona and 1996 Atlanta Olympics before retiring in 2002.
For now, the case that once defined her career has been replaced by one defined by a bank ledger — and a fortune she says she never saw slip away until it was already gone.

title: Israel's under-16 girls storm back to beat South Africa in water polo World Championship opener
dek: A five-goal burst after an early setback carried Israel to a 12-7 win in Zagreb, with Yahali Rokach and Ori Grodman leading the way as the team opened one of the busiest summers in Israeli water polo history.

verificationSources.label: Ynet
Sport5

body: Israel's under-16 girls' water polo team opened its World Championship campaign with a statement, coming from behind to beat South Africa 12-7 on Saturday at the Mladost pool complex in Zagreb, Croatia.
The Israelis conceded the first two goals of the match and looked rattled early, but settled quickly and reeled off five unanswered goals to seize control before the opening quarter was out.
By halftime Israel led 6-4, and the team pulled away for good in the third quarter, outscoring South Africa 4-1 to move ahead 10-5 heading into the final period.

Ori Grodman and Yahali Rokach each scored three goals, with Rokach named player of the match. Yara Huvino Garcia added two, while Tamara Salmon-Michaeli, Inbar Yanko, Alma Tauber and Tamar Orhan each found the net once.

"The excitement was evident at first, but once the girls settled in, they showed they are the stronger side," head coach Edan Kaftori said afterward. "Tomorrow we have a very tough match against Hungary, one of the gold-medal contenders. The girls will rest, regroup and prepare for the long tournament ahead."

Israel landed in a demanding group alongside Hungary, one of the traditional powers of world water polo, along with the Netherlands, Mexico and South Africa - meaning Saturday's win was an important early step rather than a formality.
The team is due to face Hungary next, followed by Mexico and the Netherlands, as it looks to navigate the group stage of the inaugural age-group event on the world aquatics calendar.

The Zagreb opener also marks the start of what Israeli water polo officials are calling one of the sport's busiest summers on record domestically, with five youth national teams set to represent the country across three World Championships and two European Championships over the coming weeks.

For a program with modest senior-level pedigree internationally, an opening win over a nation like South Africa - and a competitive group draw against a genuine contender in Hungary - offers an early gauge of how far the age-group pipeline has progressed.

title: Norway mourns as Olympic rowing great Olaf Tufte dies at 50
dek: The two-time Olympic champion was found unconscious on his family farm days after training with the national squad; doctors say he suffered acute cardiac arrest.

verificationSources.label: World Rowing
newsinenglish.no
VG
ESPN

body: Norway is in mourning for Olaf Tufte, the most decorated rower in the country's Olympic history, who died on Tuesday at the age of 50, just a day after he was found unconscious on his family farm.

Tufte was discovered unresponsive at around 3pm on Monday at Tufte Gård, the farm he ran with his wife in Horten, on Norway's southern coast. Emergency crews administered first aid at the scene before he was rushed to Rikshospitalet in Oslo, where he died the following day.

The hospital and Tufte's family said he suffered acute cardiac arrest. An autopsy was planned to establish the full circumstances, and there were no signs of a workplace accident or witnesses to his collapse.

Tufte was, by any measure, one of Norway's greatest Olympians. He competed at seven consecutive Summer Games, from Atlanta in 1996 through the pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics in 2021, a span of 25 years at the top of his sport.

His signature achievement came in the men's single sculls, where he won back-to-back Olympic gold medals at Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008. He also took silver in the double sculls at Sydney 2000 and, at 40 years old, bronze in the double sculls alongside Kjetil Borch at Rio 2016.

Away from the Olympics, Tufte was twice crowned world champion in the single sculls, in 2001 and 2003, becoming the first Norwegian ever to win a world rowing title. He finished his career with six world championship medals in total.
In 2021 he was awarded the Thomas Keller Medal, rowing's highest individual honour, in recognition of a career that helped put Norwegian rowing on the map.

After retiring from elite competition, Tufte largely stepped back from the spotlight. He worked his family farm, served as a volunteer firefighter, and built a string of small businesses, including a concrete firm, the clothing label Tufte Wear and a brewery.

He had not fully left the sport behind. Frank Ove Reite, president of the Norwegian Rowing Federation, said Tufte had joined a joint training session with the national squad at the Årungen rowing stadium in Ås just the previous Friday, days before his death.

"It is completely terrible and incomprehensible," Reite said, adding that his thoughts were with Tufte's family in what he called an "incomprehensible situation," and describing the news as a shock that had rippled through Norway's rowing community.
Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre also paid tribute, saying Tufte "brought enormous athletic joy to us as a nation" and was remembered as one of the country's most beloved sporting figures.
Tufte is survived by his wife, Aina, and their two children.

dek: Ron Ben Yishai and Lee Liberman beat a German pair 18-7 in Antibes to seal the medal after a semifinal exit to eventual champions Brazil.

body: Israel's footvolley pair of Ron Ben Yishai and Lee Liberman claimed bronze at the Footvolley World Championship in Antibes, on France's Riviera coast, beating a German duo 18-7 in the third-place match, Sport5 reported.

The Israelis had reached the medal round on the back of a strong run through the knockout stage, before running into a Brazilian pair in the semifinal who proved too strong and went on to win the gold medal in the final, according to the report.

Rather than dwell on the near-miss, Ben Yishai and Liberman regrouped for the bronze-medal match and were comfortable winners over Germany, closing out the tournament with a podium finish for Israel in a sport still building its profile at home.

The Mondial de Footvolley is an annual fixture on the French Riviera, traditionally staged in the Antibes and Juan-les-Pins area and drawing national teams from across Europe and South America to a sport that blends beach volleyball's court and net with football's no-hands rule.

Ben Yishai is a familiar face on Israel's small but growing footvolley scene, where he also competes domestically in Tel Aviv's Ya'ez footvolley league, at times partnering Maor Ha'as. Liberman is likewise a regular fixture of that same local circuit.

For a niche sport with only a handful of organised players in Israel, a world championship medal is a notable marker of progress — proof, as Sport5's headline put it, that Israel is becoming something of a "powerhouse" in footvolley's competitive corners.

title: Israel's U18 team crush France to set up a shot at a second straight World Cup
dek: A statement 91-77 win has clinched top spot in Group A for Nadav Zilberstein's side at the European Championship in Italy — and opened a route to next year's U19 World Cup, a stage Israel only reached for the first time last summer.

body: Israel's under-18 basketball team put together its best half of the summer on Sunday, overturning a tied game to beat France 91-77 in Trento and lock up first place in Group A at the FIBA U18 EuroBasket, with a game to spare.

The sides were level 39-39 at the break, but Israel took over after halftime behind Aviv Aronov, who finished with 31 points on 5-of-11 shooting from three-point range and six rebounds, and David Mozes, who added 25 points and eight rebounds. Rom Stoler and Omri Orland chipped in off the bench as the young Israelis pulled away.

It followed an opening comeback win over Greece, 93-84, meaning Nadav Zilberstein's squad arrived at the France game already unbeaten and left it with the group sealed before Monday's dead-rubber finale against Austria.

The result matters well beyond seeding. Sport5 notes that Israel now heads into the round of 16 as one of the tournament's form teams, with the winner of that game guaranteed a place in the quarterfinals — and, under the competition's structure, a share of the five World Cup berths reserved for the tournament's top finishers.

According to Sport5's reading of the bracket, Israel's likely round-of-16 opponent is Denmark, with a possible quarterfinal draw against one of Spain, Italy, Latvia, Germany, Slovenia, Lithuania or Bulgaria — a group that includes several of the continent's traditional basketball powers. Those matchups are not yet officially locked in and will depend on how the rest of Group A's rivals finish.

The stakes are real for a program still building its recent history. Israel finished fourth at the 2024 U18 EuroBasket in Tampere, Finland, agonisingly short of a medal, and there is a sense within Israeli basketball that this crop of players — many of whom have grown up together through the junior ranks — has the depth to go further.

A World Cup place would be a landmark on its own terms. Israel's under-19 team qualified for the FIBA U19 World Cup for the first time only last summer, reaching Lausanne, Switzerland, under coach Sharon Avrahami. The team went 2-5 — the best record any Israeli side has posted at that level — and beat the host nation, Switzerland, 79-68 in the placement game to finish seventh.

That achievement was treated as a breakthrough for Israeli youth basketball. A second consecutive World Cup call-up, this time for the current U18 group once they move up an age bracket, would suggest the progress is not a one-off but part of a broader shift in the pipeline feeding the senior national team.

For now, the more immediate task is Monday's meaningless finale against Austria before the knockout rounds begin in Trento and Rovereto later this week — the stage on which Israel's actual route to another World Cup will be decided.

title: Israel's U18 side overpower France to seize control of Group A in Trento
dek: Aviv Aronov's 31 points and a monster David Musis double-double sent Israel to a 91-77 win over France at the FIBA U18 EuroBasket, setting up a Monday decider against Austria for top spot.

verificationSources.label: Ynet
Ynetnews (English)
FIBA Basketball
IBBA (Israel Basketball Association)

body: Israel's under-18 basketball team put together its most complete performance of the summer on Sunday, pulling away in the third quarter to beat France 91-77 at the FIBA U18 EuroBasket in Trento and take control of Group A.

It was a second straight statement result for Nadav Zilberstein's squad, who had opened the tournament a day earlier with a dramatic 93-84 overtime win over Greece, rallying from nine points down inside the final 90 seconds of regulation to force extra time.

Against France the game was tight for a half. Israel led 18-16 after the first quarter but the French responded to leave the sides deadlocked at 39-39 at the break, with neither team able to build a cushion.

The third quarter settled it. Israel outscored France 30-20 in the period to open a double-digit lead, and while the French chipped away in the fourth, a 22-18 final frame was enough to see the game out comfortably.

Aviv Aronov, the 17-year-old guard who has already committed to a prep-school move to the United States, was again the standout, finishing with 31 points on 5-of-11 shooting from three alongside six rebounds. He had scored 30 in the win over Greece a day earlier.

David Musis produced a huge all-round display of his own, adding 25 points and eight rebounds, while Rom Stoller chipped in 8 points off the bench. Noam Akstein and Omri Orland scored 7 points apiece, with Orland also handing out 4 assists.

France were led by Hugo Yimga, who kept his side within range for long stretches but could not prevent Israel's superior efficiency from telling — Israel shot 49% from the field and 80% from the line, both better marks than the French.

The win leaves Israel in the driving seat in Group A, which also includes Austria and Greece. Ynet reported that Israel's own fate is now in its hands: a win over Austria in Monday's final group game, scheduled for 2 p.m. local time, would secure first place outright heading into the knockout rounds.

The tournament, the first edition of the FIBA U18 EuroBasket staged across Trento and Rovereto in Italy's Trentino region, runs through August 2, with 16 nations split into four groups before the competition moves to a knockout format.

title: Inside LA 2028: Israel's Olympic officials get a rare look at the Games taking shape
dek: Two years before the opening ceremony, Ynet joined the Israeli Olympic Committee on a tour of Los Angeles venues being converted for 2028 — and paused with delegation leaders at the memorial to the 11 Israeli athletes murdered at Munich in 1972.

verificationSources.label: Ynet special report: "First pictures: a rare glimpse into preparations for the 2028 Olympics"

body: Two years out from the opening ceremony, Ynet's sports desk was given rare access to the Los Angeles venues being reshaped for the 2028 Olympics, touring the site with a delegation from the Israeli Olympic Committee led by chair Yael Arad and CEO Adi Bikhman.

The headline detail is what LA28 organisers are not building. Los Angeles will stage the Games without a single new permanent venue, according to the report — the first Summer Olympics since London 1948 to be delivered entirely on existing infrastructure. More than 40 venues across the region are being adapted to host 51 sports.

It makes Los Angeles the third city to host the Summer Olympics three times, after London and Paris, and the first American city to do so. The Games return to a city that also staged the 1932 Olympics, in the shadow of the Great Depression, and the 1984 Games — the edition that famously turned a profit through private sponsorship rather than public construction spending.

The centrepiece of that legacy, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, opened in 1923 and will host athletics as well as its third Olympic opening ceremony — but for the first time, it will share that duty. Organisers have confirmed the July 14, 2028 opening ceremony will be split, unprecedentedly, between the century-old Coliseum and the modern SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, with the Coliseum alone hosting the closing ceremony on July 30.

SoFi Stadium's own transformation is one of the more striking pieces of engineering in the plan: a temporary competition pool will be built beneath the stadium's football field for swimming and artistic swimming, with organisers targeting more than 38,000 spectators — which would make it the largest swimming venue in Olympic history. The pool is expected to be repurposed for community use once the Games end.

Other landmark venues are being folded into the programme rather than replaced. Ynet's report describes Crypto.com Arena, home of the Lakers, hosting basketball finals, gymnastics and boxing, while Dodger Stadium takes on baseball and Long Beach becomes a satellite hub for 11 sports including handball and beach volleyball. Venues further out in the San Fernando Valley will stage BMX, skateboarding and 3x3 basketball, in conditions the report notes could push past 40 degrees Celsius during the Games' late-July window.

Housing for competitors is being built around an existing campus rather than a purpose-built village: the University of Southern California's dormitories, including two- and three-bedroom units, are being converted into the athletes' village, according to the report.

Organisers are projecting between three and five million visitors over the Games, a scale that collides with Los Angeles's famously car-dependent geography. The report flags transportation as the organisers' central operational headache, with a network of dedicated shuttle routes and transit expansions being built out to move fans between a metropolitan area with comparatively little rail infrastructure.

The sporting programme itself will look different, too. Flag football will make its Olympic debut in 2028, part of the IOC's push to broaden the Games' American appeal, while lacrosse returns to the Olympics for the first time since 1908.

For the Israeli delegation, the trip was framed as more than a scouting mission. Arad, who chairs the Israeli Olympic Committee, told Ynet that American Jewish communities are eager to use the Games to connect with Israel and with younger generations, calling Los Angeles 2028 "an excellent opportunity" on that front — alongside the more familiar task of scouting logistics, accreditation and training arrangements for Israeli athletes three years out.

The most emotional moment of the tour, by the report's account, came away from the construction sites: delegation members were shown a memorial plaque commemorating the 11 Israeli athletes and coaches murdered by Palestinian terrorists at the 1972 Munich Olympics, a fixture of the Israeli Olympic Committee's presence at every Games since.

With two years still to run before the opening ceremony, much of what Ynet's team saw remains under construction or still on the drawing board. But the shape of LA28 is already clear: a Games built almost entirely on what Los Angeles already has, stretched across a sprawling, heat-prone and traffic-heavy city — and one where Israel's own preparations are now firmly under way.

title: From orienteering champion to Israeli record-breaker, Matan Ivri plots his course to the Olympics
dek: Once forging trails through Israeli forests, the 24-year-old has smashed the national 1,500m, mile and 3,000m records at Wisconsin and now has Los Angeles 2028 in his sights.

verificationSources.label: Ynet
The Jerusalem Post
World Athletics profile
Wisconsin Badgers official site

body: Three years ago, Matan Ivri's talent was reading a compass and a contour map at speed through Israeli forests, not running a fast lap of a track. Today, at 24, he owns the Israeli national records in the 1,500m, the mile and the 3,000m, and he is chasing a place on the start line at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Ivri's route into distance running began, of all places, in the sport of orienteering. He was Israel's national orienteering champion until around 2023, navigating unmarked terrain under time pressure — a discipline that demands, as he has put it, high-stakes decisions made on the move. He credits those years with building the composure that now carries him through the closing laps of a championship final.

One of the formative moments of his teenage years came at the 2019 European Orienteering Championships in Belarus, when Ivri, not yet 17, stood by the podium as Israel's flag went up to mark a sixth-place team finish on the continent — a result he still counts among his proudest as a competitor, from a sport most Israeli sports fans barely follow.

It was only when he began running to build fitness for orienteering that he discovered he had a different, and much rarer, gift. "I didn't know I had this," he has said of the speed that emerged once he put down the map and picked up spikes.

The transition has been startlingly fast. This year alone, Ivri has rewritten the Israeli 1,500m record eight times, most recently clocking 3:34.51 in Belgium on July 11 — a mark that also made him the first Israeli to dip under 3:40 for the distance.

He has done the same across the middle-distance card: a national record of 7:43.88 for 3,000m set in February, and a mile time inside four minutes that made him the first Israeli in history to break that barrier, a landmark long treated as a benchmark of serious distance-running class.

In June, Ivri took his form to the biggest stage of American college athletics, finishing fifth in the 1,500m final at the NCAA Outdoor Championships in Eugene, Oregon, in 3:37.41 — behind winner Simeon Birnbaum of Oregon — and earning First-Team All-America honors, a rare distinction for an Israeli track athlete.

All of this has unfolded at the University of Wisconsin, where Ivri trains with the Badgers on a $100,000 athletic scholarship while studying computer science and making the Dean's List. He has spoken of treating both his training and his coursework with the same analytical precision, as interlocking systems to be optimized rather than separate pursuits.

He has not strayed far from his roots. Ivri grew up in the Galilee and still trains, in spirit, with his first club, Hapoel Emek Hefer, texting his early coach and mentor Amir Ramon after every race he runs on American soil.

The next test comes fast: the European Athletics Championships open in Birmingham on August 10, and Ivri is aiming to hit the qualifying standard of around 3:33.50 to make the field — a mark just over a second inside his current personal best.

Beyond Birmingham sits the real target. Ivri has spoken of the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 not as a distant dream but as an active plan, one built race by race, second by second, on a Wisconsin track thousands of kilometers from the forests where his athletic career actually began.

Israeli distance running has rarely produced a genuine international contender; the sport has historically been a weak link in the country's Olympic program. Ivri's rapid rise, still just three years removed from his final orienteering course, has made him one of the most closely watched young Israeli athletes heading into the run-up to LA 2028.

title: Inside Messi's blueprint for life after football: a network of clubs, not one
dek: From a fourth-division side in Rosario to a Catalan academy and a stake waiting for him at Inter Miami, Lionel Messi is quietly assembling a multi-club empire for the day he finally stops playing.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 (original report)
Bloomberg — Messi buys UE Cornellà
ESPN — Messi buys Cornellà
La Nación — Leones de Rosario, run by Messi's family
Bolavip — Inter Miami's hidden ownership clause

body: Lionel Messi has never looked like a man in a hurry to leave the pitch, but the pieces of what comes after are already sliding into place. Sport5, in a detailed reconstruction of his business dealings, argues that three separate acquisitions across two continents amount to a single, deliberate plan: not one retirement club, but a network of them.

The furthest back, and the smallest, is Leones de Rosario. The club was founded by the Messi Foundation in January 2015 in his hometown, and it is run day to day by his older brother, Matías Messi, who serves as club president. For years it operated in regional Rosario leagues; this year it won direct affiliation to the Argentine Football Association to compete in the Primera C, the fourth tier of the national pyramid — a modest stage, but an official one at last.

It is not a club built around star names or a landmark stadium. What it has instead is Adidas's backing and a sponsorship from Banco Macro, plus the Messi name attached to every mention of it in the Argentine press. Messi himself was pictured in the stands at a Leones fixture in Rosario this past week, his first public appearance since Argentina's World Cup summer.

The second piece is the one everyone already knows about: Inter Miami. Messi's contract, signed when he joined the club in 2023 and since extended through the 2028 season, has long been reported to carry what is sometimes called a 'Beckham clause' — a provision, modelled on the one David Beckham secured at LA Galaxy, that lets him convert his standing with the club into an ownership stake once he stops playing. MLS rules bar active players from holding equity, so the clause only activates in retirement.

The numbers around Inter Miami since Messi's arrival make the case for why that stake matters. Club revenues have jumped from roughly $55 million to more than $200 million, the franchise has moved into a new, purpose-built stadium seating close to 27,000, and Forbes now values the team at well over a billion dollars — a valuation unthinkable for an MLS side before he signed. Co-owner Jorge Mas has repeatedly said the club expects Messi to stay involved with Inter Miami well beyond his playing days.

The newest, and in some ways the most telling, addition came in April 2026, when Messi completed the purchase of UE Cornellà, a fifth-division Catalan club based just outside Barcelona. The deal was confirmed directly by Cornellà, a 75-year-old institution whose academy has quietly produced serious talent over the years, including Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya and former Barcelona left-back Jordi Alba.

Buying a development-focused academy club in Catalonia, a stone's throw from Camp Nou, reads as more than sentiment. Sport5's framing is that Messi is assembling something closer to City Football Group or Red Bull's network model than to the single-trophy-club approach taken by earlier athlete-owners: a feeder system in Rosario, a flagship in Miami, and a European academy pipeline in Cornellà, each one able to develop or move players and generate revenue through the others.

Sport5 describes Messi as 'a process-oriented person' who, unlike some of his predecessors, 'wants to build a club for years ahead' rather than simply attach his name to one marquee project. That distinguishes his post-career trajectory from Michael Jordan's ownership of a single NBA franchise, or Ronaldo Nazário's hands-on rebuilding projects at Valladolid and Cruzeiro — both single-club bets rather than a network.

Already a billionaire by most outside estimates, Messi stands to significantly increase his wealth through this structure without taking on the daily grind of running any one club himself — leaning instead on the family at Leones, the Mas family's operation in Miami, and whatever leadership Cornellà installs under its new ownership.

None of this changes what happens on the pitch in the short term: Messi remains contracted to Inter Miami through 2028 and has given no indication of an imminent farewell. But the acquisitions themselves are already done, not hypothetical, and together they sketch the clearest picture yet of what Messi intends his footballing afterlife to look like.

title: David Moses, Israeli basketball's next big thing, delivers at Europe's under-18 championship
dek: The 18-year-old Ramat Hasharon forward, already committed to Florida Atlantic, is backing up the hype with monster numbers as Israel opens its FIBA U18 EuroBasket campaign in Italy with wins over Greece and France.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 profile: "David Moses - the next big thing in Israeli basketball"
ONE: the Israeli talent David Moses on his way to college
Walla Sport: "Breaking all the charts" — David Moses profile
FIBA Basketball: Aronov, Musis lead Israel shock over Greece
FIBA U18 EuroBasket 2026 — Israel vs Greece game page

body: Two games into the FIBA U18 EuroBasket in northern Italy, David Moses has already given Israeli basketball fans a reason to pay very close attention. In the tournament opener in Trento on Saturday, the 18-year-old forward-center put up 26 points, 19 rebounds and three blocks in overtime as Israel stunned Greece 93-84. He followed it up with 25 points as Israel beat France 91-77, sending the youth national team to the top of Group A.

For those who have watched Moses over the past year, none of it looks like a fluke. Sport5 had already anointed him "the next big thing in Israeli basketball" in a profile earlier this year, and outlets including ONE and Walla have run their own versions of the same story: a 2.10-metre forward who shoots over 40 percent from three, handles the ball like a guard and is still, by his own coaches' admission, only scratching the surface of what he can become.

Moses plays his club basketball for Ramat Hasharon, where he has spent the past three seasons rising through the youth ranks and into regular minutes with the senior Liga Leumit (National League) roster. This past season with the youth team he averaged 24.1 points and 11.4 rebounds a game across 18 appearances, shooting 62.6 percent on twos and 40.4 percent from beyond the arc — numbers that would stand out on any level, let alone for a player his size.

What makes him unusual is not just the production but the shape of it. Israeli basketball has produced plenty of tall, physical players over the years, but rarely one who can face up, put the ball on the floor and pull from three at 2.10 metres. Coaches who have worked with him describe a player who can be used as a stretch four one possession and a rim-protecting five the next.

The path here was not conventional. Moses started playing seriously relatively late, coming through Hapoel Holon's youth setup before Chanoch Mintz — the veteran developer previously credited with shaping Lior Eliyahu's career — brought him to Ramat Hasharon three years ago. He has grown roughly 13 centimetres since then, from around 1.97 metres to his current 2.10, while his skill set was built essentially from scratch alongside the growth spurt.

Ramat Hasharon's head coach, Guy Cantor, has been candid about how deliberately the club is handling him. "The dominance is exceptional," Cantor has said of Moses' performances, adding that the plan is to keep using his outside shooting while playing him at power forward rather than boxing him into a traditional centre role. Asked where it all leads, Cantor's answer was measured rather than triumphant: "We're flying with this, uncertain where it leads. Meanwhile, processes must mature."

Alongside his club coaching staff, Moses works twice a week with personal trainer Avi Even, a former Maccabi Tel Aviv coach who has overseen much of his individual skill development. "He's one of the most talented players I've worked with," Even has said, noting that "every workout, you see visible improvement."

The step up to senior basketball has come with the expected adjustment. In his appearances with Ramat Hasharon's adult Liga Leumit team, Moses has averaged 9.5 points and 4.7 rebounds in roughly 16.5 minutes a game, shooting 60.3 percent from the field. Those numbers climbed through the playoffs, where he put up 14.3 points and 7.5 rebounds in about 20 minutes across four games, capped by a 21-point, 13-rebound outing against Nahariya.

College basketball is already settled: Moses has committed to Florida Atlantic University, which reached the Final Four three seasons ago. Even has said the fit of the programme mattered more in the decision than name recognition, and Moses himself has spoken about turning his NBA ambitions into what he calls a realistic goal rather than a distant dream.

All of that context is what made his first two games in Italy so notable. The FIBA U18 EuroBasket, running in Trento and Rovereto from 25 July to 2 August, put Israel in a group with hosts Italy, Austria, France and Greece — hardly a soft draw. Beating Greece in overtime and then France in the space of two days, with Moses and teammate Aviv Aronov (who scored 30 points against Greece) leading the way, has been read at home as an early signal that Israel's age-group basketball is producing more than one interesting prospect at once.

Moses' own line against Greece — 26 points on 9-of-18 shooting, including 4-of-8 from three, plus 19 rebounds and three blocks in over 43 minutes including overtime — was, by any age-group standard, an exceptional performance. It is the kind of box score that travels fast among European scouts already tracking the tournament.

None of this guarantees anything about what comes next; European under-18 standouts do not always translate into first-team regulars, let alone NBA prospects, and Moses' own coaches keep stressing patience over hype. But between the club numbers, the college commitment and now a breakout tournament on a real international stage, the case Israeli media has been building around him over the past few months is, for now, holding up under pressure.

title: Leaked Infantino letter praised Argentina's "professionalism" as FIFA probes final brawl
dek: A private note from the FIFA president to the Argentine federation, congratulating the runners-up on their World Cup final performance, has emerged just as football's governing body investigates ugly post-match scenes in New Jersey.

verificationSources.label: Sports Illustrated
SportBible
The Mirror
ESPN
Goal.com

body: A private letter from FIFA president Gianni Infantino to the Argentine Football Association has leaked into the Argentine press and been verified by the Daily Mail, congratulating the World Cup runners-up on their "professionalism" at the very moment his own organisation is investigating their conduct in the final.

Argentina lost the 2026 World Cup final 1-0 to Spain after extra time at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on July 19, Ferran Torres settling the tie with a 106th-minute winner. The match will be remembered as much for what happened after the final whistle as for the football itself.

According to the leaked correspondence, Infantino wrote that "Argentina won the silver medal of FIFA World Cup 2026, after an intense final against Spain," adding that "these victories are always the fruit of constant work, professionalism and attention to detail." He extended his congratulations to the squad, coach Lionel Scaloni and the federation's staff.

The timing has drawn heavy criticism. Within days of the final, FIFA confirmed it had appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to examine "offensive behaviour" and a string of physical confrontations between players from both squads once the match ended.

Television footage showed Leandro Paredes grabbing Eric Garcia by the throat and shoving Gavi to the ground, while Nahuel Molina appeared to throw a punch in the direction of Spain captain Rodri. Argentina assistant coach Roberto Ayala later apologised for a separate confrontation with Dani Olmo, describing it as a shove rather than a punch.

Enzo Fernández was sent off in the chaos, and Spain coach Luis de la Fuente did not mince words afterward, telling Spanish broadcaster TVE the scenes were "intolerable and unacceptable" and that "it cannot be allowed."

Against that backdrop, Infantino's use of the word "professionalism" to describe the beaten finalists has struck many observers as tone-deaf, coming from the head of the body actively investigating the same players for misconduct.

The defeat has also triggered an extraordinary wave of fan activism. A Change.org petition demanding the final be replayed, and accusing Slovenian referee Slavko Vinčić of a "controversial and corrupt" performance, has passed 82,000 signatures.

Separately, a petition calling for Argentina to be excluded from future World Cups altogether gathered more than 29 million signatures before it was closed, while another campaign targeting Paredes specifically reached roughly 23 million names.

Sport5's original report, citing Argentine coverage of the leak, said federation president Claudio Tapia had urged supporters to accept Spain's victory rather than dwell on the refereeing controversy — a notably more measured tone than the mass petitions suggest exists among parts of the fan base.

FIFA has not commented publicly on the leaked letter itself, and it remains unclear who passed the document to media outlets or why, given the sensitivity of an ongoing disciplinary process involving the same federation the letter praises.

The disciplinary prosecutor's findings, whenever they arrive, will determine whether Argentina's players and staff face bans or fines over the post-final scenes — a process now complicated, at least in the court of public opinion, by the FIFA president's own warm words to the team under investigation.

title: Still the fastest: Noah Lyles wins third US 100m title in 9.79 seconds
dek: The Olympic champion matched his own personal best to post the world's fastest 100m time of the season at the USATF Outdoor Championships in New York.

verificationSources.label: World Athletics report
Olympics.com report
LetsRun.com report

body: Noah Lyles served notice on Friday that the two years since his Olympic breakthrough haven't cost him a step, storming to a 9.79-second victory in the men's 100m final at the USATF Outdoor Track and Field Championships in New York.
The time matched his own personal best - the 9.79 he ran to win Olympic gold in Paris in August 2024 - and stands as the fastest 100m mark run by anyone in the world this season.
It was Lyles' third US outdoor title over the distance, cementing his status as the man to beat in the sprints heading toward the next global championship cycle.

True to his usual pattern, Lyles was not fastest out of the blocks. He trailed through the early phase of the race before unleashing his trademark closing speed over the final 30 metres to pull clear of the field.

Ronnie Baker took second place in 9.88, edging out Kenny Bednarek by just five thousandths of a second - both sprinters were credited with the same 9.88 clocking, with Baker awarded the runner-up spot on a photo finish.
"I think I made that 'I'm still the world's fastest man' statement," Lyles said afterward, according to World Athletics' official report on the meeting.

The New York championships also produced a statement performance in the women's field, with Sha'Carri Richardson winning the 100m title in an equally emphatic display, giving the meet a genuine world-class sheen.

For Lyles, the reigning Olympic and world 100m champion, matching his lifetime best in a domestic final rather than a global showpiece sends a clear signal to rivals that his current form has lost nothing since Paris.

title: Hezonja gives up a bigger Real Madrid pay day to chase his NBA return with Cleveland
dek: Fresh off being named the Liga Endesa's MVP, the Croatian forward is walking into a one-year, $2.8 million deal with the Cavaliers — roughly $1.2 million a year less than he could have earned in Madrid, according to Sport5

verificationSources.label: Sport5 report
ESPN — Cavs, former lottery pick Mario Hezonja agree on 1-year deal
Yahoo Sports — Hezonja signing 1-year, $2.8 million deal, returning to NBA for first time since 2020
Real Madrid — Hezonja named MVP of the 2025/26 Liga Endesa

body: Mario Hezonja is walking away from a bigger pay cheque to chase the NBA dream again. Sport5 reports that the Croatian forward is sacrificing roughly $1.2 million a year in net income by leaving Real Madrid for a one-year, $2.8 million deal with the Cleveland Cavaliers — more than a third of what he could have kept in Spain.

The move caps a stunning individual season. Hezonja was named MVP of the 2025/26 Liga Endesa, Spain's top domestic league, after averaging 17.5 points, 4.9 rebounds and 1.9 assists a game and leading Real Madrid to the top of the standings — the first Croatian ever to win the award and the eleventh Real Madrid player to do so since it was introduced in 1991-92.

According to Sport5's breakdown, Hezonja's Real Madrid salary stood at roughly €2.4 million gross a year, which nets out to around $1.6 million after Spanish tax. His new deal in Cleveland is worth $2.8 million, but the report's own framing still puts him roughly $1.2 million a year worse off than what he was actually banking in Madrid.

The gap could have been even wider. Sport5 reports Real Madrid was ready to offer Hezonja a raise to €4.7 million a year to keep him at the Santiago Bernabéu's basketball arm — meaning the 31-year-old is effectively turning down close to €3 million annually to get back onto an NBA roster.
Leaving was not free, either. Hezonja's contract reportedly included an NBA-only exit clause priced at €850,000, which the Cavaliers are said to have covered in full to get the deal done.

None of that seems to have given him pause. Hezonja had been telling people around Real Madrid for weeks that he intended to trigger the clause and test the NBA again, and the move was widely reported by outlets including ESPN and Yahoo Sports as a $2.8 million, one-year agreement once it became official this week.

It marks his first NBA appearance since 2020. Drafted fifth overall by the Orlando Magic in 2015, Hezonja spent three up-and-down seasons in Orlando before one-year stops with the New York Knicks and Portland Trail Blazers, the latter of which waived him after the 2019-20 season. He then rebuilt his career in Europe with Panathinaikos, UNICS Kazan and, since 2022, Real Madrid.

For Cleveland, Hezonja arrives as an experienced floor-spacing wing coming off arguably the best season of his career, at a fraction of what a player of his current form might have commanded had he stayed in Europe.

The financial sacrifice underlines just how much weight Hezonja is putting on a genuine second chance in the NBA — a league he left as a disappointing lottery pick and is now returning to as a reigning MVP of one of Europe's strongest domestic competitions.

title: Israel's U18 team stuns Greece and beats France to open EuroBasket 2-0
dek: Behind a breakout run from center David Musis and a scoring surge from Aviv Aronov, Israel's youth national team has started the U18 European Championship with consecutive wins over Greece and France

verificationSources.label: Sport5 report
FIBA: Aronov, Musis lead Israel shock over Greece
FIBA: France vs Israel box score
FIBA: Israel team profile, FIBA U18 EuroBasket 2026

body: Two games into the U18 European Championship, Israel's youth national team is unbeaten, unshaken and playing the kind of basketball that has people around the program reaching for superlatives.

Israel opened the tournament in Trento, Italy on Saturday with an overtime thriller against Greece, coming back from nine points down inside the final 90 seconds of regulation to win 93-84. A day later they beat France 91-77, pulling away with a 12-0 run in the third quarter to seal a 2-0 start in Group A.

The headline act has been David Musis, the 18-year-old, 2.10-metre center who has committed to Florida Atlantic. Through two games he is averaging 25.5 points, 13.5 rebounds and 1.5 blocks a game, shooting well from outside for a player his size. Against Greece alone he had 26 points, 19 rebounds, four three-pointers and three blocks.

Musis arrives at the tournament off a domestic season in which he was named MVP of Israel's youth league, and Sport5's coverage from Trento has carried the reaction of scouts and observers who say they cannot recall an Israeli youth team with this combination of size, skill and athleticism.

He has not carried the team alone. Guard Aviv Aronov has been the tournament's leading scorer through two rounds, averaging 30.5 points and 4.5 assists — he scored 30 points with six assists in the win over Greece and added 28 in the France game. Lior Hershko has also stood out, leading the squad with three steals a game.

The Greece game was as dramatic as the U18 championship has produced this year. Israel trailed by nine with a minute and a half left in regulation before clawing back to force overtime, then closing out the extra period to seal the win — 93-84 on the scoreboard, but a far tighter story than that margin suggests.

Aronov described it as an emotional occasion off the court as well as on it. "The sweetest victory there is. We are a generation with very strong character," he said afterward, according to Walla Sport. He added that the team had to deal with a hostile atmosphere before tip-off — "there was a huge protest against Israel with flags and horns, but the guys and I gave everything for the country's sake" — before praising his teammates for not letting the noise affect them.

Head coach Nadav Zilberstein struck a measured tone despite the dramatic finish, noting the number of momentum swings in the game and the pressure on his young players. "This championship is behind us now," he said of the Greece result. "Tomorrow we face the French. Hopefully we'll improve in what we need to improve."

Israel duly delivered against France, controlling the third quarter to turn a tight contest into a comfortable win and move to 2-0 in Group A, alongside Austria and Greece as the teams still involved in a four-team pool completed by France.

The team's next group game is against Austria, with a place in the knockout rounds of the tournament — which runs across Trento and Rovereto through August 2 — very much within reach after the strong start.

For a country whose senior men's team has long punched above its population in European basketball, a youth group generating this level of buzz two games into a continental championship is being read in Israeli basketball circles as a genuine signal for the sport's pipeline over the next several years.

title: Pogačar completes fifth Tour de France title to match cycling's all-time record
dek: The Slovenian sealed overall victory in Paris after a wildfire-shortened final stage, joining Anquetil, Merckx, Hinault and Induráin as five-time winners of cycling's biggest race.

verificationSources.label: Sport5
NPR
Euronews
ESPN
Cyclingnews

body: Tadej Pogačar rode into Paris on Sunday as the outright owner of one of sport's most exclusive records, sealing his fifth overall Tour de France title and drawing level with the four riders long considered untouchable at the top of the sport's history.

The Slovenian finished the 2026 race 6 minutes and 26 seconds clear of Belgium's Remco Evenepoel, with Australia's Jai Hindley completing the podium 9:42 back. It was a margin that, by modern Tour standards, amounted to a rout.

The final stage itself belonged to someone else. Mathieu van der Poel won the sprint into the Champs-Élysées for his second stage victory of this year's race, while Pogačar simply had to stay upright and roll home in the pack to confirm the yellow jersey.

This was not the stage 21 originally planned. Wildfires tearing through southwest France forced organisers to alter three stages of the race, including trimming Sunday's finale from a scheduled 133 kilometres down to roughly 89, a decision made to free up emergency services for deployment to the fire-hit areas rather than for crowd control in Paris.

In winning his fifth Tour, Pogačar joins Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin as the only riders in the race's history to have won it five times — a club that had stood unchanged for more than three decades before this summer.

"I'm speechless. It's an incredible day, there was an incredible atmosphere," Pogačar said after the finish. "I've ridden seven Tours already and I've always finished on the podium. You might think this is a fairytale, it's incredible for me too."

The victory is his third in succession, following triumphs in 2024 and 2025 on top of his breakthrough wins in 2020 and 2021, and it came alongside five individual stage wins across this year's three weeks — a tally that underlines just how thoroughly he dominated the race from the Pyrenees to the Alps.

Elsewhere in the final classifications, Hindley's third place also earned him the white jersey as best young rider, Richard Carapaz took the polka-dot jersey as king of the mountains, and Mads Pedersen claimed the green jersey in the points competition.

Merckx, the Belgian great whose record Pogačar has now equalled, was generous in defeat of his own mark. "I congratulate him, but I believe that he will not only match me and the other champions — he will soon break our record for Tour victories," he said, a suggestion that a sixth title, and outright ownership of the record, may only be a matter of time.

title: Legal or not? Paquito Navarro's net-straddling winner splits the padel world
dek: A viral clip from an exhibition match in Ibiza has fans and pundits arguing over whether the Spanish star's audacious shot, in which he left his paddle hanging over his opponents' side of the net, should have counted at all.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 report
Padel Addict: Paquito Navarro's craftiness at the Ibiza exhibition
Paquito Navarro arrives at Can Pádel Ibiza for clinic and exhibition
Paquito Navarro — Wikipedia

body: Padel's most theatrical showman has done it again. Paquito Navarro, the Seville-born former world No. 1, produced a shot at an exhibition event in Ibiza that has split opinion across the sport: brilliant improvisation to some, a clear breach of the rulebook to others.

The clip, filmed during a clinic and exhibition match Navarro played at Can Pádel Ibiza in the relaxed, crowd-pleasing atmosphere typical of pre-season showcases, shows the ball arriving near the net. Navarro struck it, then left his paddle hanging over the net on his opponents' side as they attempted to play their return, appearing to interfere with the follow-up.

The moment came days before Navarro and his partner, the Argentine Martín Di Nenno, were due to compete in the Premier Padel P1 event in Pretoria, South Africa, and it quickly spread on social media as fans and rivals debated whether the point should ever have stood.

Padel's laws do allow a paddle to finish its swing on the opponent's side of the net, provided two conditions are met: the ball must already have crossed fully onto the striker's side before contact, and neither the paddle nor the player may touch the net or the opposing court during the stroke.

What is explicitly illegal is making contact with the ball before it has crossed the net line — and that is exactly the point of contention in Navarro's shot. Slow-motion replays circulating online have not settled the argument, with the timing of ball and net crossing close enough to read either way depending on the angle.

It is far from the first time the 37-year-old has generated this kind of debate. Navarro, world No. 1 alongside Juan Lebrón in 2019 and now partnered again with Di Nenno, has built a reputation over the years for instinctive, showman-style shots that regularly test the limits of padel's net-crossing rules, on top of run-ins over conduct at official tournaments.

No governing body has ruled on the exhibition point, which carried no competitive consequence, but the clip has reopened a wider conversation among players and coaches about how strictly padel's follow-through rule should be interpreted — and enforced — when the margins are this tight.
facts: Paquito Navarro (Francisco Jesús Navarro Compán), 37, is a Spanish padel player from Seville, world No. 1 in 2019 alongside Juan Lebrón.
He now partners Argentine player Martín Di Nenno on the Premier Padel tour.
The controversial shot occurred during a clinic/exhibition match at Can Pádel Ibiza in mid-July 2026, ahead of the Premier Padel P1 event in Pretoria, South Africa.
Navarro struck the ball near the net and left his paddle extended over his opponents' side, appearing to affect their return attempt.

Padel rules permit a paddle's follow-through to end on the opponent's side of the net, but only if contact was made after the ball fully crossed to the striker's side, and only if the net or opposing court is not touched.
Making contact with the ball before it crosses the net is illegal under the sport's rules; the exact timing in Navarro's shot has not been definitively settled by replays.
No official ruling was issued, as the incident occurred in a non-competitive exhibition match with no result at stake.

title: Abu Fani gets 61 minutes as Red Star Belgrade win Eternal Derby
dek: The Israel international featured for an hour as Dejan Stanković's side beat Vojvodina 3-1 at the Marakana to open their Serbian SuperLiga campaign with a second straight win.

body: Mohammad Abu Fani got 61 minutes of Serbian SuperLiga football on Sunday as Red Star Belgrade beat local rivals Vojvodina 3-1 in the Eternal Derby, opening their league campaign with a second straight win, Sport5 reported.

The match at the Rajko Mitić Stadium, known to everyone in Belgrade as the Marakana, was the second round of the new season. Osman Bukari, Vasilije Kostov and Dimitrije Šarić scored for the hosts, while Nardin Mulahusejnović pulled one back for Vojvodina in the 32nd minute before Šarić settled the contest deep into stoppage time.
Abu Fani started in Red Star's midfield and was withdrawn just past the hour mark as manager Dejan Stanković rotated his side in a derby that was largely settled by half-time.

It is one of the Israel international's first competitive outings since his move to Belgrade. Abu Fani signed for Red Star from Ferencváros on 13 June, agreeing a three-year deal with a club option for a fourth season, and has taken the number 15 shirt.
Stanković, who managed Abu Fani during his own spell in charge at Ferencváros, was said to have pushed hard for the signing after taking over at Red Star.

Abu Fani, 28, came through the Maccabi Haifa academy and won three straight Israeli championships with the club before leaving for Hungary in the summer of 2023. Across three seasons at Ferencváros he won two Nemzeti Bajnokság I titles and a Hungarian Cup, establishing himself as a regular for the Israel national team along the way.
The derby win keeps Red Star perfect after two rounds of the new Serbian SuperLiga season, and Abu Fani will be aiming for a fuller ninety minutes as his integration into Stanković's squad continues.

title: Bee swarm halts Brazilian youth final as players hit the deck
dek: A swarm of bees invaded the pitch during the first leg of the Campeonato Baiano Sub-20 final between Bahia and Fluminense de Feira, forcing players, coaches and match officials to lie flat on the grass in Feira de Santana.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 report

body: Play at the Estádio Joia da Princesa in Feira de Santana stopped this past Saturday not for an injury, a red card or a floodlight failure, but for bees. A swarm invaded the pitch during the first leg of the Campeonato Baiano Sub-20 final between Bahia and Fluminense de Feira, sending players, both benches and the match officials diving flat onto the grass.

Sport5 picked up the scenes under the headline "Watch: final in Brazil stopped because of a bee attack," relaying footage that had already gone viral in Brazil, where images of a football pitch full of prone bodies needed little explanation.

According to Brazilian outlets including Lance!, Correio 24 Horas and A Tarde, the bees arrived roughly ten minutes into the first half, swarming low enough over the turf that the referee halted the game rather than risk mass stings among players and staff.
Ground staff responded by switching on the stadium's irrigation system, spraying the pitch in an attempt to disperse the insects — a low-tech fix that appears to have worked.

Play resumed after a stoppage of around ten minutes, with no injuries reported among players, staff or the crowd inside the venue, one of the older football grounds in Bahia state, dating back to 1953.
Once the match restarted, there was no shortage of goals: Bahia, the youth side of the Salvador club whose first team is based at the Arena Fonte Nova, overwhelmed their hosts 8-0.

The result leaves Bahia in a commanding position for the second leg, scheduled for next Saturday, August 1, back at the Joia da Princesa. Bahia can lose that match by up to seven goals and still be crowned champions of the Campeonato Baiano Sub-20 on aggregate.

Bee interruptions are not unheard of in Brazilian football — a swarm famously halted a match between Corumbaense and Itaporã in 2011, forcing players to the ground in scenes that made headlines well beyond Brazil. Rarely, though, has an entire final been paused this way, which is why Saturday's clip travelled so far beyond Bahia's borders.

Play resumed after about ten minutes with no injuries reported.
Bahia won the match 8-0.
