title: Portland set to become the NBA's outlier as new owner guts the broadcast booth
dek: Sport5 reports Tom Dundon is folding the Trail Blazers' TV and radio operations into one lean unit, cutting veteran voices loose and following the same playbook he used to gut his hockey team's radio booth in 2018.

verificationSources.label: Forbes (Maury Brown) — Under Tom Dundon, Portland Trail Blazers Make Dramatic Cuts To Broadcast Team
Ynet — יפגע באבדיה? הבעלים של פורטלנד הוא הכי קמצן ב-NBA - והאוהדים מודאגים
NBC Sports — It's official: NBA formally approves sale of Trail Blazers to a group led by Tom Dundon

body: Three months into Tom Dundon's ownership of the Portland Trail Blazers, the cost-cutting has reached the broadcast booth. According to Sport5, the Blazers are moving to consolidate their television and radio operations into a single, leaner unit — a restructuring that would make Portland the only franchise in the NBA without fully separate, travelling crews for each medium.

The purge has already claimed several familiar voices. Michael Holton, the team's television analyst for 19 seasons, is out, along with longtime statistician Tom Haberstroh and TV hosts Neil Everett and Jamie Hudson, according to Forbes' Maury Brown, who first laid out the cuts in detail. The contracts of TV play-by-play voice Kevin Calabro and radio's Travis Demers are both up for renewal, with their futures unresolved, while producer Greg Fonseca has already left for a role at NBA Broadcasting.

Under consideration, per the reporting, is a plan to simulcast the television broadcast onto radio and to cover road games remotely rather than sending announcers on the road — a model no NBA team currently runs in full. Twenty-eight of the league's 29 clubs still maintain fully separate TV and radio broadcast teams; only the Toronto Raptors' radio operation skips travel for away games, and even that falls short of a true simulcast.

The blueprint looks familiar to hockey fans. When Dundon took over the Carolina Hurricanes in 2018, he dismantled the radio booth after Hall of Fame voice Chuck Kaiton declined an offer that would have cut his pay by roughly 80 percent, folding radio coverage into a television simulcast that has stayed in place ever since.

The broadcast cuts follow a wave of roughly 70 layoffs across the Blazers' front office since Dundon's group completed its takeover, touching both the basketball operations side and close to a quarter of the business staff — an early sign of how aggressively the new ownership intends to run the numbers on a franchise it paid a reported $4.25 billion to control.

The NBA's Board of Governors unanimously approved that sale on March 30, with Dundon's group — which also includes Portland-based investor Sheel Tyle, Blue Owl Capital co-president Marc Zahr and the Cherng family behind Panda Express — buying an 80 percent stake immediately and the remaining fifth by 2028. The Blazers had been controlled by the estate of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen since his 2018 death, with sale proceeds required to go to charity under the terms of his trust.

The broadcast overhaul fits a wider pattern Ynet has also chronicled in recent weeks: Dundon is reportedly seeking Portland's next head coach for around $1.5 million a year, well under the $7-8 million typically paid to established NBA coaches, and has been unwilling to give interim coach Tiago Splitter the raise he was hoping for after steering a shorthanded roster through the playoffs. The same reporting describes the Blazers skipping free jerseys at a playoff home opener and declining to fly two-way players to road games — small line items, but ones that have unsettled a fan base and staff still adjusting to life after the Allen era.

None of it touches the roster directly, but it lands at an odd moment for a Blazers team increasingly built around Deni Avdija, whose breakout form since his 2024 trade from Washington has made him the closest thing Portland has to an untouchable asset. How far the cost-cutting eventually reaches — and whether it stops at the broadcast booth — looks set to be one of the defining storylines of Dundon's first full season in charge.
facts: Sport5 reports the Dundon-owned Trail Blazers are consolidating TV and radio broadcast operations, on track to become the only NBA team without fully separate travelling broadcast crews, corroborated in detail by Forbes.

On-air departures include TV analyst Michael Holton (19 seasons), statistician Tom Haberstroh, and TV hosts Neil Everett and Jamie Hudson; TV voice Kevin Calabro and radio's Travis Demers have contracts up for renewal with status unresolved; producer Greg Fonseca has left for NBA Broadcasting.
The broadcast cuts follow roughly 70 layoffs across the Blazers' front office since Dundon's group completed its takeover of the team.

The NBA Board of Governors unanimously approved the $4.25 billion sale to Dundon's group on March 30, 2026; the group is buying an 80 percent stake immediately with the remaining 20 percent due by 2028, with proceeds required to go to charity from Paul Allen's estate.

When Dundon bought the Carolina Hurricanes in 2018, he dismantled the radio broadcast team after Hall of Fame announcer Chuck Kaiton declined an approximately 80 percent pay cut, replacing it with a TV simulcast.

Ynet reports additional cost-cutting under Dundon, including seeking a head coach at roughly $1.5 million annually versus a $7-8 million market rate, skipping free playoff jerseys for fans, and not flying two-way contract players to road games.

title: Hapoel Beer Sheva's European Dream Wobbles After Reykjavik Reverse
dek: The reigning Israeli champions must overturn a 2-1 first-leg deficit against Víkingur Reykjavík in Hungary next week, after a defeat in Iceland exposed cracks that had been papered over during the title run.

verificationSources.label: ONE
Haaretz
Walla! Sport
Sport1 Maariv
UEFA.com match page

body: Hapoel Beer Sheva's first taste of Champions League qualifying since reclaiming the Israeli title was a sobering one. The champions lost 2-1 away to Iceland's Víkingur Reykjavík in the first leg of their second qualifying round tie on Tuesday, leaving Ran Kozuch's side needing a comeback in the return leg to keep their European campaign alive.

Nicolai Hansen headed Víkingur in front in the 48th minute, powering in a corner past a Beer Sheva defence that has looked shaky at times even through a title-winning season. The Israelis hit back almost immediately: three minutes later Niv Yehoshua won the ball high up the pitch and teed up Kings Kangwa, who finished to make it 1-1.

Beer Sheva thought they had completed the turnaround in the 77th minute when Yehoshua wheeled away in celebration, only for the goal to be chalked off by VAR for offside. Hansen made the visitors pay nine minutes later, converting again to hand Víkingur a 2-1 win at their own ground.

The tie now moves to Hungary, where Beer Sheva will play their nominal home leg in Szombathely on Wednesday, needing at least a one-goal win to progress and a two-goal margin to avoid extra time. It is familiar territory for Israeli clubs, who have had to stage continental "home" fixtures at neutral European venues in recent seasons.

ONE's analysis of the defeat, aired on the outlet's football podcast, pointed to more than one bad night on an artificial pitch in Reykjavik. Presenters Itzik Kalipi and Dov Gabai flagged defensive lapses that have persisted through the club's rise, and a continuing shortage of a genuine creative attacking midfielder capable of deciding matches at this level.

That last gap has been a talking point in Beer Sheva for months, and according to ONE, reinforcements from the transfer market that might address it have been slow to arrive this summer, even as the club prepares to balance a Champions League push with the defence of its Ligat Ha'al title.

Kozuch, the 45-year-old former Beer Sheva full-back, led the club to the championship in May by beating Maccabi Tel Aviv 4-2, and signed a new contract through 2028 on the back of it. A shaky opening continental night does not erase that achievement, but it does underline, as ONE's analysis put it, the distance still separating this squad from the level the coach will demand of it in Europe.

Kangwa's leveller arrived amid a swirl of transfer talk that has hung over the club all summer. The Zambian midfielder, last season's Israeli Footballer of the Year after scoring 12 goals, is reportedly a target for AEK Athens, with Greek reports cited by ONE putting the Greek champions' offer in the region of €4 million.

Kangwa remains under contract in Beer Sheva until 2028, giving the club leverage in any negotiation, but the interest from Athens is unresolved and neither side has confirmed a deal — a genuine transfer link rather than a completed move.

For now, the more pressing issue is Wednesday's second leg. A win in Hungary would send Beer Sheva into the third qualifying round and keep alive the prospect of Champions League group-stage football and its financial windfall; anything less would drop the champions into the Europa League qualifying path instead, a considerably less lucrative consolation.

title: Spanish public overwhelmingly backs Rodri for the Ballon d'Or
dek: A reader poll finds nearly half of respondents in Spain want Rodri, not Kylian Mbappé, to win this year's Ballon d'Or after his Golden Ball-winning World Cup — even though a serious knee injury wiped out much of his club season.

verificationSources.label: The Score — Rodri takes Golden Ball over Messi; Mbappe claims Golden Boot again
Sky Sports — World Cup 2026 award winners: Did Rodri deserve to win the Golden Ball for best player over Lionel Messi?
Goal.com — Rodri injury return update: Double trophy target for Man City & Spain star as Ballon d'Or winner works his way back from knee ligament damage

body: A reader poll run by the Spanish sports daily Marca has produced a lopsided verdict on this year's Ballon d'Or debate, ONE reports: 49 percent of respondents want Rodri to win it, more than double the 17 percent who backed his nearest challenger, Kylian Mbappé.

Marca put five names to its readers — Rodri, Lamine Yamal, Harry Kane, Lionel Messi and Mbappé — and the Manchester City and Spain midfielder ran away with it. The case for him, as the paper laid it out, is straightforward: Rodri captained Spain to the World Cup title this summer, was named the tournament's outstanding player, and did it while Spain conceded only a single goal across the entire competition.

Spain's run through the tournament ended with a 1-0 win over Argentina in the final, settled by a Ferran Torres goal deep into extra time — the country's second World Cup title, sixteen years after its first in 2010.

It was the second time in as many major tournaments that Rodri picked up the outstanding-player honour: he was also named Player of the Tournament at Euro 2024, when Spain beat England in the final in Berlin. Few midfielders anywhere have strung together two such displays back to back.

What makes the poll notable is how little of it has to do with his club form. Rodri missed roughly half of Manchester City's 2025-26 Premier League season through injury, returning to make only 21 league appearances and finishing the campaign without a trophy at club level — a sharp contrast to the midfield force who helped drive City to a treble two seasons earlier.

The root cause was the anterior cruciate ligament tear he suffered against Arsenal in September 2024, an injury that cost him the best part of a season and left Pep Guardiola managing his return carefully through 2025 as recurring soft-tissue setbacks slowed him down. By Marca's own account, Rodri needed roughly 18 months to work his way back to the level he showed for Spain this summer.

Rodri is not new to this stage. He already won the Ballon d'Or in 2024, edging out Vinícius Júnior in one of the tighter votes in the award's recent history. With the World Cup added to his collection, he has now won the World Cup, the European Championship, the Champions League and the Ballon d'Or — a combination only Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Müller and Zinédine Zidane had achieved before him.

The other names on Marca's list have credentials of their own. Messi, now 39, captained Argentina back to a World Cup final and collected the Silver Ball as the tournament's second-best player; Mbappé topped the scoring charts at both club and international level and picked up the Bronze Ball; Yamal continued the remarkable rise that has made him one of the sport's biggest young stars for both Barcelona and Spain; and Kane's case rests on another prolific season in front of goal for Bayern Munich. But in Spain, for now, none of it has dented the sense that the World Cup settled the argument.

None of this decides anything by itself — the Ballon d'Or is voted on by journalists, not newspaper readers, and the shortlist and ceremony are still months away. But as an early read on how Rodri's World Cup has shifted the conversation in his own country, Marca's numbers are hard to ignore.

Rodri was also named Player of the Tournament at Euro 2024, which Spain also won.

Rodri missed roughly half of Manchester City's 2025-26 Premier League season after tearing his ACL against Arsenal in September 2024, returning to make only 21 league appearances and winning no club trophies that season.
Rodri already holds the Ballon d'Or, having won the 2024 award ahead of Vinícius Júnior.

title: AEK Athens Say Kangwa Pursuit Still 'Active' Despite Reports of Collapse
dek: The Greek club insists its move for Beer Sheva's Zambian midfielder remains alive, even if it costs him early-season European eligibility.

verificationSources.label: ONE
Ynet
Africa Soccer
UEFA.com match record

body: Despite a wave of reports declaring the move dead, AEK Athens have not walked away from their pursuit of Hapoel Beer Sheva midfielder Kings Kangwa, ONE reports. A source close to the Greek club described the transfer as "active and ongoing," even if completing it now costs the Zambian international his eligibility for AEK's own early European ties.

The doubts crept in after Beer Sheva fielded Kangwa in the Champions League second qualifying round first leg against Vikingur Reykjavik, a match the Israeli champions lost 2-1 in Iceland, undone by a brace from the hosts' Hansen.

The complication is a UEFA technicality: a player registered for one club in this season's continental qualifiers cannot turn out for a different club in the same competition until the group or league phase begins. By playing Kangwa against Vikingur, Beer Sheva effectively locked him out of AEK's own European playoff round if the transfer goes through immediately.

That is reportedly what prompted the Greek club's hierarchy, keen to have him available for their own playoff tie, to press Beer Sheva not to use him at all against Vikingur - pressure the Israeli champions resisted, fielding him regardless in a qualifier they needed to win.

Greek media subsequently suggested AEK had cooled on the deal or pulled their offer entirely, turning instead to other midfield options. ONE's report pushes back on that version, framing Athens' interest as undimmed despite the self-inflicted eligibility headache.

On the numbers, the two clubs have been discussing a fee in the region of €3.5 million plus roughly €500,000 in add-ons, with Kangwa said to have reached broad personal terms with AEK worth close to €1 million a year - figures still unconfirmed by either club.

Kangwa, 27, joined Beer Sheva from Red Star Belgrade in July 2024 for a reported €800,000 and is contracted until June 2028. He was voted the club's Footballer of the Year for 2025-26 after scoring 12 goals in a season that ended with Beer Sheva winning the Israeli championship.

Owner Alona Barkat and chief executive Nir Katz have steered the club's handling of the saga, standing firm that a continental qualifier would not be sacrificed to smooth a sale - the stance that produced last week's stand-off over Kangwa's involvement against Vikingur.

Attention now turns to the second leg, with Beer Sheva needing to overturn the first-leg deficit to keep their Champions League run alive. Only once that tie is settled, ONE suggests, is the Kangwa transfer likely to move toward a final resolution.

title: Man United miss out as World Cup star Summerville set for shock Al-Hilal move
dek: Netherlands winger Crysencio Summerville, fresh off a two-goal World Cup, has agreed to join Al-Hilal from West Ham after Manchester United's interest stalled and a rejected bid left Roma walking away.

verificationSources.label: Sky Sports — Crysencio Summerville: Al Hilal reach agreement with West Ham to sign Netherlands international
Yahoo Sports — Saudi splash: Al-Hilal to sign Crysencio Summerville as Premier League giants miss out
Transfermarkt — Al Hilal agree mega-money deal for Crysencio Summerville to beat Man United & Roma

body: Crysencio Summerville spent the World Cup turning himself into one of the Netherlands' most eye-catching performers. Now, according to Sport1 (Maariv), the winger is heading somewhere few had pencilled in a month ago: Riyadh, not Manchester, and not Rome either.

Al-Hilal have reached agreement with West Ham to sign the 24-year-old, Sport1 reports, a deal corroborated by Sky Sports and several other outlets, effectively hijacking a move Roma had spent weeks trying to complete and closing the door on any lingering Premier League ambitions.

Manchester United's name had circled the story for weeks, but Sky Sports reports the interest never amounted to much more than talk — 'nothing progressed beyond initial, exploratory talks,' with any serious United move dependent on first selling Marcus Rashford this summer. That sale never materialised in time, and neither did a bid.

Roma's pursuit was more concrete but ultimately came up short. The Serie A club had an opening offer of roughly £39m (about €46m) rejected by West Ham, and Sky Sports News reports Roma have no plans to raise it to match Al-Hilal's package, turning their attention instead to alternative wing targets including Norway's Antonio Nusa and Andreas Schjelderup.

The fee itself is reported slightly differently across outlets — Sky Sports puts the package at £55m guaranteed plus £5m in add-ons, while other reports have cited figures as high as roughly €80m — but all agree it represents a significant outlay by Saudi Pro League standards, with Summerville set for a medical before signing a long-term contract at Al-Hilal.

Should it go through as reported, the sale would rank as West Ham's third-highest ever, behind only Declan Rice's move to Arsenal and this summer's sale of Mateus Fernandes — underlining how far Summerville's stock has risen since he arrived at the London Stadium.

That rise crystallised at the World Cup. Summerville, capped only a handful of times before the tournament, scored a curling left-footed strike against Japan in a 2-2 draw and then came off the bench against Sweden to set up Cody Gakpo before scoring himself in a 5-1 rout — two goals and two assists in four appearances for a Dutch side that went deep into the tournament.

His form carried into the club game too. Summerville managed seven goals and five assists in 34 Premier League appearances for West Ham in 2025/26, having joined from Leeds United in the summer of 2024 after his own breakout campaign at Elland Road.

For West Ham, cashing in near the peak of Summerville's value fits a familiar pattern of selling their most coveted attacking talent for a premium; for Al-Hilal, it is another marquee name added to a Saudi project that has already reshaped the market for the league's biggest recruits. For Manchester United and Roma, it is one more high-profile miss in a summer transfer window that keeps producing them.

title: Belgrade, 7 April 1977: The night Tal Brody put Israel "on the map"
dek: A neutral-court upset over CSKA Moscow and a one-point final against Varese gave Maccabi Tel Aviv its first European basketball crown — and Israeli sport its most quoted sentence.

verificationSources.label: Wikipedia — 1976–77 FIBA European Champions Cup
Wikipedia — Tal Brody
Tablet Magazine — A New Documentary Details the Basketball Victory That Put Israel 'On The Map'
The Times of Israel — Film on Israeli basketball's 'miracle on hardwood' set to screen in the US
SA Jewish Report — Maccabi's 1977 basketball victory still makes big men cry
The Jerusalem Post — Maccabi, Tal Brody: The 'pride of Israel' was made in Belgrade

body: The scoreboard read 78-77, the clock had run out, and Tal Brody was already hoisting the European Champions Cup over his head in Belgrade's Pionir Hall when he said the sentence Israelis have been repeating for almost fifty years: "We are on the map! And we are staying on the map — not only in sports, but in everything." It was 7 April 1977, and Maccabi Tel Aviv had just beaten the Italian champions Mobilgirgi Varese by a single point to win the country's first European club title in any team sport.

The road to that Belgrade final had run, improbably, through a small gymnasium in Belgium. Since the Six-Day War of 1967, the Soviet Union had severed diplomatic relations with Israel and thrown its political weight behind Israel's Arab neighbours. When the draw for the 1976-77 European Champions Cup semi-final group paired Maccabi Tel Aviv with the Soviet army club CSKA Moscow, neither government would permit the match on its own soil — Moscow refused to host the Israelis, and the Soviets refused to travel to Tel Aviv. FIBA settled on neutral ground: the border town of Virton, Belgium.

On 17 February 1977, in front of a crowd that Israeli newspapers gleefully described as an underdog's dream — a nation of some three and a half million against a Soviet superpower of nearly 260 million — Maccabi routed the heavily favoured CSKA side 91-79. Much of Israel watched on its single state-run television channel. The Belgian gym had become, for one night, the unlikely front line of a Cold War morality play, and Israel had won it.

The victory landed at a raw moment in Israeli life. Barely four years earlier, the Yom Kippur War had shaken the country's sense of security; not five years earlier, eleven members of the Israeli Olympic delegation had been murdered at the Munich Games. Tal Brody, the team's American-born captain, later said the team "took the country out of mourning" that winter. Whatever the scoreline, the CSKA upset carried a weight that went well beyond a basketball semi-final.

Two months on, Maccabi arrived in Belgrade for the final against Mobilgirgi Varese, the reigning Italian champions and clear favourites on paper. The team Ralph Klein had built blended homegrown talent with adopted sons: Brody, a former University of Illinois All-American who had turned down a shot at the NBA to build the game in Israel; Miki Berkovich, the sharp-shooting guard who would go on to a Hall of Fame career; and Aulcie Perry, the New Jersey-born centre who had arrived in Israel only the year before and would become one of the most beloved figures in the club's history.

The final itself was as tight as the season that preceded it. Maccabi held off Varese's late surge to win 78-77, sealing the club's first European Champions Cup — the forerunner of today's EuroLeague — in the competition's twentieth edition. It was, at the time, the single biggest achievement in Israeli international sport.

What has outlasted the score, though, is the line Brody delivered on the podium. "On the map, and staying on the map" became shorthand for a country insisting on its place in the world, quoted in political speeches, television commercials and school textbooks for decades afterward. Few sentences in Israeli sport have travelled as far from the court where they were spoken.

The team's return home was itself a small piece of theatre: photographs from the reception show Brody and his teammates paraded through Tel Aviv to a public still savouring the upset, the entertainer Uri Zohar among those greeting them off the plane. The club would go on to add another Champions Cup title in 1981 and further EuroLeague crowns in the decades that followed, but 1977 remained the one that changed the conversation.

Almost fifty years later, the run through Virton and Belgrade is still the subject of documentary films and retrospectives, most notably Dani Menkin's "On the Map", which traced the story through the eyes of the Americans who came to Tel Aviv to help build it. For a country then just three decades old, still counting its losses from Munich and the Yom Kippur War, a basketball team's improbable run through a Belgian gym and a Belgrade final offered something rarer than a trophy: proof, delivered on the biggest stage the sport then had, that Israel belonged.
facts: Maccabi Tel Aviv beat CSKA Moscow 91-79 in a European Champions Cup semi-final group game played on neutral ground in Virton, Belgium, on 17 February 1977, after the USSR refused to allow the match in Tel Aviv or Moscow following the severing of Soviet-Israeli relations after the 1967 Six-Day War.

Maccabi Tel Aviv beat Mobilgirgi Varese 78-77 in the final of the 1976-77 European Champions Cup, played at the Pionir Hall in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, on 7 April 1977 — the club's and Israel's first European basketball title.

Team captain Tal Brody declared afterward, "We are on the map! And we are staying on the map — not only in sports, but in everything," a line that became one of the most quoted in Israeli public life.
The championship-winning roster included captain Tal Brody, guard Miki Berkovich and centre Aulcie Perry, coached by Ralph Klein.

The victory came against the backdrop of the 1972 Munich Olympics massacre and the 1973 Yom Kippur War, both cited by Brody and later documentarians as part of why the win resonated so deeply in Israel.
Director Dani Menkin's documentary "On the Map" chronicles the team's 1976-77 European campaign.

title: Scaloni brushes off Messi's viral locker-room video, says stars will now 'rethink' their futures
dek: Argentina's coach denied any dressing-room rift after the World Cup final loss to Spain and would not rule out Messi and Emiliano Martínez stepping back from the national team.

verificationSources.label: Fox Sports
ESPN match report
Bolavip

body: Two days after Spain snatched the World Cup from Argentina's grasp in extra time, Lionel Scaloni finally addressed the video that had consumed Argentine football since the final whistle: Lionel Messi's pre-match dressing-room address to his teammates, which spread rapidly online and fuelled theories about what went wrong in New Jersey.

Spain beat the defending champions 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium on July 19, with Ferran Torres converting the decisive goal in the 105th minute to hand La Roja their second World Cup title and first since 2010.

Footage circulating since the loss shows Messi gathering his teammates before kickoff, telling them, "Calm, let's stay calm, lads," and, "Let's forget about everything," as he tried to settle the squad's nerves. The clip's unusually tense tone set off speculation among fans and pundits back home about strain inside the camp.
Scaloni waved the theory away. "I don't see networks. I know nothing. I have no idea what you are telling me," he said, distancing himself from the online storm.
Pressed on suggestions of a rift inside the squad, he was equally blunt: "I can't believe what you are asking me. We are going another way, guys."
He was warmer about his players' effort in the final itself. "The important thing is that the boys gave their all, they showed character with this shirt, and let's keep that," he said.

The bigger question hanging over Argentine football is what comes next. Scaloni, who has led the team since 2018 and delivered the 2022 World Cup before this runners-up finish, confirmed only that his contract carries him through December. "Until December we are here," he said, without saying whether he intends to continue into World Cup qualifying beyond that.

He was similarly non-committal about Messi's future and that of goalkeeper Emiliano "Dibu" Martínez, both of whom have faced retirement questions for months. "After a tournament like this, with everything happening naturally, I think one starts to rethink things," Scaloni said, acknowledging the pair are likely weighing their own next steps.

The coach's composure gave way once he reached his hometown of Pujato, in Santa Fe province, where hundreds turned out to greet him. Visibly moved, he told the crowd: "We did not manage to win. We know that we play to make our people happy, and that is why the pain is great."

He credited Spain rather than looking for excuses. "Sometimes you win, and other times you lose. We have to admit that Spain played better, and that makes us better too," he said, as fans in the crowd chanted that Messi would not leave the national team.

Argentina are next scheduled to play friendlies in September and October — matches that could offer the first hints of whether Scaloni, Messi and Martínez intend to stay on for the next World Cup cycle, or whether Sunday's final in New Jersey was the last act for this generation.

title: Ibrahimović's parting shot: "I'd have headbutted Paredes" over final brawl
dek: In his last appearance as a Fox Sports pundit, Zlatan Ibrahimović tore into Argentina's Leandro Paredes for the ugly scenes that closed out the World Cup final — and asked why Spain's players just stood and watched.

verificationSources.label: Sport1 (Maariv) — original report

body: Zlatan Ibrahimović was never going to bow out of World Cup punditry quietly, and he didn't. On what turned out to be his last day in the Fox Sports studio, the former Barcelona and Sweden striker said that if he had been on the pitch during Sunday's ugly closing scenes at MetLife Stadium, he would have headbutted Leandro Paredes himself — and taken the red card without complaint.

"Paredes can be happy there was no player like me on the pitch," Ibrahimović said, in comments reported by Sport1 and corroborated by Fox Sports' own account of the broadcast. "If I had been there, I would have headbutted him and been sent off. It is unprofessional behavior from him."

The remark was aimed at the chaos that followed the final whistle of Spain's 1-0 extra-time win over Argentina, sealed by substitute Ferran Torres' 106th-minute goal. Argentina had already been reduced to ten men after Enzo Fernández's dismissal when full time arrived, and Paredes was shown a second red card of the night for Argentina after a physical confrontation involving Spain's Eric García and Gavi.

Ibrahimović didn't stop at Paredes. He turned his fire on Spain's own players for failing to step in, telling viewers: "I don't know what the Spanish players are doing? They are just watching another player hit their teammate." It was a pointed complaint from a player whose own career was built on never backing down from confrontation.

The comments carried extra weight given who was making them. Ibrahimović spent parts of two seasons at Barcelona and remains one of the most recognizable — and combative — figures to have played for the club, giving his verdict on a brawl involving a Barcelona-heavy Spain side an added edge.

He used the same appearance to announce he was stepping away from the punditry role altogether. "This is my last visit to the studio. For me, this was the first and last time," he told his Fox Sports colleagues, thanking Thierry Henry, Alexi Lalas and Rebecca Lowe along with the network and its viewers for the tournament.

The brawl itself has already triggered a formal response from football's governing body: FIFA opened disciplinary proceedings into Argentina's conduct in the aftermath of the final, with Paredes among the players facing scrutiny.

For all his criticism of the post-match scenes, Ibrahimović was unambiguous about the result itself, crediting Spain's defensive discipline and overall football over the course of the match as the difference-maker in a final Argentina managed just a handful of shots in.

Ibrahimović's sign-off adds one more voice — arguably the loudest yet — to a chorus of former players and pundits who have said the ugly aftermath overshadowed what was, for 106 minutes, a tightly contested final between the world's two best teams.

title: Report: Ronaldo's Portugal career set to end against Wales on September 24
dek: A Portuguese agent, cited by journalist Mohammed Awaad, says the 41-year-old plans to bow out of international football at Alvalade in a Nations League tie against Wales, closing the book on 233 caps and 146 goals.

verificationSources.label: Goal.com

body: Cristiano Ronaldo's international farewell may already have a fixture attached to it. According to a report carried by Sport1, an unnamed Portuguese agent has told journalist Mohammed Awaad that Ronaldo intends to play his final match for Portugal in September's UEFA Nations League tie against Wales.

The venue, per the report, would be the Estádio José Alvalade in Lisbon on September 24 — a ground with personal resonance for Ronaldo, whose senior career began just up the road at Sporting CP's academy before he left for Manchester United in 2003.

It is important to be clear about what this is: a report relayed through an agent, not a statement from Ronaldo, the Portuguese federation or Al-Nassr. Portugal have not confirmed a farewell fixture, and Ronaldo himself has repeatedly declined to put a firm date on his international exit.

The speculation follows Portugal's exit from the 2026 World Cup earlier this month, beaten 1-0 by Spain in the round of 16 after a Mikel Merino goal deep in stoppage time. Ronaldo was visibly emotional afterwards, applauding fans around the pitch in Arlington, Texas.

"It's normal, sad, to leave the World Cup like this," he said in the aftermath. "But, as I said yesterday at the press conference, I gave it my all, I gave my best. And I leave with a clear conscience." He stopped short of confirming it was his last game for Portugal, saying he did not want to make that call in the heat of the moment — though he had already confirmed this World Cup would be his last as a tournament.

Portugal have since moved on under new head coach Jorge Jesus, who took the job on a four-year contract and has signalled he won't be tearing up the squad Ronaldo has anchored for two decades. "I'm not stupid," Jesus said of wholesale changes. "On top of that, I don't have enough time to bring in several players who weren't called up this time."

Whenever it comes, the end will close out a record no one is likely to threaten. Ronaldo has 233 caps and 146 goals for Portugal, both the most in the history of men's international football, spanning a European Championship win in 2016 and two Nations League titles, in 2019 and 2025.

Off the pitch, Ronaldo remains under contract with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia through the summer of 2027 and has made clear he wants to reach 1,000 career goals for club and country before he stops playing altogether — a landmark that, at his current pace, could arrive before this season is out.

If the September 24 date holds, it would give Portuguese fans a proper send-off at a stadium Ronaldo knows intimately, rather than the anticlimactic ending in Texas. For now, though, it remains one agent's account of a decision only Ronaldo has the authority to make.

title: Report: Trump Wants FIFA's Infantino as Next UN Secretary-General
dek: Sport5, citing the New York Post, reports that Donald Trump is pushing for his World Cup partner Gianni Infantino to succeed António Guterres at the United Nations — a proposal that would need to clear a Security Council veto gauntlet.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 — original report
Haberler.com — corroborating report citing New York Post

body: Donald Trump's alliance with Gianni Infantino has already given the FIFA president an office in Trump Tower and a seat of honour at the World Cup he helped stage. Now, according to a New York Post report picked up by Sport5, the U.S. president wants to hand him one of the most powerful jobs in global diplomacy: United Nations Secretary-General.

The post falls vacant at the end of the year. António Guterres, in the role since 2017, is due to complete his second term on December 31, 2026, and the process to choose his successor — who would take office on January 1, 2027 — is already under way at UN headquarters in New York.

Trump's reported thinking, per the Post, is straightforward: he sees the 56-year-old Infantino as "respected worldwide" and gifted at "bringing people together," qualities forged, in the president's view, through Infantino's stewardship of the expanded, 48-team World Cup that the United States co-hosted this year.

The two men have built an unusually close relationship since Trump returned to office. Infantino has visited the Oval Office repeatedly, FIFA opened a satellite office inside Trump Tower, and in December the governing body handed Trump its brand-new, inaugural FIFA Peace Prize — a gesture Infantino defended publicly, saying the president deserved recognition for his role in brokering a Gaza ceasefire.

None of that affection translates automatically into a UN post, however. A Secretary-General cannot simply be nominated by one head of state; the appointment requires the backing of the UN Security Council, where any one of the five permanent members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France — can kill a candidacy with a single veto, before the choice goes to the General Assembly for confirmation.

That gauntlet already appears to be shaping the wider race. Other names floated for the job, including former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet and Argentina's Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, are each said to face their own veto risks — Bachelet reportedly facing U.S. resistance, Grossi a potential British objection tied to the Falklands dispute.

There is also an obvious tension in the idea. Trump has long been one of the UN's sharpest critics, once dismissing it as a club where "people talk, people have a good time, but nothing gets solved." His administration pulled the U.S. out of the UN Human Rights Council and UNESCO and cut funding to UNRWA — hardly the resume of a president eager to strengthen the body he now reportedly wants Infantino to lead.

Infantino himself has not publicly addressed the report. FIFA's presidency is an elected position, and he would presumably need to give up football's top job to pursue a UN role — a step with no indication, so far, that he is willing or able to take.

For now, this reads as a Trump-driven idea rather than a formal nomination: floated through the press, resting on a friendship built around a World Cup and a Peace Prize, and facing a Security Council process built specifically to stop any single leader from installing his preferred candidate unopposed.

title: FIFA banks record $15 billion from 2026 World Cup, nearly double Qatar's haul
dek: Gianni Infantino told FIFA's membership in Manhattan that the expanded, 48-team tournament in North America shattered every financial benchmark in the governing body's history, powered by soaring broadcast, sponsorship and ticket revenue.

verificationSources.label: Sport1 (Maariv) — original report

body: FIFA has confirmed what its own marketing department could barely have dreamed of a decade ago: the 2026 World Cup is the most financially successful tournament the organisation has ever staged, with revenue crossing the $15 billion mark for the four-year cycle.

Sport1 reports that the precise figure stands at $15.2 billion, a number Gianni Infantino delivered personally to FIFA's member associations at the Waldorf Astoria in Manhattan on the eve of the final — a deliberately symbolic setting, and a deliberately triumphant message, before the showpiece kicked off across the river at MetLife Stadium.

The scale of the jump is what makes the figure remarkable. FIFA's Qatar 2022 cycle brought in roughly $7.5 billion, meaning the North American edition has essentially doubled the governing body's income in a single World Cup cycle — a growth rate almost unheard of in global sport.

Two structural changes explain most of it, according to the report: the tournament's expansion to 48 teams and 104 matches, and the decision to stage the bulk of it in the United States, a market built around premium pricing, corporate hospitality and aggressive commercial packaging in a way European or Gulf hosts never quite replicated.

Broadcasting deals and sponsorship packages both grew sharply against the Qatar cycle, but it was ticketing — and especially the resale market — that produced some of the tournament's most eye-catching numbers. On FIFA's own resale platform, Category 1 seats for the final opened at around $11,700, with some listings reported elsewhere climbing into six and even seven figures for premium seats.

That kind of pricing drew grumbling from fans and some pointed criticism of FIFA's dynamic-pricing model, but by the governing body's own account it barely dented demand in a U.S. market accustomed to premium sports economics.

"Football is a sport, but it is also a business," the report quotes, framing the $15 billion-plus figure as, in FIFA's own words, the clearest proof yet that its bet on an American-centred, market-driven World Cup had paid off.

Infantino used the announcement to promise the windfall would flow back into the game: FIFA's Forward development fund, which distributes money to all 211 member associations, is projected to rise to $2.7 billion for the 2027-2030 cycle — an eightfold increase since the programme's launch.

The financial announcement landed just after the football itself wrapped up. Spain beat Argentina in the final at MetLife Stadium on July 19 to close out the expanded tournament, capping a month that FIFA will now point to as the commercial template for future World Cups.

body: Barely a day after Argentina's World Cup final unravelled into red cards, a brawl and a snubbed trophy ceremony, FIFA president Gianni Infantino chose a very different tone: warmth, not censure.

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium, with substitute Ferran Torres scoring the winner in the 106th minute. Argentina had already been reduced to ten men after Enzo Fernández was sent off in the 93rd minute for a reckless challenge on Barcelona defender Pau Cubarsí.

The aftermath was ugly. A brawl broke out between players from both sides moments after the final whistle, Leandro Paredes was also shown red following a confrontation with assistant referee Tomaž Klančnik, and Nicolás Otamendi squared up to Spain captain Rodri over complaints about the officiating.

As Spain's players collected their medals and lifted the trophy, Argentina's squad turned their backs on the ceremony, walking to the far side of the pitch while chants of Lionel Messi's name rang out from their own supporters in the stands.

Against that backdrop, Infantino posted a message on Instagram that steered entirely clear of the controversy and instead saluted Argentina's run to the final. "What an exceptional tournament the Argentina national team delivered at the World Cup! An unforgettable comeback and a fighting spirit that inspired millions, and gave football fans around the world timeless moments that will not be erased from memory," he wrote.

He went further, framing the runners-up finish as proof of the team's enduring class: "Reaching the World Cup final once again, after winning the title in 2022, is the best proof of excellence and the sustained high level of Argentine football."

It wasn't the first time in this tournament that Infantino had gone out of his way to praise Messi's side. After Argentina's dramatic semi-final win over England in Atlanta, he had posted a similarly effusive Instagram note calling it "an intense, emotional and incredible" match and praising both sets of fans for the atmosphere.

What Infantino's latest message notably did not do is address the ugly scenes that closed out the final - the red cards, the brawl or the snub of the podium ceremony - leaving open the question of whether FIFA will pursue any disciplinary action over the post-match conduct.
For Argentina, the defeat still means a second consecutive World Cup final appearance, a run bookended by the 2022 title in Qatar and Sunday's loss to a Spain side chasing their second world crown.

title: Kangwa levels for Hapoel in Iceland but barely celebrates amid AEK transfer talks
dek: The Zambian forward salvaged a 1-1 draw for Hapoel Beer Sheva at Víkingur Reykjavík in the Champions League, and his muted reaction was read in Athens as another sign of how close he already is to joining AEK.

verificationSources.label: Sport1 (Maariv) — original report

body: Kings Kangwa did something on a football pitch in Reykjavík on Tuesday night that transfer gossip rarely allows for: he scored a genuinely important goal and looked almost embarrassed about it.

Hapoel Beer Sheva were trailing Víkingur Reykjavík in the first leg of their Champions League second qualifying round tie when Kangwa pounced on a loose ball inside the box in the second half and drove it home to make it 1-1, the final score in Iceland. Víkingur had gone ahead through Nikolaj Hansen before the leveler arrived.

It should have been a moment of relief for a Hapoel side chasing a European run. Instead, Greek outlets zeroed in on what Kangwa did next — very little. ERT Sports' headline summed up the mood in Athens succinctly: Kangwa scored, but Hapoel Beer Sheva 'didn't smile.' He was substituted after 71 minutes.

The subdued reaction is being read across Greece as one more data point in a transfer saga that has gripped AEK Athens for weeks. The Super League champions have been negotiating to sign the 27-year-old Zambian, and according to Greek reporting the two clubs are close: AEK have offered in the region of €3.5 million to Hapoel Beer Sheva, with personal terms on a three-year contract worth roughly €750,000 a season plus bonuses already agreed with the player.

That deal appeared to hit a snag when Hapoel opted to field Kangwa in Tuesday's qualifier rather than hold him back. Greek reports said AEK had briefly stepped back from the move once it became clear he would play — featuring in Champions League qualifying now would restrict his European eligibility for AEK this season, since he would only be registrable for the Greek club from the league phase onward, missing any playoff round.

But Athens outlets were careful not to call the move dead. Sportal.gr reported that the Kangwa case 'is not entirely off the table,' citing both head coach Marko Nikolić's regard for the player and Kangwa's own stated wish to complete the switch.

Nikolić's opinion carries weight inside the AEK dressing room right now. The Serbian led the club to the Greek Super League title in his first season in charge, was named the division's Coach of the Season for 2025/26, and signed a contract extension through 2029 last month.

For Hapoel Beer Sheva, Kangwa has been close to indispensable since rejoining the club in the summer of 2024. He was part of the squad that won the Israeli State Cup in 2024/25 and the Israeli Premier League title in 2025/26, a campaign in which the club credited him as its outstanding attacking presence.

None of that resolves the immediate football problem. The tie with Víkingur Reykjavík is level after the first leg, and Hapoel now have to finish the job in the return fixture with a player whose head — by the evidence of Tuesday night's celebration, or lack of one — may already be halfway to Athens.

title: Hapoel Katamon Jerusalem Set for Historic Champions League Debut Against PAOK
dek: The reigning Israeli women's champions play their first-ever European match on Wednesday, facing Greek side PAOK in Veria with a place in the next qualifying round at stake.

body: Hapoel Katamon Jerusalem's women will step onto a European pitch for the first time in the club's history on Wednesday, opening the UEFA Women's Champions League's first qualifying round against Greek champions PAOK Salonika in Veria.

Kickoff at the Veria Municipal Stadium is set for 18:30 Israel time, with the winner advancing to a second qualifying-round meeting with Hungary's Ferencváros — the format is a compact mini-tournament, with the losing side dropping into a third-place playoff rather than being eliminated outright.

The occasion caps a rapid rise for a club that only fielded a senior women's team from the 2020-21 season, when it started out in Israel's third tier. Hapoel Katamon Jerusalem won their first Israeli women's league title in the 2025-26 campaign, edging out perennial rivals Kiryat Gat, which is what earned the European ticket in the first place.

Head coach Tzach Shamroni described a squad buzzing with anticipation before the trip. "There is great excitement for the historic debut of the team in Europe. We worked very hard last season to reach this position," he said, according to Sport5 — adding that the target for Wednesday is simple: "The goal is clear — victory."

Jerusalem reinforced over the close season with an eye on exactly this kind of test, bringing in Costa Rican goalkeeper Daniela Solera and Brazilian forward Raiza alongside homegrown additions Ella Ben-Tzvi and Tal Feingzicht, Sport5 reports.

PAOK arrive as one of Greece's leading women's sides and will start favourites on paper, but Sport5 notes organisers are expecting a travelling contingent of Israeli supporters in Veria for what the club is treating as a landmark occasion regardless of Wednesday's result.

A win would send Hapoel Katamon Jerusalem into Saturday's mini-tournament final against Ferencváros with a real shot at reaching the second qualifying round of a major European competition in the club's very first attempt — a first for Israeli women's club football.

body: Hapoel Beersheba's return to the Champions League got off to a painful start on Tuesday night, as the Israeli champions went down 2-1 away to Vikingur Reykjavik in the first leg of their second qualifying round tie in Iceland.

Nikolaj Hansen struck twice for the Icelandic champions, either side of a second-half leveller from Kings Kangwa, to hand Vikingur the advantage heading into next week's return fixture, which Sport5 reports will be played in Hungary rather than at Beersheba's usual home ground.

Kangwa pulled Beersheba level shortly after the interval, continuing the sharp scoring form that has made him the club's talisman over the past two seasons. It was not enough, though, as Hansen's second goal, deep in the second half, restored Vikingur's lead and ultimately won them the first leg.

According to Sport5, Kangwa posted a short message after the final whistle pledging that Beersheba would give everything in the second leg, telling supporters the team would fight to turn the tie around next week.

Head coach Ran Kozuk was quoted by the outlet acknowledging the difficulty of facing what he called a well-drilled, quality Vikingur side playing in their 15th season in this format, but stressed the equation was now simple: Beersheba must win next week to advance.

The defeat is a setback for a Beersheba side that enters the new season on the back of a Israeli Premier League title, but the tie is far from over — away goals and a full 90 minutes remain to close the gap.

Kangwa's evening continues a turbulent summer for the 26-year-old, whose future has been the subject of persistent transfer speculation, including reported interest from AEK Athens. For now, though, his focus and his goals remain firmly with Beersheba's European campaign.

title: Maccabi Haifa Goalkeeper Kayouf Ruptures Achilles Before Season Even Starts

body: Maccabi Haifa's preseason has taken a grim turn. Goalkeeper Sharif Kayouf tore his Achilles tendon in Tuesday's friendly against Hapoel Kfar Saba, a match Haifa lost heavily, 5-0, according to Sport5.

Kayouf needed assistance from the club's medical staff to leave the field after going down, and the initial fears were confirmed by an MRI scan showing a full tendon rupture, Sport5 reported. He will now require surgery and is expected to miss the entire season before a competitive ball has even been kicked.

The injury lands at an awkward moment for the 25-year-old. Sport5 reports he had spent several weeks waiting for Maccabi Haifa's clearance to join Hapoel Ramat Gan, a move now thrown into doubt by the severity of the injury.
Kayouf was not the only casualty of the friendly. Brazilian defender Pedrão also picked up a knock during the first half and was withdrawn, replaced by Eder Gaitán, per the same report.

Kayouf, from the Druze town of Isfiya, has been part of Maccabi Haifa's setup since signing his first professional contract with the club in 2019, working his way up through loan spells at Hapoel Kfar Shalem and Hapoel Afula before establishing himself as a squad goalkeeper in the Israeli Premier League. He has also represented Israel at youth level through the U21s.

With Kayouf sidelined long-term, Haifa will need to sort out its goalkeeping options before the competitive season begins — one more problem to manage after a lopsided defeat in a match that was supposed to be about building form, not losing personnel.

title: Versano Breaks Israeli U18 Hurdles Record as Afrifah Completes Sprint Double in Jerusalem
dek: Hila Versano set a new national under-18 mark in the 400m hurdles and Marcy Afrifah swept the 100m and 200m as the Israeli Athletics Championship closed out at Givat Ram Stadium.

verificationSources.label: ONE

body: Jerusalem's Givat Ram Stadium closed out the Israeli Athletics Championship on Tuesday with two of the meet's sharpest storylines saved for last: a national under-18 record from Hila Versano and a sprint double from Marcy Afrifah.
Versano, who runs for Maccabi Tel Aviv, clocked 59.53 seconds in the women's 400m hurdles to break the Israeli record for girls under 18. She crossed the line second overall in the race itself.

The race went to Noa Levi, the country's dominant 400m hurdler of recent seasons, who won comfortably. ONE's report puts her winning time at 48.82 seconds — a figure that would obliterate the world record and is almost certainly a misprint — so we're not repeating that number here pending confirmation from the Israel Athletics Association.

None of that takes away from Versano's night. Breaking a national age-group record while finishing runner-up to an established senior champion is exactly the kind of result that points to genuine depth building behind Israel's top hurdlers.

In the sprints, Marcy Afrifah completed a clean double over 100m and 200m. ONE did not report her winning time in the 100m, but in the 200m she held off rival Alina Drotman for the second time this season, stopping the clock at 24.19 seconds.

Afrifah, who also competes for Maccabi Tel Aviv, is the younger sister of Blessing Afrifah, Israel's European U23 200m champion and a 2024 Olympian — sprinting pedigree that now runs through the family.

The men's 200m went to Gal Ard in 20.68 seconds, while the long jump produced the day's most dramatic finish: Yishai Efraimov trailed for most of the competition before leaping 7.66m on his sixth and final attempt to overtake both Eden Sela and Nikita Mirkin, who had each reached 7.44m.

Romi Tamir added a jumps double of her own, following her long jump title with gold in the triple jump at 13.12m. Noam Mamo took the men's 800m in 1:53.50, and Kroan Halabi-Kabalan closed out a distance double, backing up Monday's 1,500m win with victory in the women's 800m in 2:07.09.
For Israeli track and field, though, it's Versano's mark that will carry furthest — a new bar for the country's under-18 hurdlers, set on the biggest stage the domestic calendar offers.

title: Partizan Belgrade joins Hapoel Jerusalem in race for Wendell Moore Jr.
dek: The Serbian giant is chasing the free-agent forward as a replacement for the departed Sterling Brown, putting it in direct competition with Hapoel Jerusalem for the 24-year-old NBA journeyman.

body: Hapoel Jerusalem's pursuit of Wendell Moore Jr. just got more complicated. ONE reports that Partizan Belgrade has entered the race for the 24-year-old American forward, turning what looked like a straightforward Israeli signing into a competitive chase.

Hapoel Jerusalem had already flagged Moore as a target for the coming season, according to the report. Now the Serbian EuroLeague power wants him too, and Partizan carries obvious pull: bigger stage, bigger money, and the promise of Europe's top continental competition.

Partizan's interest is not just a rumor picked up second-hand. The Belgrade sports outlet FanSport reported separately that the club sees Moore as its primary target to replace Sterling Brown, the guard-forward who left Partizan over the summer. FanSport described Moore as a modern, multi-positional defender who thrives in transition — exactly the profile Partizan is said to be missing on the wing.

Moore, 1.96 meters tall, arrives with a real basketball pedigree even if his NBA career never quite settled. He won the Julius Erving Award as college basketball's top small forward in 2022, capping a breakout junior season at Duke in which he averaged 13.4 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.4 assists while shooting 50 percent from the field.

The Dallas Mavericks took him 26th overall in the 2022 NBA Draft, but he never played for them — he was dealt to the Houston Rockets as part of the Christian Wood trade before the season even began, then moved again to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Since then Moore has bounced between rosters and two-way deals, appearing for the Detroit Pistons, the Charlotte Hornets and the Boston Celtics, with stints in the G League for the Iowa Wolves, the Greensboro Swarm and the Maine Celtics. That path — flashes of promise, no fixed NBA home — is precisely why he is now available to European suitors.

For Hapoel Jerusalem, adding a defender of Moore's draft pedigree and college accolades would be a statement signing ahead of a season in which the club will again try to compete on multiple fronts domestically and in the EuroCup. Losing him to Partizan, by contrast, would be a reminder of how often Israeli clubs find themselves outbid once a bigger European name joins the conversation.
Nothing is finalized. Both interests are still at the reported stage, and Moore remains unsigned as talks are believed to continue on more than one front.

title: Chelsea complete British transfer-record signing of Morgan Rogers

body: Chelsea have officially completed the signing of Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117 million, ONE reported, a fee that makes the 23-year-old England international the most expensive player in British football history.

The deal also becomes Chelsea's own record purchase, surpassing the £115 million they paid Brighton for Moises Caicedo in 2023, and was confirmed by the club itself in an official statement on chelseafc.com rather than left as unconfirmed transfer talk.

"I'm so excited. For me, Chelsea are the biggest club in London and a club I've always admired since I was a kid," Rogers said in Chelsea's announcement. "I'm really excited about the project with the new manager, the players we've got and where the club is heading."
Rogers has signed a long-term contract running to 2033, tying him to Stamford Bridge for years to come as Chelsea continue to build a young, high-ceiling squad around head coach Xabi Alonso.

Sky Sports and ESPN, both reporting the same £117 million figure, noted that Rogers had also been a top target for Arsenal but ultimately opted for Chelsea, with Alonso's project said to be a decisive factor in his decision.

At Villa, Rogers will be remembered for a remarkable rise: signed from Middlesbrough in 2024 for a fraction of his eventual sale price, he broke through under Unai Emery and became one of the Premier League's most productive attacking midfielders.
In the 2025-26 season alone he scored 14 goals and added 12 assists in 55 appearances, helping Villa qualify for the Champions League while also lifting the Europa League trophy.

At Chelsea, Rogers reunites with Cole Palmer, a former teammate from their days together in Manchester City's academy, giving Alonso two attacking players with a shared history at the heart of his rebuild.

Rogers has become a regular fixture for England since his senior debut in November 2024, winning 22 caps and featuring for the Three Lions at this summer's World Cup, including appearances against Ghana and Panama.
The size of the fee has already stirred debate in the English game over transfer inflation, but for Chelsea it underlines the scale of their ambition under Alonso heading into the 2026/27 season.

title: Ronaldo Likes Instagram Post Accusing FIFA of Rigging World Cup for Argentina
dek: Days after Portugal's own elimination, Cristiano Ronaldo's verified account liked a Spanish TV clip branding FIFA a "mafia" that favored Lionel Messi's Argentina all the way to the final.

verificationSources.label: ONE
LADbible

body: Cristiano Ronaldo's World Cup ended in Dallas on July 6, beaten by the country that would go on to lift the trophy itself. Two weeks later he was back in the headlines anyway, not for anything he did on a pitch but for what his thumb did on Instagram.

Ronaldo's verified account liked a video post from the Spanish breakfast show Espejo Público, aired on Antena 3, that accused FIFA of tilting the tournament in Argentina's favor and openly floated the idea of institutional corruption at the sport's governing body.

The clip centered on remarks from journalist Pilar Rodríguez Losantos, who told viewers "Argentina should have been eliminated at least five matches ago," and suggested FIFA president Gianni Infantino's organization wanted to see the trophy handed to Lionel Messi.
Fellow panelist Rubén Amón went further on air, describing FIFA as "a mafia organization, shameful and corrupt" in his assessment of how the tournament had been managed.

The segment aired in the buildup to the final, but Ronaldo's like registered publicly only after Argentina's run actually ended — a coincidence of timing that turned an obscure Spanish talk-show clip into a global talking point almost overnight.

Ronaldo's own tournament had already finished in the round of 16, where Spain beat Portugal 1-0 at Dallas Stadium on a stoppage-time strike from substitute Mikel Merino — a defeat widely described as the last World Cup match of Ronaldo's international career.

Argentina, defending champions from 2022, made it all the way to the final only to fall to the same opponent. Spain won 1-0 after extra time in New Jersey on July 19, Ferran Torres scoring in the 106th minute as Emiliano Martínez made a record 11 saves in a losing effort. Messi, playing what is expected to be his last World Cup final, left the field in tears after collecting his runner-up medal.

FIFA has not addressed the specific Instagram post, but tournament refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina has previously dismissed suggestions of bias in officiating decisions during the tournament, and Argentina defender Lisandro Martínez said he found the standard of officiating "excellent."

No evidence has surfaced to support claims that matches were manipulated in Argentina's favor. Ronaldo has not commented publicly on the like, and a single tap on a post is not proof he endorses every claim within it — but given the long rivalry between him and Messi, and the raw nerve still exposed after Sunday's final, the gesture was enough to set off a fresh round of debate across football social media.

body: Luka Modrić is not done yet. AC Milan's 40-year-old midfield metronome has agreed to extend his stay at San Siro for another season, ONE reports, with the formal signing expected within days.

Citing transfer specialist Fabrizio Romano and Italian sources, ONE says Modrić has agreed a new one-year deal that will run until June 2027 — closing, for now, the retirement speculation that had trailed him since Croatia's exit from the World Cup.

Italian outlets including SempreMilan and Yahoo Sports, drawing on reporting from MilanNews and Fabrizio Romano, say the extension keeps Modrić's terms broadly unchanged from last season: roughly €3.5 million a year plus performance bonuses.
The new contract is expected to be put on paper this week, with several reports pointing to Wednesday as the likely signing date.

Modrić joined Milan as a free agent last summer after 13 years at Real Madrid, where he became one of the most decorated midfielders of his generation, winning the Champions League repeatedly and the 2018 Ballon d'Or.

His first season in Serie A produced 37 appearances across all competitions, with two goals and three assists, a workload interrupted at times by a jaw injury but otherwise a rare show of durability for a player who turned 40 in September.

The renewal comes just weeks after Croatia's run at the 2026 World Cup ended in the round of 32, beaten 2-1 by Portugal — a result that reopened questions about how much longer Modrić intends to keep playing at the top level, at club and country alike.

For Milan, locking down their captain-in-all-but-name for a second season answers at least one of those questions: whatever he ultimately decides about international football, the Rossoneri will have him running their midfield again in 2026-27.

title: Another suspect held over grenade attack on restaurant chain owned by Beitar Jerusalem's owner
dek: A man in his 20s from Bat Yam was arrested and taken in for questioning over a stun grenade thrown at a Japanika branch linked to Beitar Jerusalem owner Barak Abramov, the latest arrest in a wider wave of attacks tied to a criminal turf war.

body: Police have arrested another suspect in the investigation into a wave of grenade and gun attacks on branches of the Japanika restaurant chain owned by Beitar Jerusalem's controlling owner, Barak Abramov, ONE reports.

The suspect, a man in his 20s from Bat Yam, was detained by the Central Unit of the Tel Aviv Police District and transferred for questioning at the district's headquarters, according to the report. He is suspected of throwing a stun grenade at the Japanika branch in Kiryat Ono in the early hours of July 13.

Police told ONE he is due before the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court, where detectives will ask for his remand to be extended while the investigation continues. Officers said the probe is ongoing and that "all investigative directions are being examined." As is standard practice before any indictment, his name has not been released.

The Kiryat Ono incident is one of more than a dozen attacks reported against Japanika branches across the country since early July, according to Israeli media, with grenades thrown at outlets in Ramat Gan, Afula, Netanya, Givatayim and Rosh Pina and gunfire directed at the chain's Herzliya branch. Several suspects, including an alleged crime organisation leader, have already been arrested over the wider wave.

Japanika is the restaurant chain built and controlled by Abramov, who consolidated it and other ventures into his Andorra Investments Group before completing his takeover of Beitar Jerusalem in August 2022, buying the club after previously owning second-tier side Bnei Yehuda.

Investigators believe the attacks stem from a feud between rival crime organisations rather than any dispute involving Abramov personally, and have described him as a victim of the campaign rather than a suspect.

Abramov has sought to reassure Beitar's fan base as the case has unfolded, telling Ynet that "we are confident that recent events will not affect the club, and that nothing will spill over into Beitar's path in the league and in Europe."
With further arrests already made and the court process for this latest suspect still ahead, police say the investigation into who ordered and carried out the attacks remains active.

title: Naor Barkol Leaves Youth Ranks Behind to Coach Holon Yermiyahu
dek: After more than a decade exclusively in youth football, the Holon-born coach takes his first senior job at Liga Alef South side Holon Yermiyahu.

verificationSources.label: ONE - Naor Barkol appointed Holon Yermiyahu coach

body: Naor Barkol is coming home. The 39-year-old, who spent more than a decade coaching only in youth departments, has been named head coach of Liga Alef South club Holon Yermiyahu for the coming season, ONE reports — his first senior job at adult level.

Barkol is a Holon native through and through. He came up as a central defender in the youth ranks of Tzafririm Holon and went on to play for the club's adult team, before injury forced him into early retirement at 27 — the moment he pivoted into coaching, starting out in that same Tzafririm Holon youth department.

His most recent post was in charge of MS Ashdod's youth team, a job that ended abruptly and, by his own account, mysteriously. "To this day I don't know how to put my finger on the reasons that led to my dismissal," he said, referring to a departure that reportedly came a day after his side won 1-0 away to Ramat Hasharon. Before Ashdod, he had coached Ramat Hasharon's own U-17 side.

Now he is stepping up. "After so many years in the youth departments, I feel I've exhausted that chapter," Barkol said. "I see the opportunity I've been given as a springboard to the higher levels of Israeli football."

Holon Yermiyahu are preparing for their tenth consecutive season in Liga Alef South. The club, founded in 2014 and renamed in 2017 in honour of Holon playing great and former assistant coach Haim "HaSilon" Yirmiyahu, finished last season's shortened campaign in mid-table — and the ambitions are rising this time around.
Club owner Lior Shulman and sporting director Mousa Ben-Haim, who has his own long history with the club as both player and coach, brought Barkol in to lead the new project.
His bench will include two more former players: assistant coach Haim Pontormeli and goalkeeping coach Doron Rosenkovich round out the staff, per the club's presentation of the new setup.
"We're building a team with high aspirations," Barkol said. "We are choosing players for the squad carefully, and holding on to the ones we're very satisfied with."

dek: Israel midfielder Mohammed Abu Fani started as Crvena Zvezda led Larne 1-0 early in the second half of their Champions League second qualifying round first leg in Northern Ireland, Bruno Duarte converting a VAR-awarded penalty.

body: Mohammed Abu Fani took his first competitive step onto the European stage for Red Star Belgrade on Tuesday, starting in central midfield as the Serbian champions led Larne 1-0 shortly into the second half of their Champions League second qualifying round first leg at Inver Park.

The only goal, and the one Red Star carried into the interval, came from the penalty spot. In the 26th minute the referee stopped play to check an incident on the pitchside monitor and pointed to the spot; Bruno Duarte stepped up and side-footed his effort low into the bottom corner, sending the visitors in front.
As of the 47th minute — the point this report captures — Red Star's lead remained intact, with the tie still live for Larne on home soil and the second half only just under way.

For Abu Fani, this was his first taste of continental football in Red Star colours, coming five days after he played every minute of the club's 5-0 SuperLiga-opening rout of Mačva Šabac — his first appearance since arriving from Ferencváros in June on a deal Serbian outlets valued at around €1m over three years.

The Israel international has quickly become a fixture in Dejan Stanković's midfield plans. After the Mačva game, the head coach said Abu Fani, still working back to full sharpness, had his "blessing" to lose the ball occasionally given the calm and control he brings to Red Star's build-up play.

Larne arrived at this stage having never before reached a Champions League second qualifying round tie in the club's history. The Northern Irish side eliminated San Marino's Tre Fiori in the first round, winning 1-0 away on 7 July and 2-1 at home a week later, to earn Tuesday's visit from one of European football's most decorated clubs.

Red Star, chasing a place in the competition's league phase for the third time in four seasons, arrive as clear favourites, having retained the Serbian SuperLiga title last season by a ten-point margin. Austria forward Marko Arnautović also featured for the visitors, back in club colours days after his country's run at the 2026 World Cup.

The tie moves to Belgrade for the second leg next week, with Red Star defending a 1-0 lead at the Rajko Mitić Stadium — without the cushion of an away-goals rule UEFA scrapped in 2021, meaning a single Larne goal in the return fixture would level the tie again.

body: Hapoel Be'er Sheva's hopes of taking a foothold in their bid for a first-ever Champions League campaign proper were still alive but unresolved deep into the first half in Reykjavik on Tuesday, with Israel's champions locked at 0-0 against Víkingur Reykjavík 44 minutes into their Champions League second qualifying-round opener, ONE reported from the Icelandic capital.

It is the first competitive meeting between the two clubs. Víkingur are hosting the first leg on their compact, artificial-turf ground at Víkingsvöllur; the return fixture follows next week at Turner Stadium in Be'er Sheva. The aggregate winner advances to the third qualifying round, one tie away from the Champions League's league phase, while the loser is dropped into Europa League qualifying.

Hapoel arrive in Iceland as Israel's freshly restored champions, having ended an eight-year wait for the title in May under coach Ran Kozuk. Their build-up to Europe, however, was jolted by a defeat in the traditional season-opening Super Cup meeting against Maccabi Tel Aviv, who won that fixture 3-1, according to Ynet and Sport1. "Disappointing — I expected a lot more," Kozuk said afterwards, per Ynet.

That match also cost Hapoel their marquee summer arrival. João Victor, the Brazilian defender signed for a reported €1.7 million, went down with what the club fears is a significant hamstring tear after coming on as a stoppage-time substitute. ONE reports he is expected to be sidelined for roughly one to one-and-a-half months. "It doesn't look promising, but we'll wait for the tests and hope for the best," Kozuk said, according to Sport1-Maariv.

Víkingur are no pushovers at home. Iceland's reigning champions needed two legs to see off Hungary's Győr, winning 3-2 on aggregate in the first qualifying round, and they have lost just once in their last eight matches on home soil across all competitions. Their squad includes the well-travelled Gylfi Sigurðsson, formerly of Tottenham and Everton, alongside forward Nikolai Hansen.

Neither side had broken through by the midpoint of the first half, leaving the tie finely poised heading into the second period in Reykjavík — and, whatever the final score in Iceland, into next week's second leg in the Negev.
