body: Blessing Afrifah, the sprinter who holds Israel's national 100m record, has withdrawn from both the 100m and the 200m at the national athletics championships in Jerusalem, pulled at the last moment by a hamstring injury.

According to the report, he had been troubled by the hamstring for several weeks before he was struck from the entry lists shortly ahead of the meeting at the Givat Ram stadium. Medical staff judged it safer to rest him than risk aggravating the muscle further.

Afrifah is the fastest man Israel has produced. He set the national 100m record of 10.09 seconds in Jerusalem in July 2025, ending a mark that had stood for more than two decades, and he also holds the national 200m record of 19.96, run as a teenager in 2022.
Now 22, he won the 200m at the 2022 World Under-20 Championships and took the European Under-23 title in both 2023 and 2025. He had arrived in Jerusalem as the defending champion in both sprints.

The decision to hold him back is tied to the calendar. By the report's account, the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham are only about a month away, and his team preferred to protect his fitness for the continental stage rather than chase domestic titles at home.

The withdrawal lands on a weekend already heavy with meaning for Israeli athletics, marking as it does the close of decathlon record-holder Ariel Atias's competitive career, whose retirement this desk reported separately.

No return date has been given, and for now the withdrawal rests on a single Israeli report. His condition in the run-up to Birmingham is likely to be the more telling measure of how serious the injury proves to be.
facts: Blessing Afrifah was withdrawn at the last moment from the 100m and 200m at the Israeli Athletics Championships in Jerusalem (Givat Ram) with a hamstring injury, according to the source report.
The hamstring problem had troubled him for several weeks, and the medical staff chose to rest him rather than risk further damage.
Afrifah holds Israel's 100m national record of 10.09 seconds, set in Jerusalem in July 2025 — the fastest ever run by an Israeli (World Athletics).
He also holds the national 200m record of 19.96 (2022) and was 200m champion at the 2022 World U20 Championships and the 2023 and 2025 European U23 Championships.
The withdrawal is aimed at protecting his fitness for the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham, which the report places roughly a month away.
The same weekend marked the retirement of decathlon record-holder Ariel Atias, covered separately by this desk.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv are on the verge of adding to their attack, with Israeli reports on Monday indicating that the club have reached a principle agreement to sign Slovenian striker Ester Sokler from Serbian side Radnicki 1923. The framework of the transfer is said to be settled between the two clubs, though the player has not yet put pen to paper and the move should not be treated as complete.

According to the Israeli coverage, the fee involved is in the region of one million euros. That would represent a substantial return for Radnicki, who only turned Sokler's loan from Aberdeen into a permanent transfer in January 2026, and it reflects the impact the forward made across the second half of the Serbian SuperLiga campaign.

The reporting describes the deal as roughly ninety-five per cent complete, with those close to the negotiations expecting matters to be finalised within about forty-eight hours. Israeli outlets have also indicated that Sokler's wages would be upgraded on the terms he holds in Serbia, with figures of around 200,000 to 250,000 euros a year cited, although those numbers have not been formally confirmed by either club.

Sokler, who turned 27 in June, enjoyed the most productive season of his career in 2025-26. Across his loan and permanent spells with Radnicki he registered 15 goals in 29 league appearances, a tally that helped the Kragujevac club preserve their top-flight status after a difficult campaign. That scoring rate is understood to have made him a priority target for Maccabi's recruitment staff.

A native of Krsko in eastern Slovenia, the striker came through at NK Krsko before spells with Brezice, Celje and Radomlje. He moved to Scotland with Aberdeen in the summer of 2023, where he spent close to three seasons and won the 2025 Scottish Cup, before the loan to Serbia reignited his form in front of goal.

At international level Sokler is a recent addition to the senior picture rather than an established name. He earned his first cap for Slovenia in June 2026, coming off the bench in a 1-1 draw with Cyprus, and remains uncapped beyond that single appearance as he looks to build on his breakout club season.

Should the transfer be completed as expected, Sokler would arrive as a central striking option and a reported priority of Maccabi's new sporting leadership. Other clubs, including Sweden's Malmo and Serbia's Partizan Belgrade, were said to have monitored his situation, but for now the momentum is firmly with the Israeli champions. Until the signature is confirmed, however, the deal stays in the advanced-but-pending category.

title: Tearful Scaloni puts Argentina future in doubt, commits only to seeing out contract to December
dek: After the 1-0 World Cup final defeat to Spain, Argentina's coach said losing "hurts me in the soul", vowed to complete his contract through December and left the room in tears without announcing a definitive departure.

body: A tearful Lionel Scaloni left his press conference early in East Rutherford on Sunday night, saying Argentina's 1-0 World Cup final defeat to Spain "hurts me in the soul." He committed only to seeing out his contract, which expires in December, before deciding whether to continue as national team coach.

Ferran Torres's goal in the 106th minute of extra time settled the final, ending Argentina's bid to become the first side since Brazil in 1962 to retain the trophy. Enzo Fernández had been sent off late in regulation, leaving the holders to chase the game a man down.

Asked directly about his future, Scaloni stopped short of a resignation. "I will complete my contract and then see," he said. "I will talk with the president, but I more or less have an idea of what I want to do."
"Honestly, I feel the need to think," he added, "because I don't know if we'll be able to do something as grand as this."

The 48-year-old struggled to hold his composure as the questions continued. "Bear with me, I don't know if I can continue," he said, before standing up and apologising. "It's really painful, I am very sorry," he told the room, and walked out to applause from the Argentine journalists present.

He offered a glimpse of how heavy another cycle would feel. "In order to continue you need a great deal of things, especially resetting your mind, rebooting, creating a group like this again," he said. The likely first step, he added, was "to relax and to stop for a bit."

Scaloni has led Argentina since 2018, when he took over on an interim basis after a chastening tournament in Russia. He rebuilt the squad around Lionel Messi and delivered the Copa América in 2021, ending a 28-year title drought.
That triumph was followed by the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and a second Copa América in 2024, cementing his place among the most successful coaches in the country's history.

His deal with the Argentine federation runs to the end of 2026, and a decision on his future is expected only after he sits down with president Claudio Tapia. For now, the coach who restored Argentina to the top of the world game has promised nothing beyond December — and made no secret of how much Sunday cost him.
facts: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the World Cup final on 19 July 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey; Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute.
Scaloni on the defeat: "Losing hurts me in the soul."
On his future: "I will complete my contract and then see" — the deal expires in December 2026; no explicit resignation was announced.
He left the press conference in tears, apologising, and was applauded out of the room by Argentine media.

title: Kings of the world: Ferran Torres strikes in extra time as Spain beat Argentina 1-0 to win the 2026 World Cup
dek: The European champions suffocated Lionel Messi's Argentina at MetLife Stadium, survived Emiliano Martinez's record 11 saves and a disallowed goal, and won their second World Cup through Ferran Torres' 106th-minute volley — while more than 10,000 Israelis watched together at Menora Mivtachim Hall in Tel Aviv.

source.originalTitle: Spain edge Argentina after extra time to win 2nd World Cup title

body: Spain are champions of the world. On a heavy summer night at MetLife Stadium, the European champions beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time to win the 2026 World Cup, their second star arriving sixteen years after their first. It took 106 minutes, a red card, a disallowed goal and the finest goalkeeping display a final has ever seen before Ferran Torres, a 62nd-minute substitute, finally broke Argentina — volleying into the roof of the net after Nico Williams headed Pedro Porro's cross into his path.

For 90 minutes the pattern never wavered. Spain passed, probed and pinned Argentina into their own third, finishing with 65 per cent of possession and 20 shots to Argentina's two. The holders did not manage a single shot on target all night, a statistic without precedent in a World Cup final of the modern era.
That it remained goalless so long was down to one man. Emiliano Martinez's 11 saves were the most ever recorded in a World Cup final, according to figures carried by ESPN and the Associated Press.

The match turned in stoppage time of the 90. Enzo Fernandez, booked in the 82nd minute for dissent, launched into a reckless challenge that sent Pau Cubarsi somersaulting, and Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic showed the Chelsea midfielder a second yellow card in the third added minute. The decision was widely reported as justified, and it condemned Argentina to face half an hour of extra time with ten tired men against the deepest squad in the tournament.

Even then Argentina were reprieved twice. Martinez clawed away a Williams effort in the 93rd minute, and when Williams did put the ball in the net early in extra time, the goal was ruled out for a foul on Nicolas Otamendi in the build-up — a call the AP described as another that went Argentina's way.

It only delayed the inevitable. In the 106th minute Porro crossed from the right, Williams cushioned a header across goal, and Torres — the Barcelona forward sent on to stretch a wilting defence — thrashed his finish past Martinez at last.

The records tumbled with the final whistle. Spain's unbeaten run now stands at 38 matches, surpassing the world record of 37 set by Italy between 2018 and 2021, and they conceded just one goal in the entire tournament — the fewest ever by a World Cup winner. As holders of the European Championship they are now, without argument, kings of both their continent and the world, the first side since their own 2010-12 generation to hold both crowns at once.

For Lionel Messi, 39, there was only heartbreak in what is widely expected to be his last World Cup. He became the first player to start three World Cup finals and the oldest outfield player ever to start one, but he spent the night starved of the ball, shackled by Rodri and Cubarsi, and left the pitch a beaten captain as Spain's players streamed past him towards their supporters.

In Israel, the final was a midnight festival. More than 10,000 fans packed Menora Mivtachim Hall in Tel Aviv for a municipal viewing party — moved indoors from Charles Clore Park after every ticket sold out — watching the drama unfold on giant 360-degree screens with the atmosphere of a home fixture, Israeli media reported. When Torres scored, the basketball arena, more accustomed to Maccabi Tel Aviv's European nights, shook like it does for a buzzer-beater.

The night may also have settled football's next great argument. Lamine Yamal, 19, quiet by his standards yet always threatening, adds a World Cup to a Euro at an age when most players are still waiting for a debut, and Goal.com's power rankings already listed him as the bookmakers' Ballon d'Or favourite before kick-off.

The tournament's official verdict followed within the hour. Rodri, Spain's metronome, was named player of the tournament ahead of Messi; Unai Simón took the Golden Glove after a record 650 consecutive minutes without conceding; Pau Cubarsí was voted the best young player; and Kylian Mbappé's ten goals had already sealed the Golden Boot. As Messi's era closed in New Jersey, the succession was standing 30 metres away, wearing the same number ten — for the other side.
facts: Final: Spain 1-0 Argentina after extra time; Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute (ESPN, FIFA match centre, AP).
Enzo Fernandez was sent off at 90+3 for a second yellow card after a reckless foul on Pau Cubarsi; his first booking came in the 82nd minute for dissent (ESPN, AP, NBC News).
Emiliano Martinez made 11 saves — the most ever recorded in a World Cup final (ESPN, AP via Yahoo Sports).
Spain led possession 65%-35% and shots 20-2 (12-0 on target); Argentina did not register a shot on target (ESPN Gamecast statistics; also per NBC News).
A Nico Williams goal early in extra time was disallowed for a foul on Nicolas Otamendi in the build-up (AP; incident corroborated by Sky Sports).
Spain extended their unbeaten run to 38 matches, breaking Italy's world record of 37 set between 2018 and 2021 (ESPN, AP).
Spain conceded one goal in the entire tournament — the fewest by any World Cup winner (ESPN, AP).
More than 10,000 fans attended the Tel Aviv municipality's viewing party at Menora Mivtachim Hall, relocated from Charles Clore Park after tickets sold out, per Israeli media reports.

Spain swept the individual awards: Rodri the Golden Ball ahead of Messi, Unai Simón the Golden Glove (record 650 consecutive minutes unbeaten), Pau Cubarsí best young player; Kylian Mbappé won the Golden Boot with ten goals (ESPN, Yahoo Sports, Sports Illustrated, Manchester City official).

body: Maccabi Haifa's summer-long goalkeeping saga is all but over. Both halves of the club's planned reshuffle — the sale of Heorhiy Yermakov to Ukrainian side Metalist Kharkiv and the return of Israel international Omri Glazer from Red Star Belgrade — have been agreed, an Israeli sports outlet reported on Sunday evening, with the deals expected to take full effect within 48 hours once all parties have signed contracts.

Glazer, a 30-year-old goalkeeper with 23 senior caps for Israel, has agreed a contract for the next four years, according to the report, which puts the fee due to Red Star Belgrade at an estimated 600,000 dollars. The Serbian champions had initially pushed for the Israeli to stay in Belgrade or command a substantially higher price, but subsequent Israeli reports said the club formally cleared him to leave, with a medical examination among the final steps before signing.

The move would open a second spell at the club for Glazer, who was on Maccabi Haifa's books from 2016 to 2021, a period that included a loan at Sektzia Ness Ziona. He established himself as first choice at Hapoel Be'er Sheva between 2021 and 2023 before joining Red Star Belgrade, where he made more than 50 appearances and played European football. His contract in Serbia had been due to run until June 2027.

Travelling in the other direction, at least figuratively, is Yermakov. Metalist will pay three million euros for the 24-year-old Ukrainian, per the report — a figure broadly consistent with earlier Israeli reporting that described an offer of 2.8 million euros rising to three million through add-on clauses. The goalkeeper, who is said to be tripling his wages in Ukraine, leaves Haifa after a single season.

Kyiv-raised and a product of the Shakhtar Donetsk academy, Yermakov arrived in Israeli football via FC Oleksandriya, where he spent a further season on loan after Haifa acquired his rights, before joining up with the Greens' first team and making over 30 appearances last season. His willingness to move had reportedly been secured earlier in the window, with the two clubs left to close the gap on the fee.

It is worth underlining what has and has not happened: both transfers are agreed rather than officially announced. Neither Maccabi Haifa, Red Star Belgrade nor Metalist has confirmed the deals, and the report frames the coming 48 hours — signatures, paperwork and formal unveilings — as the window in which the agreements become official.

For Haifa, the double deal resolves the position that has dominated their summer and lets the recruitment department move on: having completed the signing of Wanderson Tsunami, a left-sided defender who can also cover at left-back, the club has reportedly turned its search toward a right-footed centre-back as preparations for the new season continue.

body: Jeff Dowtin Jr is heading to Italy. Napoli Basket officially announced the signing of the American point guard for the 2026-27 season on Monday, confirming a move Israeli and Italian media had already reported as agreed the previous evening.

The deal ends a summer of uncertainty for the 29-year-old, whose single season at Maccabi Tel Aviv finished with an early parting of ways. Dowtin had also been in negotiations with AEK Athens, but that path closed, leaving Naples rather than Athens to host his second European season.
He had arrived in Tel Aviv in August 2025 on a three-year contract, his first stop outside North America after NBA spells with Golden State, Milwaukee, Orlando, Toronto and Philadelphia.

His numbers in yellow and blue were respectable rather than commanding. He averaged 9.6 points and 4.3 assists in around 21 minutes a game in domestic play, and 8.1 points with 2.4 assists in just over 17 minutes a night in the EuroLeague.
It was not enough to see out the contract. Maccabi and Dowtin agreed to part ways in May, before the season had even finished, and the guard re-entered the market.

Napoli represent an ambitious landing spot. The Serie A club are returning to European competition for the first time in nearly two decades, drawn into a EuroCup group featuring Bourg-en-Bresse, Tofas Bursa, Buducnost and Trentino, among others.
For Dowtin, the EuroCup offers a stage a rung below the EuroLeague nights he knew in Tel Aviv, and a chance to run a team of his own in a city rediscovering its basketball appetite.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's basketball club confirmed on Sunday that it will begin the coming season outside Israel. "At the moment — we will open the season in Sofia," the club told supporters, extending the arrangement that defined its historic first EuroLeague campaign.

The explanation came in an official statement issued in the club's name rather than attributed to any individual executive. "In light of the heating-up of the security situation, and in order to prepare in the best possible way for the coming season, it was decided to maintain activity bases both in Sofia and in Israel," the statement read.

The wording was deliberately provisional. The club said the main activity base will sit in Sofia "at this stage," that it will continue to monitor developments, and that if the security picture in Israel improves, the possibility of moving the principal base back home will be examined. No end date was given, and the club did not specify which competitions, or how many fixtures, the arrangement will cover.

The decision continues rather than begins Hapoel's Bulgarian chapter. Throughout 2025-26 — the club's debut season in the EuroLeague — home games in the competition were staged at Arena 8888 in Sofia, the hall formerly known as Arena Armeec, under the alternative-venue arrangements the league put in place for Israeli clubs while the security situation kept top-tier European basketball from being played in Israel.
That debut campaign was itself the product of a breakthrough. Hapoel earned their EuroLeague place by winning the 2024-25 EuroCup, sweeping Gran Canaria in the final.
In their first season among Europe's elite, they reached the 2026 playoffs, where they met Real Madrid, before the title was decided in Athens, where Olympiacos were crowned champions.

A squad member, quoted without being named in one of the Israeli reports, suggested the players had been braced for the news. "They said we'd start in Bulgaria and progress from there. There are still security matters, but we're going with whatever the team decides," the player said.

For Hapoel's supporters, the announcement lands as a familiar disappointment: a second consecutive season, at least at its outset, in which the biggest nights of the club's European life will begin some 1,600 kilometres from Tel Aviv. The club's own framing, though, leaves the door conspicuously open — the operative words remain "at the moment," with everything after that contingent on quieter times at home.

The arrangement is explicitly provisional: the club will monitor developments and examine returning its main base to Israel if security improves.

Hapoel qualified for the EuroLeague by winning the 2024-25 EuroCup and reached the 2026 EuroLeague playoffs; Olympiacos won the 2025-26 title.

body: Hapoel Jerusalem have made an opening bid to bring former Denver Nuggets forward David Roddy to the Israeli capital, offering the 25-year-old American a contract worth approximately $2.2 million over two years, according to a report published in Israel on Sunday evening. Roddy is said to have rejected that first proposal, but the two sides remain in negotiations.

The report, by a named Israeli basketball correspondent, indicates that Jerusalem view the rejection as a step in an ongoing negotiation rather than the end of the pursuit, and that the club is continuing its effort to close a deal. No other outlet has yet confirmed the talks, and neither the club nor the player has commented publicly.

Roddy, a 6-foot-5 forward built more like a linebacker than a wing, was one of the most decorated college players in the country at Colorado State, where he was named Mountain West Player of the Year in 2022. Philadelphia selected him with the 23rd overall pick in that summer's NBA draft before trading his rights to Memphis on draft night.

What followed was a well-travelled four-year NBA career: two seasons with the Grizzlies, a February 2024 trade to Phoenix, a stint in Atlanta, a brief return to Philadelphia on 10-day and two-way deals, a two-way contract in Houston and, this past March, a two-way agreement with Denver. Across 181 NBA regular-season games he averaged 6.3 points and 2.9 rebounds, and per the Israeli report he contributed 8.0 points and 4.0 rebounds in five appearances for the Nuggets last season.

The pursuit fits the shape of Jerusalem's summer. The club has appointed veteran Serbian coach Sasa Obradovic, who led Monaco to the 2023 EuroLeague Final Four, on a contract running through 2028-29, and has formally applied for a two-year EuroLeague license ahead of the shareholders' decision on the 2026-27 field. For now, the team is preparing for another BKT EuroCup campaign.

Domestically, Jerusalem are trying to close the gap on the Tel Aviv powers after a season that ended in frustration: a third-place finish in the Winner League regular season at 18-8 was followed by a semi-final exit against Hapoel Tel Aviv, while Maccabi Tel Aviv went on to claim the championship. The roster rebuild is already under way, with big man Devontae Cacok among the arrivals on a two-year deal.

An outlay in the region of $2.2 million for a single player would signal serious financial ambition by Israeli league standards, and landing a 25-year-old with 181 NBA games behind him would be a statement of intent to match the club's European aspirations. With the first offer rebuffed and talks continuing, the coming days should show whether Jerusalem are willing to raise their bid.

body: Hapoel Haifa's squad flies home from its pre-season camp in Bulgaria on Monday to an unwelcome discovery: according to a report on Sunday evening, the club is currently barred from its Beit Nagler training complex. Haifa Municipality is said to be withholding access over an alleged unpaid debt of thousands of shekels, a decision that lands six days before the club opens its Toto Cup campaign against Maccabi Haifa in the city derby next Saturday.

The story was first reported by a local Haifa outlet before the club issued a lengthy, and unusually bitter, public response — one that did not dispute the existence of a payment question, but attacked the city's treatment of the club root and branch.

"After cutting the annual support budget for Hapoel Haifa to 29,000 shekels — roughly our annual socks budget — the municipality continues to turn a cold shoulder to the club," the club said in the statement. "Unfortunately, we feel like an unwanted, unloved stepchild in the city, to put it mildly."

The statement went further, accusing the city of "failing one of the oldest and most important institutions in the city, in its 103rd year," and of forcing the club "to compete with unequal tools against rivals budgeted in the millions of shekels, including facilities provided free or subsidised by municipalities." The club also questioned the timing, calling the emergence of the ban days before the derby "puzzling."

There is history here, and it is strikingly recent. In the summer of 2025 the same municipality barred the same club from the same Beit Nagler complex over a debt then put at roughly NIS 100,000, saying training could resume once it was settled; the club responded at the time that it pays more than NIS 2 million a year for its use of Beit Nagler and Sammy Ofer Stadium and would settle any bill on formal demand. That episode was resolved; its reappearance a year on suggests a structural rather than incidental problem in the relationship.

What is missing, this time, is the city's side. Haifa Municipality had issued no statement on the fresh bar by Sunday night, and the precise size and age of the debt now claimed has not been confirmed on the record. Until it speaks, the club's furious framing stands alone.

The stakes are immediate either way. The Toto Cup derby against Maccabi Haifa next Saturday is the club's first competitive fixture of the 2026-27 season, and a side that lands from Bulgaria on Monday with its training base in doubt has, at best, a badly disrupted match week. If the last round of this fight is any guide, a payment — and a formal demand for one — would end it quickly.

title: Evenepoel conquers the Solaison as Vingegaard crashes out of the Tour
dek: Remco Evenepoel outkicked Tadej Pogacar and Isaac del Toro on the Plateau de Solaison for his first road-stage win at the Tour de France, on an afternoon overshadowed by Jonas Vingegaard's crash and first career Grand Tour abandonment.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: אבנפול ניצח בקטע ה-15, וינגגור נפצע ופרש
source.author: Dani Porat

verificationSources.label: TOUR Magazin — Stage 15: Evenepoel wins, Vingegaard forced to withdraw

body: Remco Evenepoel produced the finest road victory of his Tour de France career on Sunday, winning stage 15 atop the Plateau de Solaison ahead of race leader Tadej Pogacar. But the Alpine afternoon will be remembered as much for what the race lost as for what the Belgian won: Jonas Vingegaard, twice a champion in Paris and lying second overall at the start of the day, crashed on the approach to the final climb and left the race in an ambulance, abandoning a Grand Tour for the first time in his career.

The 183.9-kilometre stage from Champagnole delivered the first summit finish of this Tour's Alpine block — the hors-categorie Plateau de Solaison, 11.3 kilometres at around nine per cent, making its Tour debut. Inside the final kilometre Isaac del Toro launched the expected attack. Evenepoel matched the young Mexican, then countered decisively, crossing the line ahead of Pogacar with Del Toro third at six seconds. The next group, including Paul Seixas and Florian Lipowitz, conceded just under a minute.

It was a breakthrough for Evenepoel, now in his first season with Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe. His previous Tour stage wins had come against the clock; this was his first at the summit of a mountain, taken toe-to-toe with Pogacar on one of the steepest finishes of the race. With the world time-trial champion refusing to crack on the double-digit ramps, the result reframes the podium battle heading into the final week.

The decisive drama, though, came roughly 21 kilometres from the finish. With Visma-Lease a Bike driving the peloton in pursuit of the breakaway, Vingegaard's front wheel slipped as he exited a roundabout and he went down hard into the kerb, according to reports from the race by Cyclingnews and TOUR Magazin.
His teammate Sepp Kuss and UAE Team Emirates-XRG riders Isaac del Toro and Brandon McNulty were also brought down. Del Toro remounted quickly, but the Dane could not continue.

Race doctors treated Vingegaard at the roadside and placed his right arm in a sling before he was taken away in a race ambulance, with international outlets reporting a heavy impact to his shoulder. Visma-Lease a Bike had not published a full medical bulletin by the time the stage finished, and the precise extent of the injury remained unconfirmed on Sunday evening. The team's withdrawal of its leader ends his bid for a third Tour title in the cruellest fashion.

Vingegaard's exit redraws the general classification. Pogacar, who by several accounts rode in service of Del Toro's podium ambitions rather than chasing the stage himself, retains the yellow jersey — and the polka-dot jersey besides. Evenepoel moves up to second overall at five minutes, with Del Toro third at 5:58, while Mads Pedersen continues to lead the points classification. Monday's rest day now precedes a final week in which the fight is for the podium as much as for yellow.

For Israeli fans, this is the first Tour since the team founded as Israel Cycling Academy stopped down its national identity. The former Israel-Premier Tech now races as NSN Cycling Team under a Swiss licence, owned by the Never Say Never group co-founded by Andres Iniesta, after the protest-scarred 2025 season.

Its eight-man Tour squad, built as a sprint train around Biniam Girmay, includes no Israeli riders this year — Israeli champion-in-waiting Nadav Raisberg was left off the roster. A brutal summit finish like the Solaison was always going to be a day of survival rather than opportunity for the sprint-focused outfit, which The Times of Israel reports is experiencing a far calmer race since the rebrand.
facts: Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe) won stage 15 of the 2026 Tour de France on 19 July, 183.9 km from Champagnole to the Plateau de Solaison, ahead of Tadej Pogacar (same time) and Isaac del Toro at six seconds.
It was Evenepoel's first Tour de France stage win on a road/mountain stage; his previous Tour wins came in time trials.
Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) crashed about 21 km from the finish when his front wheel slipped exiting a roundabout; his right arm was placed in a sling and he left the race by ambulance.
The abandonment — reported by Cyclingnews, Reuters, TOUR Magazin and ProCyclingUK — is the first of Vingegaard's Grand Tour career; he had started the day second overall.
Sepp Kuss, Isaac del Toro and Brandon McNulty also came down in the crash; Del Toro remounted and finished third on the stage.
After stage 15, Pogacar leads the general classification with Evenepoel second at 5:00 and Del Toro third at 5:58; Pogacar also holds the mountains jersey and Mads Pedersen the green jersey.
The former Israel-Premier Tech team races this Tour as NSN Cycling Team under a Swiss licence; its eight-rider squad, led by sprinter Biniam Girmay, contains no Israeli riders.

title: Sour finish in Ljubljana: Israel under-20s beaten by Lithuania in ninth-place game
dek: Israel's reserve national team led at halftime but was outscored 30-18 in the third quarter, losing 95-79 to Lithuania and closing the FIBA U20 EuroBasket in 10th place — with top-division status already secured.

The final score and quarter scores are confirmed by FIBA's official game page; individual Israeli statistics are attributed to the original match report where FIBA's figures differ. body: Israel's under-20 national team closed out its FIBA U20 EuroBasket campaign on a sour note on Sunday, falling 95-79 to Lithuania in the ninth-place classification game at Arena Stožice II in Ljubljana. The defeat left the young blue-and-whites 10th of 16 teams in Europe's top division, with Lithuania claiming ninth.

For a half, Israel looked the likelier side to finish inside the top ten. Lithuania shaded a tight opening quarter 19-18, but Israel answered by taking the second 23-20 to go into the locker room in front, 41-39 — a scoreline confirmed quarter by quarter in FIBA's official record of the game.

The match turned decisively after the break. Lithuania piled on 30 points to Israel's 18 in the third quarter, taking a 69-59 lead — the first double-digit gap of the contest — and kept pressing in the fourth to stretch the margin to 21 points before Israel trimmed the final deficit to 16.

Gabrielius Jokubauskas did the bulk of the damage for Lithuania, finishing with a game-high 31 points on six three-pointers, according to FIBA's official box score. Israeli match reports initially carried 34, but that figure is FIBA's listed efficiency rating for Jokubauskas, not his points total.

On the Israeli side, FIBA's leaders card credits Yonatan Keller with 16 points, with Oren Sahar also on 16 and leading the game with eight assists. Captain Rany Belaga added a team-high eight rebounds in what was his final game of the tournament.

The loss capped a campaign of real swings in Ljubljana. Israel went 2-1 in Group D — wins over Romania and the Czech Republic bookending a defeat to host Slovenia — before dropping into the 9-16 classification bracket.

There, a lopsided win over Italy guaranteed Israel's place in Division A, Europe's top flight, for next summer, and a 96-74 dismissal of Latvia in the 9-12 semifinal set up Sunday's meeting with Lithuania. Belaga starred in that Latvia game with a 32-point triple-double, which FIBA noted as just the eighth in the competition's history.

It was the first major tournament for the reserve programme's new coaching staff, installed ahead of this summer. A 10th-place finish is a step back from 2025, when Israel's under-20s reached the quarterfinals and ended the championship sixth, and the Israeli match report carried no post-game comment from the bench.

Still, the bottom line for the programme is survival at the top table: Israel will play Division A again in 2027. It leaves Ljubljana with a core led by Belaga — newly signed with Hapoel Jerusalem — plus Sahar and Keller, all of whom produced against elite European opposition. Serbia, meanwhile, took the tournament title in Ljubljana.
facts: Final: Lithuania 95, Israel 79 — ninth-place classification game, FIBA U20 EuroBasket 2026 (Division A), Arena Stožice II, Ljubljana, 19 July 2026; confirmed final by FIBA's official game page.
Israel led 41-39 at halftime before Lithuania won the third quarter 30-18 to lead 69-59.
Lithuania's lead reached 21 points in the fourth quarter; Israel finished the tournament 10th of 16, Lithuania ninth.
Gabrielius Jokubauskas scored a game-high 31 points (11/16 FG, 6/10 threes) per FIBA's official box score; the widely-reported 34 was his efficiency rating.
Israel beat Latvia 96-74 in the 9-12 semifinal, with captain Rany Belaga posting a 32-point triple-double — the eighth in U20 EuroBasket history, per FIBA.
Israel's earlier classification win over Italy secured its place in Division A for 2027.
Serbia won the 2026 FIBA U20 EuroBasket title; the tournament ran 11-19 July in Ljubljana, Slovenia.

dek: The Israel Athletics Federation announced on Sunday that the country's finest combined-events athlete will end his 16-year career at Monday's Israeli Championships in Jerusalem, before joining the federation's Academy for Excellence coaching staff in September.

body: Ariel Atias, Israel's national record-holder in the decathlon and, in his federation's estimation, the finest all-round athlete the country has produced, is retiring from competition at the age of 27. The Israel Athletics Federation announced on Sunday that Monday's Israeli Championships, at the Givat Ram Stadium in Jerusalem, will close out a career spanning 16 years.

"I am finishing this chapter with a heavy heart, but a whole one," Atias said in the federation's statement. "Sometimes one of the greatest challenges for an athlete is knowing when the time has come to stop."
He added that for 16 years he had been privileged to live his dream in Israeli athletics.

The numbers behind that career are considerable. Atias made some 20 appearances in Israel colours, set eight age-group records, and collected multiple national titles, including back-to-back senior decathlon championships in 2019 and 2020. In 2020, according to the federation, he broke a national decathlon record that had stood for 26 years.

He then raised the bar further still. World Athletics lists his national record at 7,343 points, scored on 14 May 2022 at Drake Stadium in Des Moines, Iowa, while he was competing collegiately for Illinois State University at the Missouri Valley Conference championships. His profile also records an indoor heptathlon best of 5,414 points and a 4.85-metre pole vault, both set in Chicago in February 2024.

The decathlon is athletics at its most unforgiving: ten disciplines across two days, rewarding the athlete who is merely excellent at everything over the specialist who is brilliant at one thing. That Atias dominated the event domestically for the better part of a decade, while carrying his career from Israel to the American collegiate circuit and back, explains why the federation's farewell called him the best combined-events athlete in the country's history.

The goodbye is not a departure. In recent years Atias had already begun coaching alongside his own training, and in September he will formally join the staff of the federation's Academy for Excellence.
There, the federation said, he will remain an inseparable part of the athletics family and help shape the next generation of Israeli combined-events athletes.

First, though, there is one final start. "The track may end here, but my path in sport is only changing direction," Atias said. It ends where it should: at the national championships, in front of his own, with the record book still carrying his name.
facts: Ariel Atias (born 9 May 1999) is retiring at 27 after 16 years in athletics, the Israel Athletics Federation announced on Sunday, 19 July 2026.
He holds the Israeli decathlon record of 7,343 points, set on 14 May 2022 at Drake Stadium, Des Moines (World Athletics).
Per the federation, he first broke the national decathlon record in 2020, ending a mark that had stood for 26 years.
His career includes roughly 20 national-team appearances, eight age-group records and multiple national titles, including the 2019 and 2020 decathlon championships.
His final competition is the Israeli Championships at Givat Ram Stadium, Jerusalem, on Monday, 20 July 2026.
In September he joins the coaching staff of the federation's Academy for Excellence, having already begun coaching alongside competing.

title: 'He waited for my first mistake': Stav Lemkin looks back on a first season of two halves at Twente
dek: Hauled off at half-time on his Eredivisie debut and frozen out by the coach who signed him, the Israel defender ended his first Dutch season as an automatic starter in a Twente side that clinched European football.

body: Stav Lemkin has closed the book on his first season in the Netherlands with a strikingly candid verdict on how it began. In an interview with Twente's club magazine De Twaalfde Man, the 23-year-old Israel defender said of the coach who gave him his debut: "It was as if the trainer waited for my first mistake, a first chance to take me out. I was not the player he wanted, I think."

The mistrust, Lemkin said, was something he sensed from pre-season onwards, and it surfaced on the opening weekend. Handed his Eredivisie debut away to PEC Zwolle in August, he was substituted at half-time of a 1-0 defeat.

The team fared little better than its new signing. Three points from the first four league matches left the club bottom-heavy in the table and the board out of patience, and Joseph Oosting was dismissed on 4 September 2025.

Lemkin was careful not to reduce the poor start to one man's decisions. "There were many new players, and at first it was as if we were all individualists," he reflected, describing a dressing room of strangers still searching for a common idea. Even so, he admitted feeling a measure of sympathy for Oosting when the club decided to act.

The change transformed both the team and the defender's place in it. John van den Brom was confirmed as head coach on 15 September 2025, and under the veteran Dutchman the centre-back went from expendable to indispensable, establishing himself as a regular starter and finishing the campaign with 26 league appearances. "After the change, things improved very quickly," Lemkin said, "and you got the feeling that you were playing with your best friends, or with family."

The turnaround carried the club from crisis to a European place, and Lemkin reserved particular warmth for the supporters who filled the stadium through both halves of the season. "The results were good and we are wonderfully supported by our fans. The atmosphere in the stadium is incredible, and they are always clearly present at away matches," he said. "It is nice that we could also make them happy by reaching European football."

The season completes a rapid ascent for the Tel Aviv-born defender, who came through at Maccabi and Hapoel Tel Aviv before joining Shakhtar Donetsk in 2023. After a season back at Maccabi on loan, Twente paid the Ukrainian club a reported fee of around 1.5 million euros in June 2025 to sign him on a three-year contract, and the investment now looks shrewd for a player who has also won ten senior caps for Israel.

For all the vindication of the second half of his season, Lemkin insists the story is not finished, saying he knows he can still improve. His conclusion, though, was unambiguous: "I am really happy here, and glad that I get to play for this club."

body: AEK Athens have submitted an official offer to Hapoel Be'er Sheva for Kings Kangwa, the Zambian international midfielder who powered the club to last season's Israeli championship. Word of the formal bid emerged in Israel on Sunday evening, with two separate reports confirming that negotiations between the clubs are now live. The Greek side's proposal, both agreed, is the most substantial yet received for the 27-year-old.

The numbers do not yet add up to a deal. AEK's current offer is understood to exceed €2.5 million, while Be'er Sheva value their player of the season at more than €4 million. One assessment in Israel holds that a bid in the region of €3 million could bring owner Alona Barkat's club to the table — but as matters stand, the offer falls short of her demands.

On personal terms, the gap is easier to bridge. AEK are prepared to pay Kangwa around €700,000 a year, according to one report — more than double the roughly €300,000 he currently earns in the Negev. It is the kind of salary jump that tends to concentrate a player's mind once clubs start talking.

Kangwa arrived in Be'er Sheva in the summer of 2024 from Red Star Belgrade, where he had won a Serbian title and tasted Champions League football, for a fee reported at under €1 million. The investment has been repaid many times over. He scored 14 goals and set up 8 more in his first season, then followed with 12 goals and 9 assists in the championship campaign that came after, form that earned him the league's player-of-the-season award. He has 46 caps for Zambia.

AEK's approach is not the first of the summer. Levski Sofia are reported to have offered €2 million for the midfielder earlier in the window, a bid Be'er Sheva turned aside without ceremony. It now looks like the opening move in a market that has steadily warmed since.

In Greece, expectations run higher still. On the podcast Trivela Boys, Kangwa was described as the closest available match for Orbelin Pineda, the playmaker AEK are seeking to replace, with one analyst estimating the eventual fee would land "in the region of €8 million." That figure belongs to Greek media speculation rather than anything either club has put on paper, and it sits well above what has been reported in Israel.

A regulatory clock is ticking underneath the negotiation. Under Article 30.05 of UEFA's Champions League regulations, a player fielded in the qualifying rounds may represent another club in UEFA competition only from the league phase onwards. Be'er Sheva open their qualifying campaign against Vikingur on Tuesday, and if Kangwa plays, he would be cup-tied for the rest of the qualifying and play-off phase, unable to line up for AEK against his old club should the two sides meet in the play-off round, as one Israeli report noted on Sunday evening. An unused substitute is not caught by the rule; only minutes on the pitch trigger it.

The timing sharpens everything. Be'er Sheva open their Champions League qualifying campaign this week, and Kangwa is expected to be central to it, giving the champions every sporting reason to hold firm, and giving their most coveted player a European shop window in which the price may yet climb.

By Monday morning the endgame appeared to be forming, though the picture remained contested. One Israeli report said AEK were expected to improve their offer to roughly €3.8 million and that the deal could be completed within a day, adding that a transfer sealed before Tuesday's qualifier would spare Kangwa the cup-tie. A second outlet quoted sources at Be'er Sheva insisting negotiations were "not close right now," and reported figures for both the fee and the player's personal terms that differ from the first account.

Those around the player left little doubt about his own preference. "This is his time to move," his circle was quoted as saying. "Everyone understands this is the offer — we need to let him go." Unless the clubs converge before kick-off in Reykjavik, the champions' player of the season will simply play on.
facts: AEK Athens have submitted an official offer to Hapoel Be'er Sheva for midfielder Kings Kangwa, reported by two Israeli outlets on 19 July 2026.
The offer is reported to exceed €2.5 million, against a Be'er Sheva asking price of more than €4 million.
AEK are reported to be offering Kangwa around €700,000 a year, against roughly €300,000 at Be'er Sheva (single-source).
Kangwa, 27, is a Zambian international with 46 caps who joined Be'er Sheva from Red Star Belgrade in summer 2024 for a reported fee under €1 million.
He recorded 12 goals and 9 assists in the 2025/26 title-winning season and was named the league's player of the season.
Levski Sofia had an earlier €2 million bid for Kangwa rebuffed this summer (single-source).

Under UEFA regulations (Article 30.05), if Kangwa is fielded in Be'er Sheva's qualifier against Vikingur on Tuesday he becomes cup-tied for the qualifying and play-off phase, and could not face Be'er Sheva for AEK before the league phase.

On 20 July, one outlet reported AEK were expected to raise their offer to about €3.8m with a possible completion within 24 hours, while Be'er Sheva sources told another outlet negotiations were "not close right now"; reported fee and salary figures differ between publications and no agreement is club-official.

body: Maccabi Ashdod have named Noa Konfino team manager of their senior basketball squad ahead of the club's return to Ligat Ha'Al, Israel's top division, according to a report published Sunday. Konfino, 27, takes up the post for the 2026/27 season, and the report states she will be the only woman holding the position in the league.

The role of team manager in Israeli basketball sits at the hinge between the coaching staff, the players and the league office. It is an administrative post covering the daily logistics of a professional squad — travel, scheduling, registration and matchday operations — and its holder is a constant presence around the team throughout the season.

Konfino arrives from the analytics side of the game. According to the report on Sport 5, she most recently headed the statistics department at Segev Sports, the company that supplies statistical services to the Israeli Premier League and graphics for basketball broadcasts. The same report says her love of the game was formed watching basketball with her late father.

"I am thrilled and delighted to join the Maccabi Rotstein Ashdod family," Konfino was quoted as saying. "The team has made an impressive journey from the National League to the Premier League, and I promise to do everything to be part of the team's success next season."

She joins a club on a steep upward curve. Maccabi Ashdod sealed promotion on June 11, beating Ironi Nahariya 94-83 at home to close out the National League playoff final 3-1, with Robert Turner III scoring 30 points in the clincher. The victory completed a two-year climb from the third tier to the top flight under head coach Dan Katzir.

Women in senior administrative roles around Israeli men's professional basketball remain a rarity, which is what gives the appointment its wider resonance. A second, bylined report on the club's season plans, published later on Sunday, independently confirmed both the appointment and that Konfino will be the only woman serving as team manager in the top flight next season.

Ashdod's preparations for their first top-flight campaign since promotion are continuing through the summer, with the roster taking shape around the core that won promotion. Konfino's hiring adds an experienced basketball operations mind to the back office as the club readies itself for life among Israel's elite.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv send six academy graduates on loan to Kfar Shalem in one sweep
dek: The champions have reportedly moved six youth-title winners to partner club Hapoel Kfar Shalem in the second tier, clearing the pathway for playing time ahead of the new season.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv have loaned out six academy players in a single move, sending the group to second-tier partner club Hapoel Kfar Shalem, according to a report published Sunday afternoon by Sport1.

The six are defenders Ron Feldman, Idan Weinberg and Itay Barhoom, together with Rani Rival, Rom Savich and Yoav Junio. All are graduates of the club's youth department and were part of the academy side that won its championship, with several of the group regarded internally as candidates for eventual integration into the senior squad.

Their destination is a familiar one. Kfar Shalem, who compete in the Liga Leumit under coach Noam Shoham, operate as a de facto feeder side for the yellow-and-blues under a cooperation agreement between the clubs, an arrangement Kfar Shalem announced publicly and which channels Maccabi youth graduates into regular senior football in the second division.

The stated purpose of the moves is playing time. Rather than keeping the group in youth or reserve frameworks, the champions want the six exposed to weekly senior competition, with Weinberg the most prominent of the departing players: he has already travelled with the first team for European fixtures and carries squad number 52 on the club's first-team list.

The mass loan fits an established pattern at the club, which routinely farms out young professionals to gain minutes; Transfermarkt currently lists seven other Maccabi players on loan at clubs in Israel, Hungary and Ukraine, among them teenagers Daniel Tishler and Itay Zafrani.

The timing is no accident. Maccabi opened their trophy season on Wednesday with a 3-1 Super Cup victory over Maccabi Be'er Sheva, and the coaching staff are trimming and shaping the squad ahead of the league campaign and European qualification rounds, making a clear runway for the academy group elsewhere the logical step.

Loan durations and any recall or option clauses were not disclosed in the report, and at the time of publication neither Maccabi Tel Aviv nor Kfar Shalem had posted an official announcement of the six moves on their channels; the transfers are therefore attributed to the reporting outlet pending club confirmation.

title: Beşiktaş president says Salah move stalled after agent raised commission demand
dek: Serdal Adalı claims Mohamed Salah approved a move to Istanbul before agent Ramy Abbas sought a commission of roughly 35 percent — a figure the club calls unacceptable and the agent's camp disputes, with an MLS option alongside Israeli defender Or Blorian still floated.

source.name: ONE

body: Beşiktaş president Serdal Adalı has publicly accused Mohamed Salah's agent of derailing the Turkish club's pursuit of the Egyptian forward, claiming an initial understanding with the player was in place before the representative sharply raised his financial demands. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Adalı directed his frustration not at Salah — a free agent since his Liverpool contract expired — but at agent Ramy Abbas.

According to Adalı, Salah was open to the move to Istanbul and went as far as meeting the club's new head coach, Vincenzo Italiano, together with its sporting director, signalling that he wanted to come. It was only after Turkish media reported that the transfer was close to completion, the president said, that the terms changed.

"After we had already reached an initial agreement, because the media published that the deal was close to being finalised, his agent raised his commission demand to inconceivable levels — around 35 percent," Adalı said, in remarks reported by the Israeli outlet ONE. "From our point of view, there is no chance of accepting such percentages. Moreover, we do not think Salah is aware of these sums."

Adalı also denied that outside intermediaries had been involved in the negotiation, insisting the club had dealt only with Abbas directly. The commission figure is, for now, the president's account alone; the agent's side has not confirmed it, and no fee or contract terms have been made public by either party.

Abbas, for his part, has pushed back on any suggestion that a deal exists. "I personally do not know where Mohamed will play next season," the agent said this week, adding that it is not his practice to hold talks with clubs his client would not want to join. Beşiktaş had earlier issued its own statement dismissing reports of a completed transfer as fiction.

Salah's next destination therefore remains genuinely open. Beyond Beşiktaş, the 34-year-old has been linked with Saudi Arabia's wealthiest clubs and with Major League Soccer, where The Athletic has reported a possible move to Sporting Kansas City — a scenario with a distinctly Israeli subplot, as it would make Salah a teammate of Israel international centre-back Or Blorian, who joined the MLS side from Hapoel Be'er Sheva in June.

If Adalı's version holds, the impasse is about the agent's percentage rather than the player's wishes, and talks could yet be revived; if Abbas's denials prevail, the Istanbul chapter may close before it begins. Either way, one of the most decorated forwards of his generation enters late July without a club, and every stated outcome — Turkey, the Gulf, or America — remains conditional on a negotiation that is still visibly unresolved.
facts: Beşiktaş president Serdal Adalı said on Sunday that the club had reached an initial understanding with free agent Mohamed Salah before the deal stalled.
Adalı claimed agent Ramy Abbas raised his commission demand to roughly 35 percent after media reports said the transfer was near completion, calling the figure unacceptable.
Adalı said Salah met new Beşiktaş head coach Vincenzo Italiano and the club's sporting director and indicated he wanted to join.
Adalı said the club does not believe Salah is aware of the sums demanded, and that talks were held only with Abbas, without intermediaries.
Abbas denied any agreement with Beşiktaş, saying on 17 July: "I personally do not know where Mohamed will play next season" (beIN SPORTS).
The Athletic has reported a possible MLS option at Sporting Kansas City, where Israel international defender Or Blorian signed in June 2026 from Hapoel Be'er Sheva.
No transfer has been completed; Beşiktaş earlier issued a statement rejecting reports by Turkish journalist Yağız Sabuncuoğlu that the deal was done.

body: Dolev Haziza, the former Maccabi Haifa captain who left the club this summer after seven years, is expected to sign for Maccabi Netanya, Israeli sports outlet Sport5 reported Sunday, adding that the gaps between the two sides have narrowed in recent days.

Haziza's agent met with Netanya officials on Sunday, and the club hopes to complete the deal within days — ideally before Tuesday, when Netanya is due to hold its traditional season-opening training session. The club is said to have pushed that opening back by a week to finish assembling its squad.

Sunday's report fits a steady trail of coverage over the past month. Netanya's interest first surfaced in late June, when the club was said to have opened preliminary talks with the midfielder, and a report last week described significant progress after head coach Ronny Levy spoke directly with the player, though it noted that gaps over salary still remained at that stage.

Haziza, 31, spent seven seasons at Maccabi Haifa after arriving from Bnei Yehuda Tel Aviv in 2019. Sunday's report credits him with 247 appearances, 43 goals and 41 assists for the Greens, along with three league championships won during Haifa's title run from 2021 to 2023 — a period in which he also wore the captain's armband. Last season he scored nine goals and added two assists.

body: Maccabi Haifa Women's Basketball has opened an academy with the Hebrew Reali School, giving teenage players a structured way to combine high-level training with their secondary education. The programme is open to players from ninth grade upward, and it hands the city something it lacked: a defined pathway for girls who want serious basketball without stepping outside their normal school life.

The arrangement joins a club already competing inside the Israel Basketball Association system with one of Haifa's established schools. Its ambitions go beyond fielding a strong team. The academy is meant to support athletic, academic and personal development under a single structure, rather than leaving families to piece those elements together on their own.

That distinction carries real weight in youth sport. Training loads typically climb sharply through the teenage years, just as exams and travel start eating into a player's time. A school-club model can manage those competing demands more deliberately than either side working alone, though the academy has yet to publish a full timetable, an admissions process or a coaching roster.

There is already a competitive base to build on. Maccabi Haifa Women's Basketball is registered under team code 2198, with Ilan Beck and Rinat Kahana listed as club representatives and its home venue recorded at 19 Bikurim Street in Haifa. The club's girls' upper-group side finished its most recent campaign with 12 wins and two losses from 14 games, according to the association's published table.

That record matters because it means the academy is extending an active pathway rather than inventing one on paper. A player entering in ninth grade can draw a straight line between structured development work and a club that is already competing in the national girls' framework — a link that narrows the gap between introductory youth basketball and a genuinely competitive setting in northern Israel.

The launch was billed as a regional first and drew Sports Minister Miki Zohar and Haifa mayor Yona Yahav, lending the opening civic weight. But the programme's real test will come later, in details still to be settled: coaching quality, training access, academic coordination, and how many players stay in the sport through their later teenage years.

For Maccabi Haifa, the payoff is a clearer route to identifying and keeping local talent. For the Reali School, it offers a formal structure for students whose sporting commitments already resemble those of elite athletes. The framework is now in place; the evidence that will matter comes with the first full season's intake, staffing and competition schedule.

body: Tamar Steinberg finished sixth and Sharon Kantor eighth in the women's iQFOiL event at the Long Beach Olympic Classes Regatta, leaving Israel without a podium finish at the final Sailing Grand Slam stop of the season. Steinberg advanced one round further than Kantor in Thursday's medal series, but neither reached the four-athlete final that decided the medals on what will be the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic course.

Steinberg had entered the medal series in fourth place, earning a bye straight into the semi-final. A difficult launch off the line cost her the early position she needed to advance, and sixth became her final classification. Kantor arrived in better form, having climbed nine places during the qualifying series to reach eighth and a quarter-final berth, but another compromised start ended her run through the knockout ladder.

Daniela Peleg rounded out the Israeli women's iQFOiL entry in 12th, two places outside the medal-series cut. It was a narrow margin in a fleet that had put Steinberg third and Kantor fifth after the second day of racing. Britain's Emma Wilson, who had led the event from the front throughout, converted that position into the overall win.

The men's iQFOiL campaign fared worse, finishing outside the medal series altogether. Yoav Cohen was the leading Israeli in 21st, with Tomer Vardimon 27th and Olympic champion Tom Reuveny 28th. The week amounted to a development exercise rather than a continuation of Israel's medal record in the class, with the course itself and the afternoon sea breeze offering the most useful takeaways.

Israel also sent two athletes into the women's Formula Kite fleet, where Maya Ashkenazi placed 14th and Gal Zuckerman 15th. Their presence mattered beyond the results: Long Beach brought both Olympic board disciplines together for the first time, with high-speed kiteboards and foiling windsurfers racing side by side off Belmont Shore, on the same waters set to host Olympic sailing in 2028.

The regatta ran from 13 to 16 July and drew more than 100 international competitors across the four iQFOiL and Formula Kite fleets. It was the first of this summer's Los Angeles Olympic-class blocks and the closing round of the 2026 Sailing Grand Slam, giving teams an unusually early look at the Olympic venue two years out from the Games.

For Israel, going without a medal marks a meaningful break in what has otherwise been a strong women's iQFOiL season. The sharper lesson, though, came from the elimination racing itself: in a format where advancement can turn on a single short contest, the opening seconds carry outsized weight. Steinberg and Kantor both had the speed to compete for the podium — Long Beach simply showed how little room the medal series leaves for recovery once the start goes wrong.

body: The winners of Sunday's World Cup final will receive championship rings for the first time in FIFA competition history. Argentina or Spain will still lift the trophy and collect the traditional gold medals at New York New Jersey Stadium, but the winning delegation will also be assigned 30 personalised rings modelled on a familiar North American sporting tradition.

The first presentation will come immediately after the final, when the victorious captain and head coach receive temporary versions during the ceremony. Permanent rings will then be produced to measure and delivered later, each of the 30 team pieces individually numbered and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.

The design keeps the World Cup at its centre rather than simply importing another sport's jewellery. One side features the tournament trophy, while the opposite face will be completed only after the final, once Argentina or Spain have settled the match and the manufacturer can personalise it to reflect the winning nation.

FIFA has capped the total edition at 2,026 rings, a direct reference to the tournament year. Thirty are reserved for the champions, and the remaining 1,996 will be offered worldwide as officially licensed supporter pieces. No public price had been announced when the collection was revealed.

The initiative adds a commercial product to the most protected symbol system in football, but it also changes how this particular winning group will be commemorated. Medals belong to football's established presentation ritual; rings are designed to be worn and displayed as a continuing marker of membership in a championship team.

American leagues have long made that idea part of their championship culture, with bespoke rings carrying team colours, records and season references. The 2026 World Cup gives FIFA an obvious setting to adopt the practice: the final is being played in the United States, and the tournament itself has been staged across Canada, Mexico and the US.

What remains unchanged is the sporting order of importance. The ring accompanies the trophy rather than competing with it. For the winner of Argentina against Spain, though, the 2026 title will now produce three distinct keepsakes: the game's most recognised cup, the champion's medal and the first personalised ring awarded by FIFA.

body: Giannis Antetokounmpo used his first formal appearance as a Miami Heat player to define the move in championship terms. Introduced at Kaseya Center on Thursday alongside president Pat Riley and coach Erik Spoelstra, the two-time NBA Most Valuable Player said Miami offered the strongest route to competing for another title. What had been transaction news became, in that moment, the opening statement of a new Heat era.

The trade itself was substantial. Miami acquired Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis from Milwaukee in a deal approved on 6 July, sending Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kasparas Jakučionis to the Bucks along with three first-round picks, a 2030 first-round pick swap and a 2033 second-round pick. That price tag leaves little doubt about the timeline: Miami has traded away a large share of its young core and future draft control in exchange for immediate contention.

Antetokounmpo will wear No. 7 in Miami rather than the No. 34 that followed him through his entire Milwaukee career. The new number, visible during Thursday's introduction and already updated on the Heat's official roster, is a cosmetic detail with real symbolic weight — it marks the line between a 13-season Bucks career and the first major relocation of his professional life.

On the court, the fit starts with Antetokounmpo alongside Bam Adebayo, two elite defenders capable of covering unusual amounts of space and attacking the rim from different angles. That pairing is also Spoelstra's central puzzle. Neither star is primarily a high-volume perimeter shooter, so Miami's spacing, half-court creation and late-game execution will hinge on the guards and wings built around them. The defensive ceiling is obvious; the championship offense still has to be built.

Antetokounmpo brings the credentials to demand that standard be met. He led Milwaukee to the 2021 championship, won back-to-back regular-season MVP awards in 2019 and 2020, and was named Finals MVP during that title run. The NBA's official farewell tally credits him with 21,531 points in a Bucks uniform and ranks him first in franchise history in points, rebounds and assists. Miami is not simply acquiring a superstar's reputation — it is acquiring one whose peak already reshaped a franchise.

His introduction also carried an unmistakable cultural expectation. Riley and Spoelstra have spent years building Miami's identity around conditioning, accountability and postseason ambition, and Antetokounmpo's own reputation for physical preparation and sustained intensity fits that mold closely. That alignment makes the partnership coherent on paper, but it does not resolve the harder questions of health, roster depth or shot creation. Shared standards are a starting advantage, not proof of a championship.

The move also closes the book on the most successful era in half a century of Bucks basketball. Antetokounmpo delivered the championship Milwaukee had waited 50 years to reclaim, then departed as the franchise's all-time leader across its three major cumulative categories. His Miami unveiling did not erase that history — it simply opened the next question: whether his prime can be converted into another title window, now that the Heat has spent one of the summer's largest asset packages to find out.

No game has yet been played with Antetokounmpo in a Heat uniform, and Miami's final rotation remains, for now, a preseason question. Thursday's significance was strategic rather than competitive: the club presented its new centerpiece, the player accepted the pressure of a title mandate, and both sides made clear this trade will ultimately be judged in the postseason. The announcement is finished. The harder work — building a champion around No. 7 — starts now.

body: The NBA is examining the circumstances surrounding Gary Trent Jr.'s new contract with the Milwaukee Bucks, placing a significant free-agent agreement under league scrutiny days after it was reported. A league spokesman confirmed the NBA was continuing to look into the matter.
That is an active review, not a finding that Trent, Milwaukee or his representatives broke a rule.

Milwaukee officially announced Trent's return on Thursday without disclosing financial terms. The agreement has been reported as four years and $64 million, which would keep the 27-year-old guard with the Bucks through the 2029/30 season. NBA.com also records that Trent declined his player option before returning on the new multi-year deal.
At issue is possible salary-cap circumvention through a prior understanding. Trent joined Milwaukee in 2024 on a veteran-minimum contract and returned on another short agreement in 2025.

The reported concern is whether those lower salaries were connected to a promise of a larger contract once the Bucks had acquired the contractual mechanism to retain him above the cap. No such prior arrangement has been proved.

The unusual jump in salary has drawn attention because Trent's production declined in 2025/26. He averaged 8.1 points in 21.2 minutes across 65 regular-season appearances, starting 21 games — both his lowest scoring and playing-time averages since his 2018/19 rookie season. He shot 36 percent from three-point range, down from 41.6 percent the previous year.

Performance alone cannot establish circumvention, however. Teams are free to value shooting, continuity and roster fit differently from the public market, and a player's recent box score does not prove the existence of an undisclosed promise. The league's task is narrower and more evidential: determine how the sequence of agreements was negotiated, and whether any binding commitment predated the point at which Milwaukee was permitted to offer the new deal.

For the Bucks, the timing matters amid a wider roster reset. Trent's contract would create a substantial multi-year commitment to a rotation guard at the same moment Milwaukee are reshaping the team around a younger core. The review does not suspend the agreement, and neither the league nor the club has announced a timetable for a decision or any interim restriction on Trent.

The case also carries significance beyond one player's salary. The NBA's cap system depends on clubs competing within shared exceptions and negotiating windows, and if a team can secure discounted seasons by promising a later reward, that would undermine the intended balance.

Equally, treating every surprising contract as evidence of wrongdoing would interfere with legitimate negotiations — which is why the distinction between suspicion and proof must remain visible throughout the review.

Trent remains a Bucks player while the league gathers information. The verified position is therefore limited but consequential: Milwaukee have re-signed him, the four-year, $64 million terms are reported rather than club-disclosed, and the NBA is examining the surrounding circumstances. Any conclusion about a violation, penalty or contract status must wait for the league's findings.

body: Slavko Vinčić will referee Sunday’s World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at New York New Jersey Stadium. The appointment gives the 46-year-old Slovenian his fourth match of the tournament and places one of European football’s most experienced officials in charge of the game that will decide the world title.

Vinčić will work with Slovenian assistant referees Tomaž Klančnik and Andraž Kovačič. Jordan’s Adham Makhadmeh has been named as the fourth official, with compatriot Mohammed Al-Khalaf serving as reserve assistant referee. The five-man on-field group combines an established Slovenian trio with two Jordanian officials for the final assignment.

This will be Vinčić’s second men’s World Cup. He refereed Argentina’s 2–1 group-stage defeat by Saudi Arabia and Wales’ 2–0 win over Iran in Qatar in 2022. His previous experience with Lionel Messi’s team therefore comes from one of the defining shocks of that tournament, although that historical result supplies context rather than any evidence about how Sunday’s final will be handled.

Vinčić has already taken charge of three games at the 2026 tournament: Brazil’s draw with Morocco, Jordan against Algeria and Mexico’s round-of-32 victory over Ecuador. The last of those included Piero Hincapié’s dismissal. Sunday will be his first appearance since that knockout assignment and his first World Cup final as the referee in the middle.

The scale of the occasion is familiar from club football. Vinčić controlled Real Madrid’s 2–0 win over Borussia Dortmund in the 2024 Champions League final at Wembley. He also refereed the 2022 Europa League final between Eintracht Frankfurt and Rangers in Seville, which Frankfurt won on penalties. UEFA’s official record lists him as an international referee since 2010.

Klančnik and Kovačič were also Vinčić’s assistants at the 2024 Champions League final, giving the Slovenian trio experience together in a comparable one-match showpiece. That continuity is a functional advantage rather than a guarantee of an error-free night: positioning, eye contact and concise radio communication all depend on rehearsed habits when the noise and speed of a final compress decision time.

For Argentina and Spain, the practical significance lies in preparation rather than mythology around past results. Teams use an official’s recent matches to study thresholds for contact, dissent, advantage and time management. Vinčić’s established assistants matter equally: offside decisions and communication across the crew can shape a final long before a major disciplinary call reaches the referee.

body: Spain conducted their World Cup final preparations under a haze of Canadian wildfire smoke in northern New Jersey on Thursday, though the latest outlook points toward improving conditions before Sunday rather than any confirmed disruption to the match itself. The smoke visibly altered the backdrop for the finalists, but it has not produced an official change to the Argentina–Spain schedule.

The Spanish squad trained outdoors in East Hanover, roughly 15 miles from New York New Jersey Stadium, the sun dimmed behind a grey layer overhead. The first 15 minutes of the scheduled hour-long session were opened to media. Argentina, meanwhile, remained at their base in Marietta, Georgia, after reaching the final, meaning the two teams were not preparing under the same local air conditions at that point in the week.

Air quality in East Hanover began Thursday in the 'unhealthy' range before improving to 'unhealthy for sensitive groups' by mid-afternoon. The principal concern was fine particulate matter, PM2.5, carried south by the smoke. Such particles pose a genuine risk around high-intensity outdoor exercise, since players move far more air through their lungs than they do at rest — making the training environment a legitimate performance and welfare issue even in the absence of a postponement.

New York State's official air-quality advisory, covering the New York City metropolitan area, had warned that fine-particle levels could exceed an Air Quality Index value of 100. Together, those records corroborate the haze witnessed at Spain's session, without elevating a temporary advisory into a forecast for the final itself.

Treating the final as already under threat would run ahead of both the forecast and the tournament authorities.

Spain's staff retain the option to adjust exposure and workload should local readings deteriorate again, though no confirmed change to the training programme has been published. The more immediate asymmetry between the finalists is geographic rather than medical: Spain were already working close to the venue under the haze, while Argentina could continue their recovery in Georgia before travelling north. Whether that difference carries any sporting cost cannot be established from air-quality readings alone.

The next meaningful evidence will come from the weekend forecast and the teams' final training sessions.
