body: The 16th Maccabiah opened at Jerusalem's Teddy Stadium on 16 July 2001, after coming close to postponement. A deteriorating security situation had reduced expected participation and forced organizers to reconsider whether the Games could proceed at all. The eventual opening was therefore more than a ceremonial start — it was the moment months of uncertainty became an actual competition.

The Maccabiah's later official history records an emergency meeting in June and government assurances of exceptional security measures. That retrospective explains the institutional decision. Contemporary reporting shows what it looked like on the ground: athletes were assigned protection in transit, entry checks were extensive, and the opening-day account counted more than 1,000 security personnel around the stadium.

Even under those conditions, the ceremony had scale. A report filed from Jerusalem that night recorded more than 2,000 athletes representing 45 countries and an estimated 20,000 local spectators. Delegations entered to applause, with the Israeli team receiving the largest response, while fireworks, acrobats, dancers and mass performance turned the field into a stage without disguising the tension outside it.

The two athletes entrusted with the flame gave that spectacle a sharper sporting meaning. European pole-vault champion Alex Averbukh carried the torch into Teddy Stadium, and Keren Leibovitch — who had won three swimming gold medals at the Sydney Paralympics the previous year — lit it. Their roles joined elite Israeli achievement across Olympic and Paralympic sport at the exact moment organisers were asking the Games to stand for continuity.

Teddy Stadium carried its own significance: the official Maccabiah record identifies the 2001 ceremony as the first opening in the movement's history to be held there. Moving the event to Jerusalem placed the Games in a venue surrounded by the political and security pressures of the moment, rather than insulating the ceremony from them.

There was another memory the organizers could not set aside. Four members of the Australian delegation had died after the bridge collapse at the 1997 Maccabiah opening in Ramat Gan, and the 2001 ceremony included a memorial for those athletes, while the Australian team had gathered at the collapse site the previous day. The new Games were opening while responsibility, grief and trust from the previous edition remained unresolved.

The program itself had been cut back. It ran seven days instead of the usual ten, and the field was smaller than at a normal Maccabiah. Contemporary coverage before the opening expected roughly 2,000 athletes from around 40 countries, against about 5,000 participants in a typical edition — a forecast that differs slightly from the opening-night count simply because it was written before final arrivals. Together, the two describe the same reality of a reduced but still international Games.

Competition still produced an emphatic sporting record. Israel finished far ahead in the medal table with 96 golds, 74 silvers and 74 bronzes; the United States followed with 21 golds, 23 silvers and 30 bronzes. Olympic champion Lenny Krayzelburg was the leading name in the pool, while Olympic gold medallists Maria Mazina and Sergei Charikov strengthened the fencing programme. Those figures matter because they prevent the event from being remembered only as a security operation with an opening ceremony attached.

Later recollection often treats the 2001 Maccabiah as a statement of resilience, and the contemporary evidence supports that reading — though it also makes the achievement less abstract. Athletes made individual decisions to travel. Organizers accepted a compressed event. Security personnel transformed how everyone moved, and Jerusalem spectators filled Teddy Stadium anyway.
The enduring fact is not that fear disappeared on 16 July. It is that a Jewish international sporting event began in full public view while that fear was still present.

source.author: BC Žalgiris Kaunas

verificationSources.label: Official Žalgiris announcement

body: Žalgiris Kaunas have signed Jonas Valančiūnas, bringing Lithuania's senior centre back to domestic club basketball after 14 NBA seasons. The move gives the EuroLeague side one of the continent's most recognisable interior players. Its real value, though, is more specific than reputation: a half-court reference who can create efficient possessions without the offence needing to be built around perimeter isolation.

The homecoming label carries an edge. Valančiūnas developed with Perlas and Lietuvos Rytas before leaving for Toronto in 2012, and he has never returned to his former club. His last EuroLeague season came with Rytas in 2010/11, followed by a EuroCup campaign in which he averaged 10.8 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.6 blocks. Wearing Žalgiris green reconnects him with Lithuanian basketball while placing him on the opposite side of its most charged domestic rivalry.

Toronto took Valančiūnas fifth in the 2011 draft, and his NBA career then ran through Memphis, New Orleans, Washington, Sacramento and Denver. Across that six-team span he moved from long-term starter to situational veteran without losing the core of his game — scoring on the block, screening for higher-usage creators, controlling the defensive glass and accepting changing minutes as lineups grew smaller and faster.

His final season in Denver captures that last transition. Valančiūnas appeared in 65 games, started six, and averaged 8.7 points, 5.1 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 13.4 minutes behind Nikola Jokić. The modest playing time should not be mistaken for an empty role; Denver needed concentrated physical production in short stretches. Žalgiris can now offer the same skills more possessions and a clearer place in the hierarchy.

Offensively, the appeal starts with geometry. A centre who establishes deep position forces the defence to choose between conceding single coverage and sending help from a shooter, and his screens can create separation before he even touches the ball. Offensive rebounds turn defended possessions into second chances. For those advantages to hold up at EuroLeague speed, Žalgiris will need to keep enough shooting on the floor around him that the lane doesn't clog with extra defenders.

The defensive calculation is less forgiving. Valančiūnas remains a strong rebounder and a deterrent near the rim, but opponents will look to involve him repeatedly in pick-and-roll actions and drag him into space. Žalgiris can guard against that with conservative coverage, disciplined weak-side rotations and mobile defenders elsewhere on the floor. The signing supplies size; preventing rivals from turning that size into a target is the coaching challenge that follows.

His recent international form suggests meaningful high-level production is still there for the taking. At EuroBasket 2025 he averaged 15.7 points and 6.7 rebounds for Lithuania across seven games, converting 64.7 per cent of his two-point attempts. A national-team tournament is shorter than a EuroLeague season, but it showed that a larger offensive workload can still produce efficient scoring rather than ceremonial veteran minutes.

Žalgiris are, in effect, making two bets at once. The emotional one is that Lithuania's most established active centre can deepen the bond between the team and its basketball public. The competitive one is that a defined European role will get more out of Valančiūnas than the reduced assignment he held in Denver. Neither is guaranteed by the name on the shirt, but both rest on a skill set — screening, post scoring, rebounding — that remains immediately legible.

Few Israeli teenagers are assessed inside an elite European first-team programme, and Goren entered that setting at 17 while remaining part of Barcelona's youth structure — a credible step in his development, neither a ceremonial appearance nor proof that the senior transition is complete.

title: England protected a lead until they stopped protecting the game
dek: Gordon’s goal rewarded Tuchel’s shape, but retreat invited Argentina to keep returning. Fernández and Martínez exposed the difference between managing a score and controlling a match.

source.name: FIFA
source.originalTitle: England v Argentina: Live stream, team news, tickets and more

verificationSources.label: Independent full-time match report
Confirmed match chronology and final score
FIFA semi-final context and confirmed venue
FIFA tournament final schedule

body: England's semi-final plan worked long enough to create the most dangerous illusion in tournament football: that a narrow lead and control are the same thing. Anthony Gordon's 55th-minute goal vindicated the attacking structure Thomas Tuchel had chosen. Declan Rice moved the ball early, Morgan Rogers attacked beyond Argentina's compact midfield, and Gordon arrived on the far side of the defence — a coherent sequence, not a lucky break, that put England in a position from which a place in the final should have been manageable.

The distinction between a sound plan and a complete one emerged immediately afterwards. England had shown how to progress through Argentina's pressure when their midfield received with a forward picture and a runner threatened the last line. Once ahead, though, those same forward connections became intermittent, and possession stopped being a means of altering the geography of the match. It became something England were prepared to surrender in exchange for numbers behind the ball.

There is nothing inherently timid about defending deeper against Lionel Messi. A compact block can close the central lanes he uses to combine, restrict passes into the penalty area and invite lower-value circulation in front of the defence. But depth creates its own bill: clearances travel to opponents rather than team-mates, the centre-forward becomes isolated, and the defending side must execute another sequence without the relief of making the opponent retreat. England accepted that bill for half an hour and never found a reliable way to stop it accumulating.

Argentina did not require Messi to dominate every possession — his value was also gravitational. England had to preserve enough cover around him that other players could approach the edge of the area without the defensive line stepping out recklessly. When Messi supplied Enzo Fernández in the 85th minute, Fernández still needed an exceptional finish from outside the box, yet the opportunity belonged to a broader pattern: Argentina were repeatedly established in England's half, close enough to recover second balls and begin another attack before the block could breathe.

The equaliser should have changed the tactical calculation. At 1-1, England no longer had a lead to protect, so the benefits of extreme caution had disappeared while its costs remained. The required intervention did not have to be dramatic — a controlled spell on the ball, one midfielder receiving beyond the first press, or a forward winning a foul higher up the pitch would have forced Argentina to reorganise. Instead, the match retained the same direction, and England continued to defend the same territory under greater emotional pressure.

Lionel Scaloni's use of Lautaro Martínez sharpened that pressure. The substitute supplied a different reference point inside the penalty area and headed the winner in the second minute of added time. Substitutions are often assessed as isolated acts of inspiration, but this one worked because Argentina had already arranged the conditions around it: territory, repeated entries and enough players near the box to sustain attacks. Martínez changed the target; England did not change the location from which Argentina could aim at him.

Game management is consequently a more demanding idea than adding a defender or lowering the block — it is the management of risk across every phase. The team in front still needs an outlet who can secure the first pass, a midfielder willing to receive under pressure, and at least one route that makes the chasing side turn towards its own goal. Without those elements, extra defensive numbers may protect the penalty area while simultaneously increasing the volume of attacks it must absorb.

None of this means Argentina's comeback was predetermined. Fernández's strike required rare execution, and a late header can always be decided by a small positional error or an individual duel — tactical analysis becomes dishonest when it removes contingency from football. The relevant question is not whether England could have guaranteed survival, but whether their choices improved or worsened the probability of seeing the match out. By steadily reducing their own attacking threat, they gave Argentina more attempts to find the exceptional action they needed.

The chronology is unforgiving. England led from the 55th minute until the 85th and then conceded again before extra time could begin. The two goals had different finishers and different final actions, but they grew from the same sustained territorial advantage. Tuchel solved the opening problem of how to damage Argentina's shape; he did not solve the closing problem of how to keep Argentina's shape occupied while England were ahead. That is why this defeat belongs less to the language of collapse than to the finer, more useful distinction between defending a score and controlling a game.

body: Israel's men's under-20 team did not merely lose a knockout game to Greece. It crossed into a different tournament. The 79–66 defeat in the round of 16 at Arena Stožice II ended any route to the quarter-finals and dropped Oren Aharoni's side into the classification bracket for ninth to 16th place.
The next opponent is already fixed: Italy, in Ljubljana on Thursday. The winner advances towards places nine to 12; the loser falls into the bracket where relegation from Division A is decided.

Greece created a separation that Israel never recovered from. Oren Sahar scored 20 points and Rany Belaga added 19, meaning two players supplied 39 of the team's 66. That concentration did not make defeat inevitable, but it left too small a margin once other possessions stopped producing. In youth tournament basketball, where scouting time is short and physical condition shifts fast, a team needs a third scoring route once its top two options are carrying almost three-fifths of the total.

The disappointment stings more because Israel had built a credible group phase: a 78–68 win over Romania, a 90–77 loss to host Slovenia, then an 87–73 win over Czechia for a 2–1 record. Across those three games Israel averaged 80.7 points. Greece held the team nearly 15 points below that mark, narrowing a functioning offence into little more than Sahar and Belaga.

The format offered no cushion for that winning record. All 16 teams entered the round of 16, so group performance decided the pairing but bought no bye and no second route to the title bracket. One defeat was enough to remove Israel from the top half — and the same format now hands the team an immediate second assignment, this time with survival rather than a medal shaping the stakes.

Italy arrive in the same position after an 86–63 loss to Serbia, their own tournament equally uneven. Neither round-of-16 margin should be read as a forecast for Thursday, and both sides have had less than a day to reset. The more relevant contest will be over control — which team can run its half-court offence without letting the earlier defeat rush its decisions or turn missed shots into hurried defensive transitions.

For Israel, the rotation needs to create support without asking Sahar and Belaga to play any less aggressively. A third ball-handler reaching the paint, an extra shooter converting the first clean kick-out, a frontcourt player generating second possessions — any of it would change the geometry of the attack. The goal isn't balance for its own sake; it's to stop Italy loading its defence onto the two players who carried the scoring against Greece.

The relegation arithmetic is unforgiving but not yet terminal. The eight round-of-16 losers play through the nine-to-16 classification bracket, and only the teams finishing 14th, 15th and 16th drop from Division A. Beat Italy, and Israel guarantees a nine-to-12 finish, removing that danger outright. Lose, and Aharoni's team enters the 13-to-16 bracket, where just one of four final positions is safe.

That is why the response matters beyond this squad's eventual ranking in Ljubljana. Division A keeps Israel's under-20 programme inside Europe's highest annual competitive tier. The tournament Israel wanted after the group phase is gone, but the team still controls whether this becomes a contained knockout disappointment or a structural setback — and Italy is the first, cleanest chance to settle which.

body: The Recanati family have completed the acquisition of the Federman family's 29% holding in Maccabi Tel Aviv Basketball Club, lifting their own stake from 29% to 58%. The transfer of funds closed the transaction on Wednesday evening. Its value has been reported at approximately $50 million, though the private completion documents have not been published.

The arithmetic reshapes the club's ownership balance immediately. Two families no longer hold matching blocks; one shareholder now controls a majority of the equity. For an institution whose governance has long rested on several established ownership groups, that concentration is itself the central development.

The route to completion was not straightforward. Earlier reporting described an agreement under which Rapyd founder Arik Shtilman would acquire the Federman stake. The Recanati family then exercised a right of first refusal, matching the terms to secure the same 29% holding themselves. Wednesday's payment therefore did more than confirm an intention — it ended the competing transaction process and transferred the shares.

There is a historical dimension to the deal as well. The Federman family's involvement spanned decades in which Maccabi occupied the commanding position in Israeli basketball and remained a durable EuroLeague institution. Their exit removes one of the names most closely associated with that era. The Recanati family, already embedded in the club, are not arriving as outside owners — they are consolidating control from within the existing structure.

A 58% equity holding, however, does not disclose the whole system of authority. Public reporting has not set out the post-transaction board, the voting threshold for reserved decisions or the protections retained by the remaining shareholders. Majority ownership may provide decisive influence over ordinary matters, but it should not be read automatically as unilateral control over every strategic or financial choice.

The reported purchase price calls for a similar distinction. Roughly $50 million values the stake that changed hands; it is not a new player budget and does not flow by definition into basketball operations. Recruitment, coaching resources and EuroLeague expenditure depend on separate operating decisions — treating the acquisition value as available sporting cash would confuse the price of ownership with the financing of the team.

The disclosures that matter from here will be practical rather than ceremonial: who sits on the board, how responsibilities are divided, whether shareholders approve a different multi-year budget and which executives carry the resulting mandate. Those details will show whether concentrated ownership produces faster decisions, larger investment or simply a new distribution of the same obligations.

For now, the confirmed boundary is clear. The Federman family's 29% stake has changed hands, the Recanati holding has reached 58% and Maccabi Tel Aviv have entered a majority-owner phase. The transaction itself is complete; its sporting meaning will be determined by governance and capital decisions that have yet to be made public.

title: Pogačar breaks open the Tour on Bastille Day as lead reaches 3:36
dek: A decisive attack on the Col de Pertus carried the yellow jersey to a third stage win of the 2026 Tour and put Jonas Vingegaard more than three and a half minutes behind.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: מרסק הטור: פוגצ'אר ניצח גם ביום הבסטיליה
source.author: Sport5 desk

verificationSources.label: Tour de France official stage 10 report

body: Tadej Pogačar did more than win the Tour de France's Bastille Day mountain stage. His attack on the Col de Pertus split the general-classification group, erased the last survivor of the breakaway and converted a difficult but still compressed race into one governed by a lead of three minutes and 36 seconds.
By Le Lioran, the yellow jersey had taken his third victory of this Tour, forcing every rival team to reconsider what a successful final fortnight could still look like.

Stage 10 was built to expose weak management after the rest day: 166.6 kilometres from Aurillac, roughly 3,800 metres of climbing and seven categorised ascents. A 31-rider break formed only after repeated attacks, yet UAE Emirates-XRG never let its advantage grow beyond 1:25.
That control made the front group expend energy without allowing it to become a strategic threat. The stage was being prepared for the favourites long before Pogačar made his move visible.

Javier Romo spent 36 kilometres alone before being caught at the foot of Puy Mary. Richard Carapaz then took over, driving his advantage to a minute by the base of the first-category Col de Pertus. Carapaz's attack had enough quality to win a stage under different race conditions; here, it became the target against which the yellow jersey could measure his own acceleration.

Visma-Lease a Bike increased the pace through Davide Piganzoli, but Pogačar attacked one kilometre from the Pertus summit and crossed the gap to Carapaz almost immediately. He was 20 seconds clear of the Vingegaard-Evenepoel-Seixas group over the top, then kept pressing across the final ascent of the Col de Font de Cère.

The important detail was not simply that nobody followed the first acceleration. The gap continued to grow after the terrain became less selective, evidence that the damage extended beyond one explosive minute.
Pogačar finished 32 seconds ahead of Remco Evenepoel, while Paul Seixas took third. Jonas Vingegaard reached the line in seventh place, 44 seconds behind the winner.

In the overall standings, Vingegaard now trails by 3:36 and Evenepoel sits third at 4:06. Those are no longer gaps that can be recovered through bonuses, positioning or one opportunistic descent; they demand a sustained failure from the leader or a mountain offensive capable of producing minutes.

The stage also rearranged the contest behind the two principal favourites. Isaac del Toro lost 1:31 and fell to seventh overall, while Evenepoel moved onto the podium, Seixas entered the top five and Juan Ayuso climbed ahead of both younger riders. UAE therefore gained time through Pogačar while losing a second high overall position, a trade that simplifies leadership but reduces the number of cards the team can play against long-range attacks.

The victory was Pogačar's 24th Tour stage win and made him the first rider to win three stages held on 14 July. That record carries symbolism, but the sporting achievement is sharper: three victories in the opening ten stages while wearing the burden of outright favourite. He has been able to contest stages without allowing the daily race for wins to weaken his control of the overall classification.

Control now changes sides. UAE can judge breaks by composition, defend selectively and make Visma spend riders before Vingegaard attacks. Vingegaard cannot wait for Pogačar to volunteer a bad day; his team must create repeated pressure, isolate the race leader and accept the counter-attacking risk that accompanies any move large enough to recover three and a half minutes.
Stage 10 did not settle the Tour, but it rewrote its economy: Pogačar owns time, and everyone else must spend energy to buy it back.

body: John Otomewo has completed a €1.6 million move from Hapoel Jerusalem to Stade de Reims, the largest sale in Hapoel's history. The 19-year-old defensive midfielder has signed a five-year contract with the French Ligue 2 club, having completed the medical process that took him to France earlier this week.

What makes the transfer remarkable is its compression. Otomewo arrived in Jerusalem in the summer of 2025 after Hapoel identified him at a talent tournament in Nigeria. He entered through the youth team, trained with the senior group and made his first-team debut in the Jerusalem derby.

Within a single season, he moved from discovery project to regular starter to the subject of a substantial European sale. Hapoel's official player record credits him with 21 senior appearances in 2025/26 and one Israel State Cup goal.

The club's own assessment emphasises ball-winning, aggression and the ability to circulate possession in tight areas. Those are not ornamental qualities for a holding midfielder — they explain how a teenager became trusted during a relegation fight, when mistakes in central areas carry immediate consequences.

The €1.6 million fee matters beyond the headline record. Hapoel Jerusalem operate as a supporter-owned club, so transfer income is one of the few ways to generate capital at a scale that ordinary matchday and commercial revenue rarely produce.

Otomewo's sale validates a recruitment model built on finding players before better-funded markets have completed their evaluations, then giving them meaningful senior minutes rather than storing them behind established names. That model only works if the sporting pathway stays credible.

A club cannot sell the promise of development indefinitely; players and representatives need evidence that strong performances lead to responsibility and, when the right offer arrives, mobility. Otomewo now provides that evidence — he was not merely scouted cheaply and traded. Hapoel placed him in Premier League matches, absorbed the risk of his learning curve and received a record fee once the football justified the projection.

Reims are buying a different kind of risk. A five-year contract gives the French club time to develop him and protects potential resale value, but it does not remove the jump in difficulty — he must adapt to a new language, a more physically demanding weekly environment and a squad whose immediate objective is to compete near the top of Ligue 2.

His cleanest route into the side will begin with the work that accelerated his rise in Jerusalem: covering space in front of the centre-backs, winning contact without losing positional discipline, and moving the first pass quickly enough to let more creative players receive facing forward. Reims may eventually ask for a broader passing range or greater penalty-area contribution, but the transfer does not require him to become a different player on arrival.
For Hapoel, the deal closes with both sporting loss and strategic proof. Replacing a starting midfielder will cost time and money, and the success of one sale cannot guarantee the next.

Still, the club have turned a Nigerian scouting initiative, a youth-team place and 21 senior appearances into €1.6 million in a year. For Otomewo, that same sequence has produced five seasons in French football — not merely a record deal, but a development pathway made commercially real.

body: Johnathan Motley has joined Red Star Belgrade after Hapoel Tel Aviv formally ended his two-season spell on Friday. The Serbian club presented the American centre as a new signing, describing the agreement as multi-year. A reported negotiation is now a completed move between two EuroLeague clubs.

The two confirmations answer different parts of the transfer. Hapoel's farewell closed out Motley's Tel Aviv contract and removed him from the current first-team list, while Red Star's presentation established his destination. No public buyout, release payment or salary figure accompanied either announcement, so the financial mechanism behind the move remains private.

Motley leaves with a permanent place in Hapoel's modern history. He was central to the 2024/25 EuroCup title run and won the Finals MVP award as the club secured its first European trophy. Hapoel's own career record lists his spell as 2024–2026, and the farewell statement places him among the players who turned the club's European ambition into a championship.

His value went well beyond headline scoring. Motley gave Hapoel a low-post target who could seal off smaller defenders, finish through contact and pull help defenders toward the paint, and his screens, offensive rebounding and foul pressure shaped the space available to the guards around him. Losing that profile changes how half-court possessions are built, even if the replacement frontcourt produces similar overall totals.

Hapoel have already rebuilt much of that area. Their current squad lists Zach LeDay, Dan Oturu and Tai Odiase among the interior options, part of a wider roster reshaped for another demanding domestic and European campaign. body: Maccabi Tel Aviv’s summer planning has reached a genuine decision point. Walker remains under contract with Maccabi for next season. The clause, however, allows him to leave without a transfer payment if he agrees terms with an NBA team before the deadline. That distinction matters: this is not an ordinary transfer negotiation controlled by the Israeli club, but a defined contractual window in which the player can choose an NBA return.

According to Sport5, Walker and his representative are in Las Vegas while the NBA Summer League brings executives and agents from across the league into the same market. Sport5 adds that talks with Ife Lundberg are continuing and are not conditional on Walker’s decision, but the remaining guard recruitment is easier to define once Walker’s scoring, salary and minutes are either in the plan or removed from it.

The basketball question is larger than star power. If Walker stays, Maccabi retain a proven one-on-one creator and can target complementary ball-handling and defence. If he leaves, the club must replace high-volume shot creation late in possessions, a role that is difficult to reproduce with several smaller signings. The deadline therefore controls not just one name but the balance of the roster.

For now the accurate status is narrow: Walker is contracted to Maccabi, his NBA option remains open until the stated deadline, and no NBA deal was reported as complete. The next reliable update should be a signed agreement, a club announcement or the expiry of the clause—not another layer of speculation.

body: Ten-man Maccabi Tel Aviv beat Hapoel Be’er Sheva 3–1 at Turner Stadium on Thursday night to win the Israel Super Cup. Saied Abu Farchi scored twice and Sagiv Yehezkel supplied all three Maccabi goals, turning the season’s first domestic showpiece into a forceful statement by the State Cup holders.

Maccabi’s opening goal punished a serious error in Be’er Sheva’s defensive build-up, gifting Abu Farchi a direct route to goal. Be’er Sheva’s reply was more inventive: Kangwa completed the move with a backheel, restoring parity before Maccabi could settle into protecting the lead. The exchange turned what had promised to be a cautious first competitive outing into an immediate test of which side could regain control faster.

Maccabi retook the lead in the 58th minute through Dor Peretz, set up by a Yehezkel delivery. The move rewarded Maccabi for finding Peretz between Be’er Sheva’s midfield and defensive lines: Yehezkel carried the ball to the left side and supplied the final ball, and Peretz did not need maximum power, placing his finish accurately enough to beat Ofir Marciano. It also gave him a goal that stood, after an earlier effort had been ruled out for offside in the build-up.

Roy Revivo was shown a second yellow card in the 66th minute, reducing Maccabi to ten men. They refused to protect a one-goal margin passively, attacking the space behind Be’er Sheva’s advancing shape, and another Yehezkel cross let Abu Farchi complete his brace and settle the final at 3–1.

Yehezkel was briefly shown a second yellow card of his own during a late substitution, after turning back from the nearest touchline when cups were thrown towards him. Referee Aviv Klein reviewed the incident and cancelled the caution. The intervention was permitted under the 2026/27 law change that allows VAR to review a clearly incorrect second yellow when it immediately produces a red card; the substitution law also permits a different exit point for safety or security reasons.

The opening exchanges exposed the tactical burden carried by both midfields. Maccabi’s five-man unit is designed to place bodies around the ball and release Dor Peretz or Sagiv Yehezkel in support of Abu Farchi, while Be’er Sheva need Lucas Ventura and Eliel Peretz to protect transitions while allowing Kangwa to move into scoring positions. Both mechanisms produced an early reward; neither, at first, gave its defence sustained protection.

Be’er Sheva started Ofir Marciano, not new signing Marco Wolff, in goal. Guy Mizrahi, Miguel Vítor, Matan Baltaxa and Ofir Davidzada formed the back line, with Roy Levy and Amir Ganah supporting Igor Zlatanović. Maccabi selected Ofek Melika behind Itay Ben Hamo, Mohamed Ali Camara, Raz Shlomo and Roy Revivo, with Abu Farchi ahead of Yehezkel, Itamar Noy, Issouf Sissokho, Ido Shahar and Peretz.

The football began after a significant security operation around Turner. Four people were detained close to the stadium after police found several clubs during a vehicle search, and Be’er Sheva station officers transferred the occupants for further questioning while the South District deployed additional personnel in the area before kick-off.

No charge, supporter affiliation or attempt to enter the stadium was specified in the pre-match police account, and no injury was reported in connection with the stop. The established facts are the intervention, the seizure and the detentions; they do not support a conclusion about criminal responsibility or a link to either club without further official information.

The fixture was a direct rematch of the two showpieces that framed last season. Be’er Sheva won the previous Super Cup 2–1 despite playing most of the match with ten men, then went on to secure the league title, before Maccabi responded in May by beating Be’er Sheva 2–1 in the State Cup final. Thursday’s win reversed the previous Super Cup result and added a second consecutive trophy against the champions.

The European calendar gives the performance value beyond the silverware. Be’er Sheva move into Champions League qualifying against Víkingur Reykjavík, while Maccabi begin their Europa League programme later in July. Maccabi’s transition threat and response to the red card provide a strong platform, but both teams must still reduce the moments when one lost pass exposes an entire defensive structure.

title: Zach LeDay signing raises Hapoel Tel Aviv’s frontcourt ceiling
dek: The EuroLeague forward has signed a two-year deal and returns to the country where his professional career began, bringing Hapoel another high-level scoring option.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv have signed Zach LeDay through the end of the 2027/28 season, adding a proven EuroLeague scorer to a frontcourt that can now be assembled in several different ways. The appeal is not simply his résumé. LeDay gives Hapoel a forward capable of creating an advantage without forcing the offence to change shape around him on every possession.

The move also closes a circle. LeDay began his professional career with Hapoel Gilboa Galil in 2017/18, then built his European standing with Olympiacos, Žalgiris Kaunas, Olimpia Milano and Partizan before a second spell in Milan. He returns to Israel at 32 with extensive knowledge of the competition Hapoel are trying to navigate, rather than as a newcomer still learning its tactical and physical demands.

At 202 centimetres, LeDay sits between traditional frontcourt definitions. He is strong enough to hold position against many power forwards, mobile enough to attack a closeout, and credible enough from distance that a defender cannot simply retreat into the paint against him.

That versatility shows up in how he punishes mismatches. Against a switch, he can take a smaller opponent to the block; against a slow big, he can face the basket and force the first defensive rotation to arrive early.

His inside-out range is the organising value of the signing. A conventional centre often dictates where the other four attackers must stand, but LeDay can occupy the elbow, screen and pop, slip into space, or finish a possession as the nominal five. That variety should help Hapoel avoid possessions in which their spacing gives away the intended action before the ball has even crossed half court.

His recent numbers support the tactical case. EuroLeague's official record lists 12.2 points and 3.8 rebounds across 18 appearances in 2025/26. The sample was shortened, but the scoring level still matters: Hapoel are acquiring a player who carried meaningful usage for Milan, not one relying on a distant peak or a reputation detached from current production.

There are trade-offs to manage. A smaller frontcourt can concede size on the defensive glass, while lineups that pair LeDay with another scoring big will need perimeter defenders capable of containing the first action. His presence creates options; it does not remove the need to choose among them, and the most revealing pre-season decision will be how often Hapoel trust him at centre against elite EuroLeague opponents.

The two-year term makes that fit more consequential than a short rental would. Hapoel can build combinations around LeDay across more than one campaign, but they are also committing roster space to a veteran whose value depends on precision rather than raw athletic dominance. Guards must get the ball to his preferred spots, and the surrounding shooters must punish the help he draws.

This is why the signing changes Hapoel's possibilities more than it changes a depth chart. LeDay can be a scorer, a screener or a spacing device within the same quarter. Connect those roles coherently and he will make several teammates easier to use; fail to, and even a distinguished name can become one more talented player waiting for his turn.

body: Anan Khalaili’s proposed transfer from Union Saint-Gilloise to Inter has fallen through after the Israeli international failed to receive the sporting-fitness approval required for registration in Italy. Sport5 reports that the collapse ended a deal that had been moving toward completion and would have represented an exceptional transfer for an Israeli-developed player.

The distinction between a club medical and the Italian fitness ruling matters here. Inter president Giuseppe Marotta said the refusal came through the Italian Olympic Committee’s process rather than Inter’s own medical staff, and ANSA had previously reported that the authority requested additional tests before reaching its decision. No diagnosis has been made public, and privacy prevents responsible reporting from going further than the documented ruling.

Luciano Buonfiglio, president of the Italian Olympic Committee, subsequently said Italy’s more rigorous controls are designed to protect athletes, stressing that life takes priority over earnings. His remarks explain the principle behind the decision, but they neither identify Khalaili’s medical information nor establish how another country’s registration process would assess him.

The fitness outcome changes the status of every earlier transfer report. Travel, agreed personal terms and advanced club negotiations do not amount to a completed move; registration and the relevant medical approval remain essential. Khalaili therefore remains a Union Saint-Gilloise player unless and until another club completes its own process and announces a deal.

According to Sport5, Ipswich Town are now expected to intensify talks with Union. The English club made a formal approach as far back as May, the report says, and is considered capable of operating in the financial range previously discussed with Inter — though interest is not the same as an accepted offer, and neither club had announced a transfer at the time of the report.

Sport5 also describes optimism in Khalaili’s camp that a move to England can be completed during the current window. That confidence is attributed to the people around the player and should be read as their assessment, not as independent medical evidence or a guarantee that a future examination would produce a different conclusion.

Walla Sport later carried an outside cardiologist’s view that Khalaili could be approved under a different medical assessment, while Sport1 reported that his camp still prefers an English move. Neither follow-up overturns Inter’s decision or completes a new transfer; they add context to the same event and are consolidated here rather than published as duplicate stories.

From a football perspective, Ipswich would present a different development question from Inter. Khalaili’s acceleration, direct running and ability to cover the right flank are attractive qualities in an intense English game, but the decisive issue would be the role offered to him and the club’s plan for managing whatever concern stopped the Inter transaction.

The next credible milestones are clear: a formal offer accepted by Union, permission for a medical, completion of the receiving country’s fitness process and official club confirmation. Until those steps occur, the accurate headline is not that Khalaili is joining Ipswich, but that one major move has collapsed and a previously interested English club is reported to be exploring the opening.

Union Saint-Gilloise have since indicated how the next phase will run. Head coach David Hubert, quoted in Israeli reports on 18 July, said Khalaili is expected back in training next week after time with his family in Israel, and confirmed the club will conduct its own medical examinations in Belgium on his return so it can hold a complete, independent picture of his condition to share with interested clubs.

Hubert said he speaks to the 21-year-old almost daily, called the collapse hard to digest “both sportingly and humanly,” and said Union are prepared for either outcome — a stay or a sale. Those around the deal are further reported to expect a “big and beautiful move” to be completed this summer; that is the camp’s stated confidence, not an agreed transfer.

body: Eight spectators were injured close to the finish of stage nine of the Tour de France when a press vehicle left its route and entered the crowd area. Initial reports said one person was seriously hurt in an incident approximately 500 metres from the finish line.

According to the report, the driver of a vehicle associated with L’Équipe suffered a medical episode and collapsed at the wheel before the vehicle crossed the barriers. That account explains the reported sequence but remains part of an incident now subject to investigation; it should not be expanded into a definitive medical or legal conclusion without statements from the authorities.

The immediate priority is the condition of the injured spectators and the driver. A finish zone is one of the most crowded and controlled environments on a Grand Tour stage, with supporters, officials, media vehicles and race personnel moving through narrow managed corridors. A vehicle breach in that area therefore creates risk well beyond the road itself.

The event also raises operational questions for race organisers: how press vehicles are routed near the finish, what physical separation exists between vehicles and spectators, and how emergency teams reach an incident while a major sporting event is still in progress. Those questions require the evidence from the formal review rather than instant assumptions.

body: The dispute surrounding the Ironi Tiberias investigation has escalated from evidential objections into a procedural challenge. The club have submitted a petition to the Israel Football Association’s supreme judicial body seeking to halt or disqualify parts of the process, according to a report detailing the requested remedies.

The petition reportedly asks for the investigator to be removed, for any prospective indictment built on the disputed inquiry to be cancelled and for the association to disclose the material collected in the case. Those are applications made by the club, not rulings already granted by the federation, and the distinction matters while the case remains open.

Ironi Tiberias are also reported to have filed a police complaint concerning the investigator and to be pursuing NIS 500,000 in a separate civil claim. A federation petition, a police complaint and a damages action operate on different legal tracks; the existence of one does not establish the merits of another.

The new challenge follows earlier reporting that identified difficulties in the evidence and suggested five players could be cleared because the available material might not meet the disciplinary threshold. That possibility has direct sporting weight, but it remains provisional until the competent football authority issues a decision.

The club’s lawyers had previously asked the association to examine allegations concerning the investigator, including claims touching other teams and betting. Those allegations remain allegations. They should not be converted into findings, nor should the club’s confidence about the case be confused with an acquittal.

The immediate competitive issue is player eligibility. Anyone formally cleared can return to normal activity, while any remaining disciplinary exposure for players or staff will depend on the evidence admitted and the decisions issued through the association’s judicial structure.

A subsequent report says the national anti-doping agency has opened plea-arrangement discussions with some of the players in an effort to resolve part of the case more quickly. Talks are not completed agreements, and any proposed sanction would still have to satisfy the standards applied under the World Anti-Doping Code. The development therefore changes the procedural route, not the current eligibility verdict.

The positions in those discussions have now become more specific. The agency is reported to be seeking a one-year suspension for coach Eliran Hodeda, four months for Chen Sol and terms of between three and five months for the players involved. The parties are described as far apart, so those periods are demands in an unresolved negotiation rather than sanctions imposed by a tribunal.

Until the petition itself and a federation response are available in a claim-specific public record, the defensible position is narrow: Ironi Tiberias have mounted a reported legal challenge, the underlying evidence is contested and the outcome is not yet settled.

body: Spain are through to the World Cup final after beating France 2–0 in a semi-final settled by one moment of penalty-area pressure and one emphatic second-half finish. Mikel Oyarzabal converted a 22nd-minute penalty before Pedro Porro doubled the lead in the 58th minute, the reward for a performance built on territorial control and disciplined protection behind the ball.

The opening goal gave Spain the kind of control that matters more than possession figures in a knockout match: France now had to chase the game without allowing the spaces Spain's wide players are built to exploit. Oyarzabal took the responsibility from the spot and put his side ahead. It was his fifth goal of the tournament, drawing him level with Spain's record for goals in a single men's World Cup.

France's task grew harder when centre-back William Saliba went down and was replaced by Maxence Lacroix in the 30th minute, eight minutes after the opening goal. The enforced change disrupted an already stretched defensive unit, though no authoritative post-match diagnosis has established the nature or severity of Saliba's problem. It should be treated as a confirmed in-game injury substitution, not as evidence of a specific condition or recovery timetable.

Porro's goal after the interval changed the calculation completely. At 1–0, France still needed only one clean attack to reset the semi-final; at 2–0, every forward run carried the risk of leaving another transition behind it. Spain protected the lead and kept France scoreless, turning a high-profile meeting of attacking talent into a controlled passage to the final.

The result also settles the historical angle that framed the build-up. France arrived with an exceptional modern record in World Cup knockout matches, but Spain did not need to defeat that history in the abstract — they scored first, added the insurance goal and managed the match in front of them.

Didier Deschamps questioned the refereeing afterwards, particularly the sequence that produced Spain's penalty, but he also acknowledged the central football verdict: Spain controlled the contest and France operated below the level required for a semi-final. One decision can shape the game state without explaining why France never disrupted Spain once behind.

Lucas Digne accepted personal responsibility for the challenge on Lamine Yamal that produced the penalty, saying in his first public response that he was disappointed in himself. He also thanked France's supporters and looked ahead to the team's remaining tournament commitment. It adds human context without changing the wider analysis: the foul opened the scoring, but France's collective response never forced Spain out of control.

Spain's defensive record gives the final a second tactical theme. Unai Simón has recorded six clean sheets while conceding only once in seven tournament appearances, and the back line has done more than survive pressure in its own box — Spain's possession structure and counter-press have repeatedly cut down the transitions opponents can create.

This is Spain's second men's World Cup final; their first, in 2010, ended with the title. The identity of the 2026 opponent will be decided by the other semi-final, so any tactical projection for the final must wait until that fixture is done.

Spain now move from the problem of breaking France down to preparing for a different opponent and a different kind of final. Their semi-final supplied the cleanest possible foundation: a lead before the interval, a second goal before the hour, and a night without conceding.

That framing matters because outcomes alone can conceal the quality of a decision. A football side may survive several dangerous transitions and still have protected the ball poorly. A basketball roster may add the most recognisable available guard without solving the combinations around him.

A cycling leader can finish safely in the bunch while his rivals have nonetheless increased the future cost of defending the jersey. The score records what happened; structure helps explain whether it can happen again.

Hapoel Be'er Sheva's Champions League tie with Víkingur Reykjavík begins with rest defence. Víkingur advanced 3–2 on aggregate against Győr and scored twice away in Hungary, evidence that they can damage a tie when space opens beyond an opponent's first attacking line.

Look for receptions on the half-turn, progressive actions after central touches and the speed with which he counter-presses after losing possession. Tomáš Satoranský presents Hapoel Tel Aviv with a roster problem rather than a simple recruitment question. At 2.01 metres, he can see and pass over smaller guards, defend a wider range of match-ups and share the court with another ball-handler without sacrificing backcourt size.

Spain's 2–0 semi-final victory over France offers a different lesson in knockout control. Mikel Oyarzabal's penalty established the favourable game state and Pedro Porro's 58th-minute goal forced France to commit greater numbers.

The five cases also show why 'aggression' and 'caution' are inadequate analytical labels. Be'er Sheva can attack with numbers while remaining conservative about the spaces they leave. Gloukh can play between the lines without abandoning the build-up.

Hapoel can make an ambitious signing whose greatest value is flexibility rather than usage. Spain can dominate possession while treating transition prevention as an attacking responsibility. Dor Peretz will remain captain and lead the team into Kenny Miller's first full season, the club's own record confirms, closing a period in which he and his family had weighed the professional and personal case for moving abroad.

That choice carries more weight than simply retaining an experienced midfielder. Peretz is the bridge between a dressing room accustomed to title expectations and a coach still installing his authority — he offers penalty-box running, leadership and a feel for the club's competitive temperature. Just as importantly, his decision spares Maccabi from replacing a captain while rebuilding other areas of the side at the same time.

body: Oscar Gloukh has chosen continuity over another summer transfer chase. The Israel midfielder says he remains focused on Ajax unless the club decides otherwise, and he has defined his second-season objective with unusual clarity: become a regular starter. It is a more demanding ambition than simply staying, since it places the argument about his future inside the team rather than in the rumour market.

Ajax's official record makes the scale of that commitment plain. Gloukh joined from RB Salzburg in August 2025 for a guaranteed €14.75 million, with variables capable of lifting the fee to €17.25 million. He signed for five seasons, wears No. 10 and remains under contract until June 2030 — neither the investment nor the shirt guarantees selection, but both explain why a quick exit would mean abandoning the project before its shape has settled.

His first campaign contained enough production to resist any easy verdict. Gloukh's account of the season gives him nine goals and six assists in 38 appearances across all competitions. Those numbers show he affected games; they do not show that Ajax found him a permanent tactical home, particularly in a year when he worked under three coaches with different ideas and selection priorities.

The position question sits at the centre of it all. Gloukh sees his best work coming as a central midfielder or from the left with licence to move inside, where a fixed touchline role would leave him fewer chances to receive between the lines, turn toward goal and combine around the penalty area. The challenge for Ajax is to create those access points without leaving the team narrow or asking the full-back to defend an entire flank alone.

The challenge for Gloukh runs the other way. Recent work has placed greater emphasis on forward defending, rapid recovery after losing the ball and collective pressing. A creative player becomes automatic at this level once the staff trust the moments between his touches — the angle of his press, his reaction to a turnover, his discipline when another midfielder advances. Technical authority gets him into the conversation; repeatable off-ball decisions keep him in the XI.

That is why the coaching instability matters without becoming an excuse. Ajax's official record confirms the June departure of Oscar García after a brief first-team spell, another change in a season already marked by movement on the bench. Each reset altered the language used to judge the same player, and Gloukh now needs a stable reference point quickly, because a second year cannot be evaluated forever through the disruption of the first.

Eran Zahavi's earlier warning to his former Maccabi Tel Aviv team-mate fits the moment. Dutch football offered attacking possibility, he said, but the historic image of Ajax could not simply be assumed to match the institution Gloukh was joining. That advice reads less like pessimism than a demand for realism: reputation supplies opportunity, while daily structure determines whether a gifted midfielder actually develops.

For Israel, the best outcome is not a move for movement's sake. It is a Gloukh who earns a defined role, plays through difficult weeks and becomes responsible for more than highlights. His public position removes one source of noise — pre-season usage, pressing assignments and the first competitive team sheets will now reveal whether Ajax see their No. 10 as a specialist option or as part of the side's permanent spine.

body: Israel’s basketball coaches’ organisation has asked the national association to suspend changes to coach registration and licence renewal for the 2026/27 season. Sport5 reports that the organisation’s legal adviser, Amir Cohen, sent a formal letter to the association with copies to culture and sports minister Miki Zohar and a Ministry of Sport representative.

The first disputed measure is financial. The letter says that from 1 October the cost of renewing a coaching certificate after the deadline would rise from NIS 90 to NIS 200. That is an increase of more than 120 per cent. The coaches’ organisation argues that a change of that scale requires a documented economic and professional explanation rather than a simple administrative notice.

The second measure concerns continuing education. According to Sport5, the association decided to remove a requirement for professional-development hours. The coaches’ organisation says members previously invested money and time to meet that standard and that abandoning it without consultation or explanation disregards both that investment and the professional rationale behind the earlier rule.

The letter frames the argument as a governance issue, not only a disagreement over price. It contends that the Basketball Association performs a public function and therefore carries heightened duties of transparency and reasoned decision-making. That is the coaches’ legal position as reported by Sport5; it is not yet a court finding, and the association’s complete response was not included in the report.

Three demands have been set with a 14-day deadline: the full minutes of the meetings in which the changes were adopted, a written explanation of their economic and professional basis, and a structured process for coaches to present their position. If those demands are not met, the organisation says it may seek regulatory intervention, freedom-of-information material or legal proceedings.

The practical significance extends through the basketball pyramid. Registration rules affect senior, youth and development coaches, while continuing education is part of the system that establishes common professional standards. The useful next update will be the association’s reasoning and whether implementation is paused; until then, the accurate description is a formal challenge and ultimatum, not a completed legal victory for either side.

title: Paris, 1993: the night Israel turned 2–1 into history
dek: France were preparing to celebrate World Cup qualification. Israel, bottom of the group and without a competitive win, scored twice in the final eleven minutes to leave the Parc des Princes in disbelief.

body: The scoreboard at the Parc des Princes read 2–1 to France, and the clock had entered its final eleven minutes. For the hosts, this was supposed to be the night a place at the 1994 World Cup became official. For Israel, bottom of Group 6 and still without a win in the campaign, there was no qualification prize left to chase.
That imbalance is what makes the ending endure. One team had the ticket almost in hand; the other played as though the match itself was enough.

Ronen Harazi had given Israel a 20th-minute lead. France responded with the authority expected of a side built around Eric Cantona, Didier Deschamps, Jean-Pierre Papin, Laurent Blanc and Marcel Desailly. Franck Sauzée equalised in the 28th minute, and David Ginola made it 2–1 in the 39th.
The Israel Football Association's official record confirms that score at half-time — a familiar shape for a favourite briefly inconvenienced before control is restored.
Control never became comfort. Shlomo Scharf's Israel stayed close enough for one moment to matter. In the 64th minute, Eyal Berkovic replaced Avi Nimni.

With eight minutes of normal time remaining, the substitute scored the equaliser. The IFA records it in the 82nd minute; FIFA's retrospective places it at 82 minutes as well. Either way, the effect was immediate: France had gone from celebration to calculation, and the stadium was waiting for the whistle rather than a party.

Then came the goal that fixed the match in Israeli sporting memory. In the second minute of added time, Reuven Atar scored to make it 3–2. The official records agree on the scorer and the final result.

UEFA later quoted Atar describing it as the greatest moment of his career. It was also his first goal for the senior national team, delivered in Paris against a side that believed its evening had already been written.
The result did not send Israel to the World Cup. The IFA's campaign record shows a team that finished sixth with one win, three draws and six defeats — the victory in Paris was that lone win.

Its meaning came from a different place. Israel had lost the reverse fixture 4–0 and had conceded heavily elsewhere in the group. The Parc des Princes offered no broader redemption, only proof that one match can break entirely from the season around it.
For France, the shock became the first half of a national sporting trauma. They still had one home qualifier left and needed only a draw against Bulgaria.

A month later, Emil Kostadinov's late winner made it France 1–2 Bulgaria and sent the visitors to the World Cup instead. FIFA's histories connect the two Paris defeats, but the Israeli victory deserves to stand on its own — it created the danger before Bulgaria delivered the final consequence.
More than three decades later, the game remains powerful because its facts resist embellishment. Israel trailed at half-time. Berkovic entered from the bench and equalised. Atar scored in added time.
A team with nothing left in the table found something permanent in the record instead — and that precise sequence is why people still tell the story.

title: Mexico, 1970: the goal that put Israel on the World Cup map
dek: Three minutes after Sweden took the lead in Toluca, Mordechai Spiegler answered from distance and created a moment that still stands alone in Israeli football history.

body: Israel arrived in Mexico in 1970 as World Cup debutants, having qualified against Australia and stepped into a tournament whose scale the squad had previously only watched from a distance. The opening group match brought a 2–0 defeat by Uruguay. That result left Emanuel Sheffer's side needing a response against Sweden in Toluca — not for symbolism, but simply to stay alive in the competition.

The pressure had a simple shape. Israel had only three group matches and no cushion for a slow start, with two points awarded for a win under the scoring system of the time. Another defeat would have left the final fixture against Italy with almost no competitive leverage. Sweden, in other words, was the match where participation had to become resistance.

The first half on 7 June ended goalless. Sweden broke through in the 56th minute through Tom Turesson, according to the Israel Football Association's official match record. For a debutant already behind in the group, the goal could have made the tournament suddenly feel very short. Instead, Israel answered almost immediately.

Mordechai Spiegler equalised in the 59th minute. FIFA's retrospective describes a strike from around 20 metres, while the IFA record confirms both the scorer and the 1–1 final score. The distance matters: this was not the product of a slow passing move worked into the six-yard box, but a decision taken early and struck cleanly enough to change the match before Sweden could settle into its lead.

The goal remains unique. The IFA's campaign record shows Israel scored only once across its three matches in Mexico, making Spiegler the country's sole men's World Cup goalscorer. Stripped of context, that distinction can sound like a museum label. In its real setting, it was an equaliser struck three minutes after falling behind, under the pressure of possible elimination.

Its timing also reshaped the tactical picture. Sweden never got the chance to protect its lead through a long spell of slower possession or a deeper defensive block, because Israel removed that game state almost as soon as it appeared. The remaining half hour became a contest for the next goal rather than an attempt to escape a settled Swedish advantage — holding the draw was active match management, not survival after a late consolation.

Israel's team was built on collective discipline rather than reliance on one star to carry every phase of play. The line-up against Sweden read: goalkeeper Itzhak Vissoker, captain David Primo, Itzhak Shum, Giora Spiegel and Spiegler. FIFA later recalled the squad's club-like cohesion, with preparation, shared responsibility and an absence of ego central to how the players believed they could compete.

Four days later, Israel drew 0–0 with Italy in the same city, an Italian side that included Luigi Riva and Gianni Rivera, according to the IFA record — and did so without conceding. Combined with the result against Sweden, it meant the debutants left Mexico with two points under the scoring system then in use, and only three goals conceded across three matches.

Israel have not returned to the men's World Cup since 1970, an absence that adds extra weight to every surviving photograph and replay. But the achievement needs no romantic inflation. The sequence speaks for itself: a first tournament, an opening defeat, an immediate response against Sweden, a clean sheet against Italy, and one goal that still stands as the country's entire World Cup scoring record.

That distinction matters because the agreement itself is unusually large, even by NBA offseason standards. The proposed package would send Leonard to Toronto, with Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick moving to Los Angeles alongside unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033, second-round picks in 2030 and 2033, and a 2027 first-round pick swap. It was agreed in principle on 30 June, but it remains listed as on hold rather than completed.

Toronto explained its position on 9 July. The club said it had been informed that acquiring Leonard would also mean assuming the risk of any outcome from the investigation that might affect the player, and so the Raptors elected to wait for the process to finish. They stressed, however, that they still want to bring Leonard back. On the public record, the pause is not a renegotiation of the basketball package; it is a response to uncertainty over the status of the contract and the player.

The underlying review concerns whether a reported $28 million endorsement agreement between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC breached NBA salary-cap rules. The league opened the investigation in September 2025 and appointed outside counsel to conduct it. No violation has been established, and the existence of an investigation should not be treated as a finding against Leonard, the Clippers or any individual involved.

Silver's latest intervention narrows one point without resolving the central problem. He said the external inquiry must run its course, and while he maintained a summer target, he stopped short of giving a fixed completion date. For Toronto, that leaves a major part of its 2026–27 roster plan suspended: the club cannot build with certainty around Leonard while the players and draft assets in the proposed exchange remain attached to an uncompleted transaction.

The sporting stakes are significant. Leonard is coming off a season in which he averaged 27.9 points, 6.4 rebounds and 3.6 assists across 65 games. Toronto, meanwhile, improved by 16 wins, finished fifth in defensive efficiency and took Cleveland to seven games in the first round. Adding an elite half-court scorer and defender would raise the Raptors' ceiling, but the cost — two rotation players and control of multiple future draft assets — makes the unresolved risk impossible to dismiss as paperwork.

Los Angeles is waiting on the other side of the same transaction. The Clippers have already moved toward a younger roster, and the proposed return of Ingram, Dick and long-range draft capital would accelerate that reset. Until the investigation concludes and the trade is formally processed, though, neither franchise can treat its intended return as settled inventory.

The accurate position, then, is narrower than the most dramatic versions of the story suggest. Leonard has not completed a move to Toronto, the agreed framework has not been cancelled, and the NBA has not announced any sanction. Silver has expressed an expectation that the review will finish this summer, but the calendar remains open. The next decisive event will be the investigation's conclusion — not another round of trade speculation.

title: World Cup final halftime reportedly set to stretch towards 30 minutes
dek: The planned 11-minute performance would require a substantially longer interval than the 15-minute maximum in Law 7, although FIFA has not publicly confirmed the final restart timetable.

body: FIFA is reportedly preparing to stretch half-time at the World Cup final to somewhere between 25 and 30 minutes — roughly double the conventional break — to accommodate the tournament's first-ever final halftime show at New York New Jersey Stadium. The longer timetable has not been publicly confirmed by FIFA, and should be treated as a reported operational plan rather than a settled amendment to the match schedule.

The technical conflict is straightforward. Law 7 of the Laws of the Game entitles players to a half-time interval not exceeding 15 minutes. Competition rules must state the duration, and the interval can be altered only with the referee's permission, but the published law still sets 15 minutes as the ceiling. A 25-to-30-minute pause would not be a minor scheduling tweak; it would need a clear explanation of how match authorities intend to apply that provision.

FIFA has confirmed the entertainment component. The governing body describes an 11-minute live broadcast featuring Madonna, Shakira, BTS and Justin Bieber, with Burna Boy, Gustavo Dudamel and the PS22 Chorus also listed alongside Coldplay. The final takes place on Sunday, 19 July.

What remains unannounced is the full interval window needed to move production equipment and performers onto the field, deliver the show, and clear the playing surface in time for the second-half restart.

That distinction between performance time and interval time matters. An 11-minute show cannot simply be dropped into an ordinary 15-minute break: players and staff still need time to leave the pitch, receive tactical and medical instructions, return through the tunnel and complete any permitted re-warm-up, while production crews install and remove staging around those football operations. The reported 25-to-30-minute figure reflects that total logistical window, not the duration of the music alone.

From a performance perspective, the concern isn't that an extra quarter-hour automatically causes injury — it's the break in routine at the highest-intensity point of the tournament. Players normally manage hydration, treatment and tactical adjustment against a predictable restart, and a substantially longer pause could require revised warm-up procedures, particularly for substitutes and for starters whose muscle temperature drops while they wait indoors.

The referee's role also needs precision. Law 7 allows the referee to approve an alteration to the interval, but that is different from improvising an event schedule on matchday. Teams, match officials and broadcasters would need a single documented restart plan in place before kick-off, including the warning sequence for players to leave the dressing room and the point at which the field returns to sporting control once the production has cleared it.

For now, three facts can be separated cleanly: the final and its 11-minute show are official; the Laws of the Game retain a 15-minute half-time maximum; and a 25-to-30-minute interval is being reported without a matching public FIFA timetable. Until that operational notice appears, the scale of the extension — and the mechanism used to authorise it — remains the unresolved part of the story.

body: Ironi Kiryat Ata have added Nike Sibande to their backcourt, a 1.93-metre guard whose recent European résumé takes in Spain's Liga Endesa and a EuroCup season with NINERS Chemnitz. The signing gives Kiryat Ata a physically stronger perimeter option who is comfortable attacking from either guard spot, reshaping a rotation that has already retained Tomer Asayag.

Sibande was born in Indianapolis on 6 June 1999 and is listed by FIBA as representing Uganda as well as holding United States nationality. His official EuroCup profile names him as a guard and records NINERS Chemnitz as his 2025–26 club.

That blend of size and international experience should let Kiryat Ata vary defensive match-ups without changing personnel whenever an opponent switches between a small point guard and a bigger scoring guard.

His college career was already a study in adaptation. Sibande moved from Miami University in Ohio to Pittsburgh and was named the Atlantic Coast Conference's Sixth Man of the Year in 2023 — recognition for a player who learned to influence games without needing every possession run through him, a useful trait for an import joining an Israeli rotation with established domestic guards.

The professional path since has ranged even wider. Sibande began with Kataja in Finland, then played for Maroussi and Merkezefendi before reaching Spain with Girona, and Darüşşafaka and Chemnitz added two more tactical environments along the way. Kiryat Ata are therefore not asking a first-year professional to solve the usual problems of travel, scouting adjustments and shifting roles at the same time as he learns the league.

The ACB's official record lists 25 league appearances for Girona in 2024–25. The number matters less as a headline than as evidence of the level he has already had to process: Liga Endesa demands quick reads in pick-and-roll coverage, disciplined off-ball positioning and the ability to manufacture a usable possession late in the shot clock. Kiryat Ata are buying into that accumulated experience as much as any single scoring average.

Tactically, his value starts with pressure. A guard of his size can attack a switching defender, crash the defensive glass to start transition, and absorb contact when the first option does not open a clean lane. Kiryat Ata will still need to settle how much primary creation he carries and how the shooting load is spread around him, but the signing widens the range of line-ups in which the team can defend with comparable size across three perimeter positions.

What comes next is integration rather than reputation. Sibande has changed leagues repeatedly in the early part of his career, so role clarity will matter — who initiates the offence, where he receives the ball, and which opponent he guards to start games. If Kiryat Ata can make those responsibilities stable, his broad résumé gives them a guard built for more than one kind of contest.

body: Ronen Hanzis is returning to competitive football with Ironi Beit Dagan after two seasons away from the senior game. The 24-year-old left-sided attacker joins a club in Liga Bet South A, Israel's fourth tier, at a point when the prestige of his development years matters far less than his capacity to train, recover and contribute every week.

The pedigree remains unusual for this level. Hanzis moved from Maccabi Petah Tikva into Maccabi Tel Aviv's youth system in 2019, reached the senior side the following year and made his first-team debut in the 2020 Super Cup. He later came off the bench in Maccabi's Champions League play-off against Salzburg, an appearance that placed him one tie from the group stage while still a teenager.

His clearest evidence of sustained senior production came during a loan at Beitar Tel Aviv Bat Yam, where Maccabi's official career record credits him with six goals in 22 appearances. The same record lists 33 youth-international appearances and six goals for Israel, a reminder of how regularly he was selected within the national pathway before his club momentum slowed.

None of those numbers can substitute for current match fitness. Hanzis last appeared in the 2023/24 season, so Beit Dagan are not receiving a player whose recent output can be projected neatly from one campaign to the next — they are receiving a footballer with high-level references and a long competitive interruption. That combination creates upside, but it also makes patience and workload management central to the signing.

Beit Dagan's setting changes the terms of his career. At Maccabi, a young winger had to win isolated minutes inside a squad built to chase titles and European qualification; in Liga Bet, Hanzis can pursue continuity and a larger share of attacking responsibility. The opportunity is greater, but the entitlement is not — his place must still be earned against teammates who already understand the division's tempo and physical demands.

The useful performance markers go beyond goals. Beit Dagan need to see whether Hanzis can repeat high-speed runs, receive under contact and recover quickly enough to press again after an attack breaks down. His movement without the ball and the quality of his final action will reveal more than a single sprint or an eye-catching dribble, since a returning winger has to reconnect the sequence between anticipation, acceleration and decision.

Liga Bet is not a controlled rehabilitation environment. Matches can become direct, second balls carry disproportionate value, and surfaces or game states do not always favour a technically accomplished wide player. That should not diminish Hanzis's advantages so much as sharpen the test: if he can impose his timing and touch without withdrawing from the physical work, his background ought to become visible in repeatable actions rather than in reputation alone.

This is a reset with a measurable first objective — remain available and accumulate a serious run of matches. Goals, assists and a possible route back up the pyramid can follow, but they are downstream of continuity. Hanzis has already been close to elite football and has already spent a long period outside the competitive rhythm; Beit Dagan now offer him something more valuable than a nostalgic label — the chance to make his present-day game the subject again.

title: Wærenskjold wins the fastest stage in Tour de France history
dek: The Uno-X rider took the Nevers sprint after 161.3 kilometres at an average 50.91 km/h, eclipsing a record that had stood since Mario Cipollini’s 1999 victory.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: מהאגדות: ניצחון ענק והיסטורי לסורן ורנסקיולד בקטע ה-11 בטור
