body: Søren Wærenskjold won stage 11 of the Tour de France in Nevers, completing the 161.3 kilometres from Vichy in 3hr 10min 06sec for his first Tour stage victory. The peloton's average speed of 50.91 km/h made it the fastest road stage in the race's history.

The finish was nothing like a sprint assembled around one dominant lead-out train. Wærenskjold launched early, in a broken sequence, held his speed and denied Olav Kooij the space to come past. Jasper Philipsen was classified third after the finish review.

The Norwegian's advantage lay in recognising the moment before the sprinters' trains had imposed their usual order, then committing without waiting for reassurance. That distinction matters, because raw speed alone does not explain the result.

Wærenskjold is a powerful classics rider who can survive demanding terrain and produce a heavy acceleration, not a pure sprinter whose programme is built entirely around the final 200 metres. In Nevers those broader attributes became sprint weapons: stability in a disordered approach, enough strength to open early, and the resistance to keep his effort from collapsing before the line.

The stage record adds a second layer to the day. Mario Cipollini's 1999 win between Laval and Blois had set the previous road-stage benchmark at 50.355 km/h; Wærenskjold's stage beat it by more than half a kilometre per hour despite two fourth-category climbs and an advertised 1,400 metres of elevation gain. The short route and a sustained tailwind helped, but neither could produce that number on their own — the race had to refuse to settle.

Nelson Oliveira, Mathis Le Berre and Anthon Charmig kept the breakaway alive until 5.5 kilometres remained, forcing the sprinters' teams to keep chasing rather than negotiate position. Julian Alaphilippe had already lost contact. The prolonged pursuit fed straight into a frantic final approach, with no lull for the peloton to reorganise.

Uno-X Mobility converted that tempo into a specific opportunity. Moving Wærenskjold forward before the narrowed run into Nevers did not give him a long, uninterrupted lead-out — it gave him contact with the front and the freedom to choose his own launch. His early move was a tactical response to uncertainty, not a substitute for pace.

The general classification stayed intact: Tadej Pogačar finished safely in the main group, still 3min 36sec clear of Jonas Vingegaard, with Remco Evenepoel third at 4min 06sec. But a day without time gaps was not a day without cost — after the Massif Central, the contenders and their teams were denied the calmer transition the profile had promised.

For Uno-X Mobility, it is the team's second Tour victory, after Jonas Abrahamsen's breakthrough in 2025. For Wærenskjold, it changes how rivals must read fast finishes: he does not need a conventional sprint to be dangerous, and disorder may suit him better than order. Nevers will stay in the record book at 50.91 km/h, but the real lesson was less mechanical — the rider who read the finish first was still strong enough to make that reading count.

body: Hapoel Eilat have appointed Rani Cohen as chief executive as the club prepares to return to Israel's top basketball division. The timing makes the role more than a routine administrative change. Eilat are moving from a dominant National League campaign into a competition with different licensing demands, salary pressures and roster risk, and Cohen arrives with experience inside both a major club and the league's central administration.

The promotion itself was earned emphatically. Eilat secured their place in April with an 84–70 win in Ashkelon, then closed out the National League regular season with 29 victories from 30 games. The first clock is administrative: licensing, registrations, budget controls and commercial commitments all have to be ready for a division that applies far more financial and operational pressure. Decisions that could once be made in separate departments during a National League season now have to run through a single top-flight plan.

The second clock is sporting. A roster built to control a long second-division campaign must now survive weekly match-up disadvantages without signing contracts that damage the club beyond a single year. Foreign-player balance, domestic depth and the relationship between coaching priorities and the available budget become connected decisions rather than isolated recruitment choices.

Eilat's geography adds a further layer of difficulty. The club must recruit players and staff to Israel's southernmost top-level market, manage the travel and training logistics that come with it, and convert the momentum of a 29–1 season into a stable local audience. None of that is solved by the promotion record alone — Cohen's value will be measured by whether the club can build repeatable systems around those constraints, rather than lean on the emotional lift of returning to the league.

No contract length or detailed executive structure has been made public. What is verified is that Cohen takes charge of a promoted club with an unusually strong statistical base and a compressed transition window. The sporting department must still assemble a roster capable of defending top-flight space and pace; the new chief executive's job is to make that ambition financially and operationally sustainable.

title: The final is not Messi against Yamal. It is a contest over where risk lives
dek: Argentina can make Spain’s possession uncomfortable; Spain can make Argentina defend choices rather than players. Sunday’s final will be decided by the spaces around its two headline names.

source.name: Associated Press
source.originalTitle: The World Cup final is set, with Messi and Argentina facing Yamal and Spain for the title on Sunday

verificationSources.label: Confirmed finalists and current championship context
FIFA final date, venue and competition schedule
FIFA historical context for an Argentina–Spain final

body: The temptation is to market Sunday's World Cup final as a private appointment between Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal. It is an irresistible image: the defining player of one generation opposite the young attacker already being asked to carry the next. It is also a poor tactical description. Messi and Yamal will shape the final most profoundly through the decisions they force from players nowhere near them, and the trophy will go to whichever team can move that risk into ground it is prepared to defend.

The competitive frame is unusually rich. Argentina reached New York New Jersey by recovering from a 55th-minute deficit to beat England 2-1; Spain arrived through a controlled 2-0 victory over France. FIFA's schedule places the final on Sunday, 19 July, and it will be the first World Cup final between the reigning world champions and the reigning European champions. Argentina can become the first side since Brazil in 1962 to retain the trophy, while Spain are chasing the second world title in their history.

The coaches add a layer of familiarity to that history. Luis de la Fuente taught Lionel Scaloni during his coaching education in Spain, and both have spoken publicly about their friendship. It will sharpen the contest without removing either man's need to solve what the other team has become.

Spain's central question is how aggressively to use the width that has helped them dictate territory. Yamal can receive outside the opposing block, carry a defender towards him and open an inside lane for a midfielder or overlapping runner. The value is not the isolation alone but the chain reaction it triggers: Argentina must decide whether the nearest midfielder shifts across, whether the full-back steps out, and who then protects the pass released behind that pressure. Spain want the defending side making several connected choices at speed.

Argentina's answer cannot simply be to assign more bodies to Yamal. Every extra defender pulled towards Spain's right side widens the space elsewhere, especially if the first clearance is not secured. Scaloni's team need the near-side pressure forceful enough to delay the attack and the far side compact enough to contest the next pass — a problem of distances rather than bravery. Let those distances stretch and Spain can keep the move alive without asking Yamal to beat two players himself.

Messi poses the inverse problem. He does not need to stay fixed in one lane, so Spain cannot solve him with a permanent marker without damaging their own midfield geometry. Follow him with a centre-back and Argentina gain depth for a runner; drop a midfielder too early and Spain lose pressure on the next pass; leave him unattended and he receives facing forward. Spain must defend the handover — the moment responsibility for him passes from midfield to defence without either line losing shape.

That makes possession after possession loss the final's most consequential phase. Spain can advance for long stretches with structure intact, but the players stationed behind that attack must be ready for Argentina's first forward pass. Messi's threat multiplies when he receives before the Spanish block has reset and a runner can attack the space beyond him. Spain do not need to eliminate every turnover — only to stop it becoming a clean, central transition where Argentina choose the timing of the final ball.

Argentina face a related burden once their own attacks end. Their comeback against England was built on sustained territory late in the match, but Spain are far more comfortable using the ball as a defensive instrument. A press that arrives in separate waves lets Spain pass around the first challenge and forces the defending midfield to cover too much ground. The champions need a clear trigger — an awkward touch, a backwards pass, a player facing his own goal — rather than energy spent on pressure Spain can see coming.

The midfield contest will therefore turn less on raw possession than on the quality of each side's next action. Spain can dominate the ball and still be exposed if their circulation leaves no cover for the loss. Argentina can accept less of it and still control the important moments if their first recovery pass escapes pressure. Neither patience nor disruption belongs to one side alone; both will need each, often within the same sequence.

Spain's first New Jersey session added a small but relevant availability question. Yamal and Pedro Porro worked separately from the main group, which the Spanish federation described as precautionary workload management. Porro has been managing a minor hamstring problem, while Yamal carries aches and bruising from the France semi-final; both are expected to be available on Sunday. Tactically it matters because Spain can protect Yamal's training load without redesigning the right side, while Porro's condition affects the depth available behind it.

The venue adds its own load. Kick-off is set for 15:00 local time in an outdoor stadium, and Spain have three days to adjust to New Jersey's heat and humidity. FIFA says the final pitch was installed in May after years of research and hybrid-stitched for consistency across the tournament, though players and teams have still criticised how the surface has played. A physically draining afternoon, or a ball that does not move as cleanly as either side expects, would favour compact distances and controlled accelerations over continuous pressure.

The bench may prove decisive given how differently the match could unfold. Argentina's late semi-final winner came from substitute Lautaro Martínez, a reminder of how a fresh reference point in the penalty area can change the value of territory already won. Spain's task is different: their replacements must preserve the spacing and counter-pressing that make their possession coherent, not simply add fresh dribbling. A final that stays level will reward control of fatigue; an early goal will test whether the leading side can keep making its opponent defend.

Messi and Yamal deserve the billing because they can do things almost no one else on the pitch can. But the more revealing contest lies in the architecture built around that talent — how much structure Spain are willing to place ahead of the ball, how much territory Argentina can concede without losing access to the next attack. The iconic photograph will probably contain one of the two stars. The winning mechanism is more likely to be found a few metres away, in the player who recognised where the risk had moved before the rest of the stadium did.

body: A coroner has concluded that a brain condition caused by repeated heading contributed to the death of England World Cup winner Nobby Stiles. Senior coroner Alison Mutch reached the finding at an inquest in Stockport, almost six years after Stiles died in October 2020 at the age of 78. The ruling is deliberately more precise than a claim that football alone caused his death: it identifies a specific disease process, its cause in his case, and its contribution to the final medical picture.

Postmortem examination showed severe dementia associated with both Alzheimer's disease and chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. Neuropathologist Daniel Du Plessis attributed the CTE to Stiles's repeated heading during his playing career. The inquest heard an estimate of roughly 140,000 headers across his career, a figure that describes the scale of exposure presented to the court. It does not mean medicine can assign equal damage to every header, or calculate an individual player's future risk from a simple total.

The distinction between Alzheimer's disease and CTE matters. They are different neurodegenerative conditions, though both can contribute to cognitive decline, and CTE is established through characteristic changes found in brain tissue after death. The inquest's conclusion concerns Stiles as an individual, based on his medical evidence and exposure history. It adds a powerful legal finding to football's brain-health debate without turning one case into a universal diagnosis for former players.

Stiles's stature gives the ruling unusual resonance. The Football Association's official record shows that he played every minute of England's victorious 1966 World Cup campaign, won 28 international caps, and spent 11 years in Manchester United's first team, helping the club win two league titles and the 1968 European Cup. The image of his Wembley victory dance, the Jules Rimet Trophy in one hand and his false teeth in the other, became part of English football's visual memory.

The wider evidence already points to an elevated burden of neurodegenerative disease among former professionals, even as the exact mechanism remains under investigation. The 2019 FIELD study compared 7,676 former Scottish professional players with 23,028 matched controls. Neurodegenerative disease was recorded as the primary cause of death in 1.7% of former players against 0.5% of controls, an adjusted rate about three and a half times higher. Crucially, that study did not establish whether heading, concussion, another feature of the sport, or a combination of factors explained the difference.

Football has nevertheless changed its practice on a precautionary basis. Professional guidance in England recommends no more than ten higher-force headers in a training week, focusing on actions such as meeting long passes, crosses and set pieces. At grassroots level, the phased removal of deliberate heading from younger age groups has expanded over successive seasons. Those policies acknowledge a potential cumulative risk while research continues; they should not be misread as proof that every form of heading carries the same danger.

The Stiles finding will intensify scrutiny of the game's historic duty of care and its support for former players living with dementia. His family is among those pursuing separate civil claims against football authorities. An inquest determines the medical cause and circumstances of a death; it does not decide negligence or damages. The coroner's conclusion is therefore highly significant evidence, but the broader questions of legal responsibility remain for a different process.

For the sport, the responsible response is neither denial nor an exaggerated promise that the science is complete. Stiles's case establishes that repeated heading caused his CTE and that the resulting brain condition contributed to his death. The population research shows a wider association between professional football and neurodegenerative mortality but cannot yet apportion the cause. Holding both truths at once is the basis for better rules, better long-term care, and a more honest account of the physical cost carried by an earlier generation.

title: Israeli football records fewer racism convictions and pitch pyrotechnics
dek: New figures point to a meaningful improvement after tougher anti-racism rules, although unequal reporting periods and missing match-level denominators limit the headline percentages.

body: Israeli football has reported substantial reductions in two of its most persistent stadium problems: racist chanting and pyrotechnic devices thrown onto the pitch. The new totals are encouraging, particularly because they follow a deliberate change in disciplinary policy. But they are not yet a complete measure of supporter behaviour. The available figures count convictions or identified incidents, not every occurrence, and they offer no per-match or per-attendance denominator.

The racism figures behind the headline decline: 19 club convictions in the first six months of the 2025/26 season, before the amended rules took effect, against five in the following four months. As a raw count, five is 74% lower than 19. But because the periods are unequal in length, that is not the same as a 74% fall in the monthly rate — the average moves from about 3.2 convictions a month to 1.25, a reduction of roughly 61%. Both calculations point the same way; only one adjusts for time.

The rule change was approved by the Israel Football Association in December and took effect on 1 February 2026. Its official notice expanded the disciplinary response to racism and discrimination: higher, escalating fines, restrictions on away-ticket sales, and the option for clubs to submit structured prevention programmes. The design tries to shift incentives before an offence occurs, rather than leaving post-match punishment as the entire policy.

That domestic trend has to be read alongside a separate FIFA decision. In March, world football's governing body found multiple breaches of the disciplinary provisions covering offensive behaviour and discrimination, fined the IFA CHF150,000, issued a warning and ordered a prevention plan. The new conviction totals do not cancel that ruling, and the ruling does not prove the later measures failed — the two address different periods and different institutional questions.

The pyrotechnics comparison spans a longer stretch of time. Fifteen cases of devices being thrown onto the playing surface were recorded in 2022/23, against eight in 2025/26 — close to a 50% reduction. That distinction matters for safety: a flare in a stand and an object landing on the pitch are not the same risk.

Yet the published totals again lack the number of fixtures monitored, the competitions included, and a consistent account of detection methods, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a final incidence rate.

Policy can move those numbers through more than severity alone. A sanction that targets away access or competitive consequences gives organised supporter groups a direct incentive to police their own section, while club prevention plans can address education, reporting and stewarding. The risk is that a lower disciplinary total may also reflect under-reporting or shifting enforcement rather than genuinely better behaviour. Public confidence will depend on transparent definitions and season-by-season data, not isolated percentages.

The most responsible conclusion is positive but provisional. Racism convictions fell sharply after the February amendment, even once the unequal time periods are corrected, and pitch-thrown pyrotechnic incidents are well below the 2022/23 total. The next step is to publish match-normalised figures, distinguish allegations from convictions, and show whether the improvement survives a full season under the new rules. If it does, Israeli football will have evidence of behavioural change rather than only a favourable snapshot.

title: Kunin doubles up as Mazkeret Batya retain national artistic-swimming cup
dek: A two-point club contest and Katy Kunin’s solo-duet double gave Israel’s summer championships a finish defined by both collective depth and senior quality.

source.name: Sport5

body: A.L.E. Mazkeret Batya have retained Israel's senior artistic-swimming cup, but only just. The club closed out the combined winter-and-summer standings on 103 points, with Maccabi Tel Aviv breathing down their neck on 101 and Hapoel Jerusalem a more distant third on 88. The national federation lists the summer meet as having run from 12 to 14 July at the Wingate Institute, the country's principal aquatic venue, bringing the domestic senior season to a close.

A two-point margin tells its own story. Mazkeret Batya won the previous edition by 31 points, so watching Maccabi Tel Aviv close that gap to within a single routine's reach changes the picture entirely: retaining the cup this time took depth across the whole programme rather than one dominant performance. Jerusalem's 88 points, meanwhile, kept three clubs meaningfully in contention — a healthier competitive shape than a runaway table would have produced.

Individually, nobody swam better than Katy Kunin. The Hapoel Jerusalem athlete won the senior solo with 231.2763 points, more than 36 clear of Yogev Dagan of Mazkeret Batya on 195.0625 and Maccabi Tel Aviv's Noya Tzarfati on 190.2950. It was a margin that separated the event's established international-level performer from a podium that otherwise reflected the discipline's widening domestic base.

Kunin then completed the double in the duet, teaming up with Noga Levi for a winning score of 240.4263. Aya Mazor and Shia Shar Shalom Nechmad took second on 207.3038, with Noa Kagan and Tzarfati third on 190.7254. The result carries an extra wrinkle: Kunin and Mazor currently form Israel's senior duet on the international stage, so the domestic event put regular national-team partners on opposite sides of a title race before they return to shared international work.

Mazkeret Batya's most emphatic event win came in the acrobatic team routine, where their total of 164.9625 opened a wide gap over Maccabi Tel Aviv's 110.1466 and Artswim's 104.8472. Maccabi Tel Aviv had their answer elsewhere, winning the separate team event with 146.0160 — a result that fed directly into the club's late push up the overall cup table.

There is a broader point behind the medals. Artistic swimming is built from several competitive units — solo, duet, mixed work, team routines and acrobatics — and national-team depth depends on athletes being tested across all of them. A tight club table offers more useful selection evidence than isolated training scores ever could, and Dagan's senior podium finish adds visibility for men in a discipline whose international programme has been expanding mixed opportunities.

Mazkeret Batya leave Wingate with the cup, but not with uncontested control of the field. Maccabi Tel Aviv cut a 31-point deficit from the previous edition down to two, Jerusalem produced the outstanding individual champion of the meet, and several national-team combinations found themselves separated rather than grouped together. The trophy stayed in the same hands; the balance of power around it did not.

dek: The 23-year-old guard arrives after one professional season with Promitheas, bringing shot creation and positional flexibility to Holon’s backcourt rebuild.

body: Hapoel Holon have signed guard Claudell Harris Jr for the 2026/27 season, converting an agreement reached earlier in the week into a formal deal. Harris, 23, joins after his first professional season in Europe with Promitheas Patras. The move reads less as a purchase of finished production and more as a bet that a young scorer can turn scattered highlights from Greece into a consistent role in Israel.

The numbers frame him as a work in progress. FIBA lists Harris at 190 centimetres, and across five Basketball Champions League appearances for Promitheas he averaged 9.2 points, 1.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists. In the Greek league he posted 10.1 points and 2.6 rebounds per game on 36% shooting from the field — the profile of an adaptable rotation guard rather than a primary offensive weapon.

His ceiling flashed on occasion. Harris scored 21 points away to Heidelberg and later added 17 points with seven assists in Promitheas's double-overtime victory over Rytas Vilnius. The gap between those nights and his season-long averages sits at the heart of Holon's evaluation: he has already created and scored at continental level, just not yet over a sustained stretch.

Head coach Predrag Krunić has pointed to Harris's ability to cover multiple perimeter roles, create his own shot and function within the team's offence. New sporting director Daniel Ravitz described the signing in similar terms, citing youth, athleticism and versatility. The overlapping language suggests Holon are building for pace and interchangeable backcourt assignments rather than filling one narrow need.

The developmental risk is real. A 36% overall field-goal rate in Greece leaves room to sharpen shot selection and finishing, and the Champions League sample is only five games. Holon will need to separate productive aggression from difficult volume, particularly once Harris is asked to initiate possessions rather than attack defences already bent out of shape by a teammate.

The fit still looks promising for the Israeli league. A bigger guard capable of shifting between on-ball creation and secondary scoring gives a coach more answers against switches and ball pressure. If Harris can also guard both backcourt positions, that versatility would extend beyond a lineup card and let Holon keep pace without giving up size — though that defensive side of his game has yet to be tested in the new environment.

Holon's expectation is a substantial step forward in year two. The evidence supports that possibility without guaranteeing it: Harris has age, length for the position and two high-level scoring performances behind him, but also modest efficiency numbers and a thin European résumé. The signing will be judged a success if Holon can turn isolated peaks into dependable possessions, rather than asking a still-developing guard to carry the offence alone.

title: Fenerbahçe turn Marcus Bingham’s breakout year into a two-season bet

body: Fenerbahçe have signed Marcus Bingham Jr on a two-season contract, handing the 26-year-old centre his first EuroLeague assignment after the most productive year of his professional career. The move caps a steep climb through three Israeli clubs — Hapoel Haifa, Hapoel Holon and Hapoel Tel Aviv — before a move to UNICS Kazan turned him into far more than a situational rim protector.

The official VTB United League record explains why a reigning European champion would commit two years to him. Bingham appeared in 54 games for UNICS in 2025/26, averaging 15.6 points, 7.1 rebounds, 1.4 steals and 1.8 blocks. At 2.13 metres, he combined conventional size around the rim with unusual activity away from the basket.
Those steals and blocks matter together. They describe a defender capable of affecting possessions at different heights and in different spaces, not merely a shot-blocker waiting near the paint.

His offensive development was just as important. Bingham left Israel with a reputation built mainly on reach, vertical finishing and shot deterrence, but in Kazan he carried a much heavier scoring load across a full domestic and playoff programme. Fenerbahçe are not recruiting him off one tournament burst or a short run of favourable match-ups — 54 appearances is a substantial sample, and the VTB League named him to its team of the semi-finals.

The next level will ask different questions of him. EuroLeague offences repeatedly pull centres into screening actions, force them to defend a second and third decision, and punish a late rotation with an open corner three. Fenerbahçe can use Bingham's mobility to play more aggressively at the point of the screen, but that value depends on the back line rotating with him — length alone does not solve the spacing and speed of an elite possession.

There is also a clear role question at the offensive end. Kazan production does not guarantee the same number of touches in Istanbul. His most transferable work will be running hard after defensive rebounds, creating pressure as a lob target, screening with precision and turning offensive boards into efficient second possessions.

A lower scoring average could still coexist with a more demanding and more valuable role, provided those actions hold up against EuroLeague frontcourts. His years in Israel now read as part of a development route rather than a finished evaluation. Exposure to several tactical environments gave him repeated work in switch-heavy line-ups and in systems that asked the centre to cover ground behind the ball, while UNICS supplied the volume to prove the athletic profile could sustain real production.

Fenerbahçe are paying for that combination — Israeli experience, a breakout season and physical tools that remain scarce even at EuroLeague level. The contract rewards what Bingham has already become while leaving room for another jump: he is no longer an intriguing project, yet he has never played a EuroLeague minute, and the two-year deal gives both sides time to absorb that transition.

The first measure of the signing will not be whether he reproduces 15.6 points immediately. It will be whether his defence, screening and rim pressure survive the competition's tighter margins often enough to earn a place in Fenerbahçe's closing lineups.

body: Hapoel Eilat have added American forward Aaron Wheeler as they rebuild for a return to the Israeli Basketball Premier League. He stays in the competition after spending 2025/26 with Hapoel HaEmek, which means the promoted club gets a player already used to the league's pace, travel and foreign-player match-ups rather than another newcomer facing a full period of adjustment.

The league's official record lists Wheeler at 2.05 metres, with 14 appearances last season. He averaged 7.9 points and 5.0 rebounds in 19.6 minutes, shooting 52.4% on twos and 38.6% on threes. His 1.3 steals and 1.4 blocks per game are unusually active defensive numbers for a forward working fewer than 20 minutes a night.

Those figures point to a complementary role rather than a high-volume creator around whom an offence must be reorganised. Wheeler's value lies in possessions that connect a lineup: running the floor, finishing after the defence has shifted, contesting from the weak side and keeping the paint open by making enough of his threes. His 17 made three-pointers came from 44 attempts — a useful rate, though still a modest sample.

Eilat sealed promotion in April with an 84–70 win over Elitzur Ashkelon, a result that secured top position after 26 wins in 27 games and returned the southern club to the first division following a two-season absence. It was an emphatic campaign built on week-to-week superiority rather than one successful playoff run.

That promotion record is a foundation, not a forecast. Dominating the National League and surviving in the Premier League are different assignments, since the size and speed of opposing rotations change immediately. Eilat must add top-flight athleticism without losing the ball movement, defensive discipline and competitive stability that made last season so consistent.

Wheeler addresses several of those needs at once. His rebounding can help finish defensive possessions, while his steals-and-blocks combination suggests he can disrupt passing lanes and protect the rim behind an initial rotation. Eilat will still have to decide whether he is best used as a mobile power forward or in smaller lineups at centre, a call that will depend on the size and shooting deployed around him.

The signing also comes with a sensible limit. Fourteen games are enough to show Wheeler can contribute in Israel, but not enough to establish him as a guaranteed anchor across a full season. It falls to Eilat's coaching staff to turn efficiency in a restricted role into dependable availability and production over a longer schedule.
If that transition holds, the club will have found a two-way piece who can make the promoted roster more adaptable without demanding control of the ball.

title: Four appointments complete a generational change in Israeli basketball’s disciplinary court
dek: A year-long handover has replaced four long-serving judges with a salaried panel, while the association’s rules preserve the court’s formal independence and route of appeal.

source.name: ONE

source.author: ONE Sports Desk

verificationSources.label: Israel Basketball Association current disciplinary regulations

body: The Israel Basketball Association has completed a major overhaul of its disciplinary court, appointing attorneys Gadi Zilberberg, Lior Boner, Amir Pavve and Yishai Zilberberg to replace four judges whose terms have ended. The incoming panel will serve on a salaried basis, following a handover the association says was a year in the making.

The outgoing judges — Tagar Amiel, Tzvika Roizen, Eli Levin and Ezra Hausner — leave a body whose work sits at the boundary between competition administration and legal process. The disciplinary court rules on player and coach conduct, club responsibility, crowd offences and alleged breaches of the association's own rules, and its decisions can alter fines, suspensions and even the conditions under which games are staged.

Under the association's current disciplinary regulations, the court is described as independent and sovereign in its decision-making. Judges are instructed to rule according to the association's statutes and regulations as well as their own conscience, with appeals proceeding to a separate supreme court. The constitution requires a panel of three to five legally qualified judges, appointed personally by the general assembly.

That framework makes the method of renewal almost as significant as the names involved. A salaried panel may give the association more predictable availability and faster case management, but payment cannot be allowed to blur the institutional distance between the court and the body whose rules it interprets. The formal safeguards already exist in the regulations — credibility from here will be built through consistent reasoning and the publication of decisions.

The transition has not begun from a standing start. Gadi Zilberberg already appears in the association's published decisions from the 2025/26 season, evidence that part of the handover was under way before the completed panel was announced. The association has also moved some hearings online and revised regulations as part of a wider reform process.

Remote hearings can ease travel and scheduling pressure in a national competition system, particularly for clubs based outside the centre of the country. But they demand careful procedure: participants must be able to hear the case against them, present their response and know which materials the judge considered. Convenience only holds value if the record stays complete and the process remains intelligible.

Association chairman Amos Frishman presented the appointments as a continuation of institutional reform and thanked the outgoing judges for their service. The more meaningful test, though, will come in the ordinary cases that follow rather than in the announcement itself — comparable offences should draw comparable treatment, written reasoning should make distinctions clear, and appeal outcomes should feed back into future rulings.

Israeli basketball's disciplinary court rarely draws attention when it functions well, yet its rulings shape competitive fairness, supporter sanctions and the relationship between clubs and the governing body. Replacing four judges at once marks a genuine break with the previous era. The new panel now inherits both that authority and a public record against which its independence, speed and consistency will be measured.

Be'er Sheva's official squad page still lists the 30-year-old attacking midfielder, and the Israel Football Association continues to maintain his current playing record. His importance to the team is not in question — he supplies set-piece quality, shooting and passes between the lines — but that footballing value does not justify turning a deliberately limited health update into a speculative injury report.

For now, the club is approaching its immediate fixtures with no public return date attached to Biton's name. Any tactical adjustment is a matter for the available squad; any medical conclusion belongs to the player and his clinicians. Until one of them says more, the accurate account remains narrow but meaningful — Biton is in a medical process, working towards a return, and has asked for space while that work continues.

body: Beitar Jerusalem have been ordered to pay M.S. Ashdod ₪450,000 in training and development compensation for Noam Mocha. The player-status ruling supplies the figure that had remained unresolved since the midfielder committed his future to Beitar, turning an open acquisition cost into a defined obligation between the two clubs.

The distinction inside the decision matters. This is compensation for Ashdod’s role in training and developing the player, not a conventional transfer fee negotiated as part of a sale — the award recognises work performed before the move, rather than putting a price on an active contract.

Mocha had reached the end of his contractual route with Ashdod and was free to agree his next employment, but that did not automatically erase the originating club’s claim under the player-development system. Freedom to choose the next club and an obligation to compensate the developing club can exist side by side.

Beitar formally announced Mocha on a three-year contract in March, describing him then as a young midfielder arriving from Ashdod and the youth national-team environment. A later pre-season update placed him among the new arrivals beginning work for 2026/27, so the sporting move was already in motion while the clubs awaited a financial determination.

That sequence separates two processes often compressed into the single word “signing.” Beitar and Mocha settled the employment relationship first — length, start date, his place in the new squad. The compensation question sat between Beitar and Ashdod, and Thursday’s ruling closes that inter-club valuation without touching the three-season term already attached to the player.

For squad planning, certainty is more useful than a headline argument about who won the case. Beitar can now set ₪450,000 against the cost of completing Mocha’s move rather than carrying an unpriced liability into the season — the ruling converts uncertainty into a known acquisition expense.

That figure should not be confused with Mocha’s salary, his bonuses or the annual first-team budget; none of those numbers are established by the decision. Nor does the award amount to extra sporting revenue earmarked for Ashdod’s next signing. It is one specific payment between two clubs, with employment costs and operating budgets sitting entirely outside it.

Ashdod, for their part, receive a concrete return for development work the committee has now formally recognised. The ruling does not put a market value on the rest of Mocha’s career, nor does it forecast what he may eventually contribute in Jerusalem. Its function is narrower and more institutional: deciding what one club owes another when a developed player moves on after the relevant contract period.

The football question now belongs entirely to Mocha and Beitar’s coaching staff. A three-year contract gives the club time to develop him, but the compensation payment guarantees nothing in terms of minutes or status — it simply clears the last documented financial uncertainty around the move. Beitar know the cost, Ashdod know the award, and Mocha can begin the season with the dispute no longer attached to his place in the squad.

dek: Huddersfield have tied the Suriname centre-back to a contract through 2028, forcing Haifa to redirect a defensive search that had reached an advanced stage.

body: Radinio Balker has extended his Huddersfield Town contract through 2028, closing the immediate route that could have taken the centre-back to Maccabi Haifa. Huddersfield published the extension on Thursday. What had been an advanced Israeli recruitment possibility is now a firm two-season commitment to the English club.

The distinction between interest and a completed move matters here. Haifa had explored Balker as part of their search for a foreign central defender, but neither club had announced a transfer agreement. The authoritative event is the new Huddersfield contract, and it means Haifa cannot treat the player as available without a fresh negotiation with a club that has just extended its hold on him.

Balker is not an unknown development player being retained for depth. Huddersfield's first-team records list him as squad number 12 and show him starting in central defence throughout the 2025/26 League One season. The club also identifies him as a Suriname international, a status he earned with a senior debut in September 2025 before scoring his first goal for the national team the following month, in a World Cup qualifier away to El Salvador.

Those details explain the appeal for Haifa: senior European league experience, current international football and a profile built around central defending rather than a positional conversion. They also explain Huddersfield's decision to secure him now. A defender already integrated into the starting XI is worth more under a longer contract than as a player approaching the point where his negotiating leverage might shift.

For Haifa, this should be read as a recruitment reset rather than a failed signing. No completed transfer has been reversed, because none was ever made public. The practical consequence is still significant, though: one of the clearest centre-back options is no longer available on the terms that made an Israeli move plausible, and the club must now decide whether to redirect its search or test Huddersfield's resolve with a different proposal.

That decision cannot be separated from squad construction. Haifa need enough reliability at centre-back to support an aggressive defensive line through a season in which availability rarely stays constant. Chasing a player who has just renewed can burn time and budget without improving the squad, and moving quickly to the next verified option may now be more valuable than clinging to a negotiation whose economics have changed.

Huddersfield, meanwhile, gain clarity before the English season starts. Balker can prepare as a retained first-team defender rather than a player weighing two possible destinations, and the club now holds a stronger contractual position should interest resurface later. Haifa's task is equally clear: the defensive need has not disappeared simply because this route has, and the next move must solve that requirement rather than merely swap another name onto the shortlist.

body: US President Donald Trump will attend Sunday's World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at New York New Jersey Stadium, placing the head of state of the tournament's largest host nation inside the venue for the concluding match. The White House announced the visit on Thursday, three days before the 15:00 local kick-off in East Rutherford.

The trip begins before matchday. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump will travel to New York City on Friday for a FIFA reception at Trump Tower before appearing at the final on Sunday. That sequence links the political hosting operation to FIFA's own closing programme without changing the competitive terms of the match itself.

Argentina and Spain arrive with sharply different historical targets. Argentina are the defending champions and are seeking a fourth title, which would also make them the first country since Brazil in 1962 to retain the World Cup. Spain, meanwhile, are chasing a second championship to add to the one they won in 2010.

The fixture is match 104 of the first 48-team men's World Cup, and FIFA's event plan turns Sunday into a long stadium operation. Gates are scheduled to open at 11:00, the closing ceremony begins at 13:30, and kick-off follows 90 minutes later. Jennifer Hudson is due to perform the United States national anthem as part of a ceremony designed to close a tournament staged across the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Presidential attendance adds another layer to an operation already built around federal, state and tournament coordination. The White House's World Cup task force says its interagency framework covers transportation, tourism, safety and security across the 11 US host cities. New York New Jersey is the final stop for that system as well as the site of the trophy match.

There is also a direct stadium precedent. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump attended the 2025 Club World Cup final at the same East Rutherford venue, and official White House records show the president participating in the post-match ceremony alongside FIFA president Gianni Infantino. That history makes Sunday's visit part of an established relationship between the administration and FIFA rather than an isolated late addition.

Any role beyond attendance should still be treated separately until the final ceremony plan is fixed. The durable facts for now are the White House confirmation, the Friday reception itinerary and the president's planned presence on Sunday.

On the field, the final remains the collision the tournament produced: Argentina's 19-goal attack against a Spain side that have conceded only once. The head of state will be in the building, but the title will still be decided by the teams.

title: Yehezkel made Maccabi’s width a Super Cup weapon
dek: Three assists told the story, but the more important lesson was how one wide outlet kept changing the point of attack—even after Maccabi Tel Aviv went down to ten men.

source.name: Walla Sport
source.originalTitle: וזוהי רק ההתחלה: מכבי תל אביב זכתה בתואר אלוף האלופים

body: Sagiv Yehezkel's three assists in Maccabi Tel Aviv's 3–1 Super Cup win are easy to treat as a spectacular individual line. The more useful conclusion is structural. Maccabi always had a route out of pressure because Yehezkel could receive wide, move the attack across the pitch and deliver before Hapoel Be'er Sheva's defensive line had reset. He was not simply the last passer three times; he was the mechanism that stopped possession becoming predictable.

The opening goal established the pattern. Itamar Noy's pass released Yehezkel into the right channel, and the ball across goal left Saied Abu Farchi with a simple finish in the 10th minute. Be'er Sheva had already failed to secure their defensive possession, but Maccabi still needed to turn that error into an uncontested shot. Width did the conversion: Yehezkel stretched the recovery run, Abu Farchi held the central lane, and the final pass arrived before the cover could close.

The second assist was different enough to matter. Yehezkel supplied Dor Peretz from the left side in the 58th minute, and the captain placed his finish rather than overpowering Ofir Marciano. He later created another headed chance for Peretz from the same kind of movement. Switching sides of the attack made him harder to contain than a winger fixed to one touchline — Be'er Sheva could identify the danger, but not a single zone in which to trap it.

Roy Revivo's dismissal in the 66th minute should have changed the match's geometry. Ten-man teams normally sacrifice their highest wide outlet, narrow the distances between defenders and accept longer spells without the ball. Maccabi did not abandon the threat. Six minutes after the red card, Yehezkel delivered the third assist and Abu Farchi completed his brace — tactical insurance, since Be'er Sheva could not commit everybody forward while the best supplier on the pitch still had space to attack.

That is the sharpest criticism of the champions' response. Kings Kangwa had already shown the value of varied movement, equalising with a backheel and helping Be'er Sheva take control before half-time. Once they gained the extra player, though, their possession did not consistently force Maccabi's reduced block to turn. Too many attacks met the defence in front of it, while the space left behind became more dangerous than the numerical advantage was productive.

Maccabi's own performance was not without risk. Their pressure produced early openings, but the match also contained enough loose transitions to warn against reading one July trophy as a finished model. Revivo's second yellow created an avoidable emergency, and Be'er Sheva struck the frame before the interval. A system that gives Yehezkel freedom must still protect the spaces he leaves when an attack breaks down.

The encouraging part for Kenny Miller is that the width did not depend on sterile crossing volume. Yehezkel's first assist followed a timed release behind the line, the second came after he appeared on the opposite side, and the third punished a team chasing the game. Three different match states, solved by the same player without demanding the same move twice.

European qualifying will test whether that outlet survives against opponents who press the receiver earlier and recover with greater discipline. Maccabi will not always be able to create an empty goal or let Peretz arrive untracked. But the Super Cup offered a credible principle to carry forward: keep one wide player capable of receiving under pressure, crossing early and changing sides, and the whole attack has somewhere to breathe.

Abu Farchi's brace and Peretz's finish won the trophy; Yehezkel's choices connected them. That distinction is why the performance deserves more than a celebration of three assists. Maccabi's best attacking idea was portable across scorelines, sides of the pitch and even a red card — on the first competitive night of the season, the strongest evidence yet that the cup holders have more than a single result to build on.

body: Or Blorian completed 75 minutes on his Major League Soccer debut as Sporting Kansas City lost 3–2 to St. Louis CITY SC at Energizer Park. The Israel centre-back started on the left side of Sporting’s central defence and helped his new team recover from two goals down, but Eduard Löwen’s late penalty decided a five-goal return from the World Cup break.

St. Louis built their advantage in eight first-half minutes. Jeong Sang-Bin converted from close range in the 28th minute before Marcel Hartel finished Simon Becher’s transition pass in the 36th. Sporting answered before the interval when Capita struck from outside the area in the 42nd minute, cutting the deficit to 2–1 and changing the second half from damage limitation into a genuine chase.

Blorian’s first assignment was demanding because St. Louis played with two forwards close enough to occupy both centre-backs while Hartel attacked the space behind them. The 26-year-old remained in the starting back line alongside Jansen Miller, with Jayden Reid and Ian James completing the defence in front of goalkeeper Stefan Cleveland. It was his first senior appearance for Sporting after joining from Hapoel Be’er Sheva this summer.

The debut ended after an injury delay in the 74th minute. Blorian received treatment on the pitch and Ethan Bartlow replaced him in the 75th, with no diagnosis or recovery timetable announced. Sporting equalised almost immediately: Dejan Joveljić met Manu García’s pass in the 76th minute and finished left-footed to make it 2–2.

The comeback did not survive the final phase. Löwen converted a penalty in the 85th minute to restore St. Louis’s lead, placing the kick beyond Cleveland for the winning goal. Sporting pushed through nine minutes of stoppage time but could not find a third response. St. Louis goalkeeper Benjamin Lundt and midfielder Daniel Edelman were booked late; Capita received Sporting’s only yellow card in the 78th minute. No player was sent off.

For Blorian, the most significant fact is that his first MLS appearance began as a start rather than a late introduction. Sporting trusted him in an away rivalry fixture immediately after the long league pause. His 75 minutes supplied a first measure of the speed, spacing and transition volume he will face in the competition, even if the treatment that preceded his substitution leaves his short-term availability to be clarified.

Sporting had signed the Israeli international to a contract running through the 2028/29 season, with club options beyond it. He arrived after winning the Israeli Premier League and Super Cup with Be’er Sheva and after breaking into the senior Israel squad. The move therefore carries an expectation that he can compete for a regular place rather than serve only as defensive depth.

The result belongs to St. Louis, whose two-goal opening and late penalty survived Sporting’s response. Blorian’s debut belongs in a different category: an incomplete individual night within a complete team defeat. He started, played 75 minutes and left with the score still 2–1; Sporting levelled after his departure and then conceded the winner. The next useful evidence will be whether he is available to continue building minutes in the following round.

title: Maccabi Haifa tie teenage striker Adrian Ballout to a new three-year deal
dek: The 2010-born forward from the Galilee village of Mi'ilya — credited with 103 goals in three junior seasons — has signed until 2029 after one championship-winning year in the academy.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: אדריאן בלוט חתם על חוזה ל-3 שנים במכבי חיפה

body: Maccabi Haifa have moved to keep one of the most prolific junior goalscorers in northern Israel, announcing on Friday that Adrian Ballout, a striker born in 2010, has signed a three-year contract with the club's youth department. The deal, reported to run until 2029, arrives only one season after the teenager left M.K. Mi'ilya, the tiny Galilee village club where his scoring record first brought Haifa's scouts north.

"Ballout continues in green," the youth department wrote in its announcement, confirming that the forward will begin his second season in the academy after winning the league championship with the club's under-16 side last term.

Ballout was on the fringes of the squad that coach Eliezer Ben Aharon guided to the under-16 title — the top national division for his age group — and contributed five goals across all competitions, according to Israeli reporting on the deal. Those are modest numbers for a player signed as a pure finisher, which makes the length of the new commitment the real story: Haifa are paying for a trajectory, not for last season's output, and have chosen to secure the years in which that trajectory will be decided.

His background is unusual even by the standards of Israeli academy recruitment. Mi'ilya, perched in the hills of the western Galilee, has around 3,300 residents, almost all of them Melkite Greek Catholic Christians, and its youth club was founded barely a decade ago. Ballout only began organised football in the 2022-23 season, starting out at a football school in the neighbouring village of Fassuta before joining Mi'ilya's youth section at 13.

What happened next is why Haifa acted. Across three seasons at Mi'ilya he scored 103 goals in 69 appearances, according to ONE, which profiled him when he made the move last summer. In his final year he finished as the northern district's leading scorer in the under-16 league despite playing a year above his age group — 48 league goals for a side that placed fourth while fielding mostly 2010-born boys against older opposition. Andrei Fran, who founded Mi'ilya's youth department and coached him there, said at the time that Haifa had needed only two training sessions before deciding to sign him.

The new contract also has a defensive logic. The Galilee's Arab and Christian villages have long supplied talent to rival academies — earlier Mi'ilya products reached senior top-flight football after moving through Bnei Sakhnin's youth system — and a productive village striker who has already banked a championship season with Haifa would not have lacked suitors. Tying Ballout down until 2029 keeps every forthcoming pathway decision inside the club.

Those decisions come quickly now. The deal covers the under-17 and under-19 years, the stage at which Israeli academies separate genuine professional prospects from strong junior scorers, and the first call is whether Ballout continues with his own 2010 cohort or is pushed up an age group again, as Mi'ilya did with him. His first Haifa season suggested the step up in defensive quality is a real adjustment; the contract says the club believes the goals will follow.

For Mi'ilya, a village that had no youth club at all until the middle of the last decade, a second contract at the academy of one of the country's biggest clubs is a measurable return on a very small footballing economy — and a reason for Haifa's scouts to keep driving north.

body: Israel Police say preparations are complete for Saturday evening's meeting between Beitar Jerusalem and Hapoel Tel Aviv at the Miriam Stadium in Netanya, and have published a detailed set of instructions for supporters ahead of the 20:30 kick-off. According to the announcement, reported by ONE, hundreds of officers, stewards and security guards will be deployed around the ground and in the surrounding streets from early afternoon.

Entry will be tightly controlled. Gates open at 18:30, and everyone arriving will pass through what the force describes as rigorous screening, with supporters urged to come early and follow instructions. Access to the stadium area is restricted to ticket holders, and no tickets will be sold on the day.

Weapons are barred outright, with no facility to deposit them at the gates. Alcohol may not be brought in, anyone judged to be under its influence will be refused entry, and flying drones during the match is prohibited.

The sharpest warnings concern pyrotechnics. Supporter displays require prior approval from the police and fire service, while flares and similar devices are banned altogether — the police statement calls them a danger to life, warning that setting them off can bring a 3,000-shekel fine and criminal proceedings. Throwing or igniting anything towards the pitch, it adds, is an offence that could halt the game.
A separate instruction bars balaclavas, neck gaiters or any garment that obscures identification, on pain of a 500-shekel fine and refusal at the turnstiles.

Traffic around the stadium will be reorganised from the afternoon. The eastern and southern car parks close entirely and the western car park is reserved for invited guests, with supporters directed instead to parking at Cinema City, Gan Tzipor, the HaTzoran car parks and the Naimi Mall. HaYahalomim Boulevard will be shut in both directions from Rami Levy Square to the corner of HaEtztadion Street and Lantos Boulevard, and drivers coming from HaTzoran Street will not be able to turn left towards the ground.

The security posture reflects both the pairing and the moment. Meetings between Beitar and Hapoel Tel Aviv are among the most heavily policed in Israeli football, with the two support bases occupying opposite poles of the domestic game's culture. This one, staged at a neutral venue and listed by fixture services under the Toto Cup programme — the source itself does not name the competition — doubles as a final competitive outing before both clubs open their UEFA Conference League second-round qualifiers on 23 July, Beitar against AEK Larnaca of Cyprus.

The clubs will not be strangers for long either way: the fixture list published in June sends them straight back into each other's company on the opening day of the Ligat ha'Al season on 22 August. For now, the police message is plainer. The force closed its announcement by urging supporters to obey officers and stewards, avoid physical or verbal violence, and preserve, in its words, "a sporting atmosphere and an enjoyable experience for everyone".

Hours before kick-off, the operation produced its first arrests. Five suspects — one minor and four adults, residents of the centre of the country and Jerusalem — were detained by officers of the Netanya station during preparations around the ground, according to the police account as reported. Two were found carrying a substance suspected to be a dangerous drug, while the other three were held over suspected involvement in a violent incident. All five were taken for questioning at the Netanya station; neither weapons nor pyrotechnics featured in the account of the arrests.

body: A 12-year-old from Herzliya stood on the top step of an international dance podium in Thessaloniki this week, an Israeli flag around her shoulders. Emily Elkobi, a pupil of the Dance Factory studio, won her solo category with a routine titled 'Cat Women', according to the report of her result published on Friday afternoon.

The competition that brought her to Greece is run by All Dance International, whose own records show its Intercontinental & Europe 2026 championship taking place at the TIF Helexpo exhibition grounds in Thessaloniki from 12 to 19 July. The Hebrew-language report describes the gathering as one of the biggest occasions in competitive dance and says entrants travelled from ten countries.

A note of precision is owed on the title itself. The Israeli report crowns Elkobi a world champion; the organiser's published structure lists Thessaloniki as its combined Intercontinental and European championship, one rung of a pyramid whose world finals proper are scheduled for Orlando, Florida, from 19 to 23 November. Category winners at each tier carry official All Dance titles, but which precise wording appears on her trophy could not be independently confirmed by the time of writing.

What is not in doubt in the account of the week is the scale of the double. Beyond her solo gold, Elkobi competed with Outrage, a crew from the same studio, which also finished first in its category. The group's coach, named in the report as Eyal Levi, came away with a Golden Ticket — an invitation to compete in Orlando, which tallies with the organiser's November world finals at the city's Hilton resort.

The routine that won the solo prize was built with choreographer and coach Irina Freidin. Behind it sat a training load that would make older athletes wince: five sessions a week through the year, rising in the final months before the championship to daily work of three to five hours, seven days a week.

Dance Factory Herzliya, directed by Tal Malka, is an established name on this circuit. Israeli coverage of the studio's earlier trips to world-level events records podium finishes for its crews, including category wins at a world dance championship in Portugal attended by delegations from dozens of countries.

The report does not state which age division Elkobi entered. Under All Dance's published rules, a 12-year-old falls within the Pre-Youth bracket for dancers aged 11 to 14, with solo, duo, trio and group subdivisions contested at each level.

The image the report dwells on is the flag. Receiving her trophy wrapped in it, the account notes, carried particular weight for an Israeli delegation competing abroad at present — a 12-year-old's small, deliberate gesture at the end of a very long season.

title: Israel's under-20s swept aside 35:23 by Iceland with a World Championship place still on the line
dek: Shorn of four squad members, Israel trailed 20:9 at half-time at the Turda Arena and must now beat the loser of Croatia's tie with Romania on Sunday to claim 15th place — and with it a World Championship berth.

body: The road to a World Championship place has narrowed to a single match. Israel's under-20 handball side were beaten 35:23 by Iceland at the M20 EHF EURO in Romania on Friday lunchtime, a placement-round defeat at the Turda Arena that leaves Sunday's fixture — against the loser of Croatia's meeting with hosts Romania — as the last remaining chance to secure 15th place, the finishing position that Israeli reports say carries qualification for the age group's World Championship.

Israel arrived severely under-strength. Hebrew-language coverage of the squad, known domestically as the reserve national team, put four players out of contention: the first-choice goalkeeper and a centre back through injury, a third player suspended for the rest of the tournament, and a fourth sidelined since the opening match. Against opponents of Iceland's pedigree, the gap in numbers told quickly.

It did not begin badly. Iceland squandered two penalties in the opening minutes and would finish the afternoon nought from three from the seven-metre line, according to the official match sheet, while Israel edged 2:0 in front.

The lead proved a mirage. Iceland moved 4:2 ahead and pulled steadily clear, through 16:6 to 20:9 at the interval, as Israel's attack broke down repeatedly against a well-drilled defence and a goalkeeper who ended the day with 20 saves from 43 Israeli attempts.

The second half was played out with the result beyond doubt. Israel's coaching staff used the closing period to give court time to players who had featured only sparingly across the tournament, while Iceland kept scoring through a strikingly even spread — ten different Icelandic players found the net. Just 78 spectators were recorded at the Turda Arena for the midday throw-off.

Ben Gross led Israel's scoring with five goals, Yonatan Pelach added four, and Liam Madar and Idan Mena contributed three apiece. In goal, Yehonatan Benshitrit was kept busy, credited with ten saves from 36 shots faced.

The defeat caps a bruising fortnight. Israel finished third in Group F, losing 42:33 to Sweden and 39:31 to Romania either side of a 43:33 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina, before a 30:35 defeat to Czechia in the rankings phase. Their best result of the trip followed, a 39:31 victory over Poland, but Thursday's 33:31 loss to the Faroe Islands routed them into Friday's meeting with Iceland.

Everything now rests on Sunday. Beat whichever of Croatia or Romania loses their placement tie, and this depleted group will have salvaged a World Championship ticket from a difficult campaign; lose, and the tournament ends in Turda with nothing to show for it but hard lessons.
facts: Iceland beat Israel 35:23 (half-time 20:9) on 17 July 2026 at the Turda Arena, Turda, Romania, in the placement round of the M20 EHF EURO (official EHF match 078; 12:00 local throw-off, 78 spectators).
The Israeli side is the men's under-20 national team, known in Israel as the reserve (atuda) national team.
Ben Gross top-scored for Israel with 5 goals; Yonatan Pelach scored 4, Liam Madar and Idan Mena 3 each; goalkeeper Yehonatan Benshitrit made 10 saves from 36 shots.
Iceland converted none of their three seven-metre throws yet had ten different scorers; their goalkeepers combined for 20 saves from 43 shots.
Israel play the loser of Croatia v Romania on Sunday 19 July for 15th place, which Israeli reports state secures qualification for the age group's World Championship.

Israel's tournament arc per official EHF records: lost 33:42 to Sweden, beat Bosnia and Herzegovina 43:33, lost 31:39 to Romania, lost 30:35 to Czechia, beat Poland 39:31, lost 31:33 to the Faroe Islands.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv's youth department has taken on two boys from the 2012 age group, with Liroy Oretzki and Marom Kadosh arriving from Nahalal Yizrael, the young Jezreel Valley club, ahead of the 2026/27 season. According to a report published on Friday by the Hebrew-language outlet ONE, the pair will be registered with the under-14 side — nearim gimel, in Israeli age-grade terms — based at the club's Kiryat Shalom training complex in south Tel Aviv. This is academy recruitment, not a senior transfer: both players are several years away from professional football.

Oretzki is described in the report as a centre-back who can also sit in front of the defence as a holding midfielder, while Kadosh is an out-and-out striker. The two spent last season together in Nahalal Yizrael's under-13 team, which competed in a regional Kids A division alongside the junior sides of Maccabi Tel Aviv North, Maccabi Petah Tikva North and Hapoel Tel Aviv North.

Kadosh's numbers stand out even at this level. The report credits him with 40 per cent of Nahalal Yizrael's goals last season — a striking share for any forward, whatever the age group. He began his football education in Hapoel Gilboa's youth setup, where he spent three consecutive seasons before making the short move across the valley.

Oretzki followed a similar path, joining Nahalal Yizrael after four straight seasons at Hapoel Gilboa. The report describes him as a fixture of the team's defensive spine and notes that he contributed six goals from the back — an unusual return for a player in his position.

Their team's collective record helps explain Maccabi's interest. Nahalal Yizrael finished third in the division with an 81 per cent success rate, conceding just 22 goals — the second-meanest defence in the league behind Maccabi Tel Aviv North, who topped the table at 95 per cent. Those figures come from the report itself; the Israel Football Association's registry could not be independently checked for this age group at the time of writing.

Nahalal Yizrael is a genuine grassroots success story. Relaunched under new ownership in the summer of 2023, on grounds where Maccabi Haifa previously ran youth activity, the club now works with more than 200 children from the Jezreel Valley and beyond, and fields league teams across most junior age groups at the top regional tier.

The move was brokered by Play It, the Israeli agency owned by Oren Sterling, a former Hapoel Haifa youth department director and chief executive, who attended the signing according to the report. Agency involvement in a deal for players this young reflects how early representation now begins in Israeli football's talent pipeline.

For Maccabi Tel Aviv, whose academy at Kiryat Shalom has supplied the first team for decades, the recruitment is routine business with a notable footprint: reaching into a two-year-old valley club for players who impressed against its own northern junior sides. For the two boys, it is the biggest step of their short careers — though at this age, nothing about the path ahead is guaranteed.

body: Hapoel Petah Tikva have turned to a familiar face ahead of the new Israeli Premier League season. The club announced on Friday that French forward Franck Rivollier is returning on a one-year contract with an option for two further seasons. The 25-year-old comes back barely a year after leaving, with the news arriving as the squad worked through its pre-season camp in Pravets, Bulgaria.

The signing carries an edge that goes beyond routine squad-building. Rivollier spent last season with Maccabi Petah Tikva, Hapoel's neighbours and rivals, and Hebrew-language coverage reached for the city's well-worn shorthand for such transfers: crossing the road. Having made that journey once already, from Hapoel to Maccabi last summer, the striker is now making it in reverse.

His first spell in blue was brief but well-timed. Rivollier arrived in January 2025 from Bulgarian side Spartak Varna and slotted into a team chasing promotion under head coach Omer Peretz, scoring four goals in 19 appearances as Hapoel sealed their return to the top flight at the end of that campaign. His contract then ran down and he moved across the city.

At Maccabi he managed six goals over the course of last season — steady rather than prolific. But the return will inevitably be read through the prism of local rivalry: direct switches between the two Petah Tikva clubs are uncommon enough to sting, and Rivollier has now made one in each direction inside twelve months.

The player, for his part, leaned into the reunion rather than the rivalry. "I am excited to pull on the Hapoel Petah Tikva shirt again," he said in remarks released through the club. "My connection with Omer and with the crowd was something exceptional in my previous spell, and I am thrilled to open my second chapter at the club, in the top flight. I will do my utmost to prove myself and help the team meet its goals."

Born in Saint-Étienne and standing 1.92 metres, Rivollier came through in France with Lyon's reserves and Stade Rennais' B side, taking in a loan at Stade Briochin before a spell with Olympic Charleroi in Belgium. He first arrived in Israel in 2023, and his 11 goals for Hapoel Afula in 2023-24 remain his most productive season. A half-year detour to Spartak Varna followed before Petah Tikva, in both of its footballing colours, became home.

One detail is worth flagging. While one of the two reports stated flatly that the striker has signed, the fuller account described an agreement with the formal signature still to come, after which Rivollier is expected to link up with the squad during the Bulgaria camp. Neither suggested any obstacle remains.

For Peretz, the logic is straightforward: Hapoel go into the 2026-27 top-flight campaign wanting more physical presence and depth up front, and Rivollier offers both, along with an existing relationship with the coach and a dressing room he already knows. For the player, returning to the club where his promotion cameo made his local name is a chance to establish himself in the Israeli Premier League properly — this time from the first day of pre-season rather than a January arrival.

body: One flight of barriers into her continental championships, Hila Varsano already owns a faster Israeli under-18 record. The 17-year-old from Maccabi Tel Aviv clocked 1:00.02 for the 400m hurdles in Friday's opening round of the European U18 Championships in Rieti, finishing third in her heat at the Stadio Raul Guidobaldi to move into Saturday's semi-finals.

The run trimmed 0.13 seconds from the national age-group best of 1:00.15 she had set in Tel Aviv on 4 July, a mark World Athletics already lists as the Israeli U18 record. The senior national record, Irina Lenskiy's 56.09 from June 2000, remains in another realm. But Varsano, born in April 2009, now has a sub-minute clocking squarely in view.
It was not her first record of the summer. In May she ran a leg in the quartet that set an Israeli U18 4x100m relay best of 47.49, according to her World Athletics profile.

Rieti is staging the fifth edition of the biennial under-18 championships, running from 16 to 19 July, and Israel's day extended well beyond the hurdles. Ido Noam and Aviv Ochman both came through the 2,000m steeplechase heats to reach Sunday's final, clocking 5:53.23 and 5:53.63 respectively.

Neither had a clean race. Ochman, of Leader Jerusalem, stumbled at the final water jump but held on to qualify, while Noam, who trains with Hapoel Emek Hefer and the excellence academy at the Wingate Institute, clipped one of the standard barriers in the second heat and likewise recovered.

Itay Magidi, the Israel Athletics Association's professional director and still the national record holder over the distance, made clear he would be happy to see that mark go. Both runners, he said in comments carried by Israeli media, had come through their mishaps to qualify, and he believes each is capable of a top-eight finish on Sunday if they recover well in time.
Varsano's semi-final follows on Saturday. Her trajectory this month, from 1:00.15 down to 1:00.02 inside a fortnight, suggests the new Israeli record may not survive the weekend either.

She finished third in heat 1 and advanced to the semi-finals scheduled for Saturday 18 July.
Her previous best of 1:00.15, set on 4 July 2026, is listed by World Athletics as the Israeli national U18 record (NU18R).
The senior Israeli women's 400m hurdles record remains 56.09, set by Irina Lenskiy in June 2000.
The championships are being held at the Stadio Raul Guidobaldi in Rieti, Italy, from 16 to 19 July 2026.

Ido Noam (5:53.23) and Aviv Ochman (5:53.63) qualified for the men's 2,000m steeplechase final, set for Sunday 19 July; Israel Athletics Association professional director Itay Magidi, the Israeli record holder over the distance, said both could finish in the top eight.
